chapters.title: Chapter 2: and tether them
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon squeezes his eyes shut, trembling.

It’s okay.

He will go to the Nether Realm, and he will meet everyone from the village again. His parents will be proud of him for surviving so long, and he will introduce his new friend to Cyrene, and they will teach him to talk together, and they will have fun without worrying about anything. And no one else will die because of Phainon. Because down there, everyone is already dead.

So, it’s okay.

Chapter Notes

TW: disturbing themes, temporary character death

It’s a regular day, by what became the norm for 'regular' over however much time has passed.

They eat, they walk, Phainon talks, they come up with new gestures as they try to communicate. They also find some nests, which makes Phainon wish they had a pan of sorts, and they switch who holds the torch now and then.

They pick a spot where they can light a fire after hours of walking, spreading their things around as they always do. Then the boy skins one of their catches and digs the bones out before handing it to Phainon to cook, and they eat together. They try creating some structure from the small bones, Phainon giggling as his companion’s attempts end in miserable failures.

With the blankets wrapped around each of them—tightly around Phainon, very loosely around the boy—they finally quiet down in preparation for sleep.

Until a loud crack sounds to the right of Phainon, and everything appears to freeze.

“Aw, shit.” A strange voice rings quietly in the air, but it might be the loudest thing Phainon has ever heard.

His heart threatens to leap out of his ribcage as he scrambles out of the blanket, frantically throwing a look over his shoulder to find his friend already crouched low to the ground and staring with narrowed eyes at the trees. At least whatever it is, it’s closer to Phainon.

He swallows the lump in his throat. He can’t panic like this. Maybe it’s nothing, maybe it’s just an animal, and Phainon is hearing things—

A tall man steps out from the cover of the thick tree trunk, leaning his hand on it as he glances down at the two of them. He doesn’t seem very intimidating, mostly apologetic. It doesn’t calm Phainon down very much.

“Sorry, didn’t mean to startle ya,” he says with a thin smile. In the firelight, his eyes look like endless pools of black to Phainon, threatening to swallow him whole. “Was supposed to be quick and painless, but I fucked it.” He scratches the back of his head with the other hand, looking from Phainon to the other boy. “You’re just two brats? That’s pretty worthless. Was thinking you would be teens at least with how you were movin’.”

Worthless? Are they supposed to be worth anything? They are camping out in the wild. Of course they don’t have a lot of things.

“You’ve lost your edge,” a new person speaks clearly from somewhere behind Phainon. When he whirls around to check, he sees another man standing among the trees over his friend’s shoulder, an axe held loosely in his hand and propped over his arm. Phainon’s throat closes up with panic. “We gotta talk after this one.

His friend backs up to keep both of the strangers within his field of view, eyes jumping between the two with a glare, lips bared. Phainon angles himself a little to keep the boy behind him.

“Yes, yes.” The first guy waves the words off lazily, clearly unconcerned. “What’s the big deal? Everythin’ is fine.”

“We will give you all our things,” Phainon butts in desperately, voice cracking. He’s got a sword, and there is one knife, and— and even scissors. Any weapon should be good for something in the forest, right? A flask is also useful. And there are the gold bracelets he keeps at the bottom of his backpack, too. “It’s not much, but it’s still something. We won’t make any trouble, please, just let us leave, we—”

He flinches when he is cut off by loud laughter. The man who accidentally alerted them comes closer, looming over them. He seems taller than anyone Phainon has ever met. “Your things? Why would we want those?” He crouches down about two steps from Phainon.

He’s got a short beard, a little uneven on the left side. Hair tied in a small bun at the back of his head, some light wrinkles here and there. And eyes so black that they barely reflect the firelight.

“See, there ain’t much food in these parts, I’m sure you’ve noticed. Maybe you two li’l things can get by on worms and shit, but we can’t. No hard feelings, y’know. We woulda preferred if you were all grown up, too. But gotta make do whenever we find a bigger prey, aye?”

Phainon feels his blood run cold, all of his muscles tensing at once. “What?”

For once, he is glad his friend doesn’t understand a single word being said. It can’t mean whatever Phainon’s brain just jumped to. There is no way. Maybe they’re just after their food supplies? That’s fine. Phainon can give them those. He can even hunt some more if it means they can get away in the end.

Understanding or not, the boy seems to sense his distress just fine. Something like a short growl comes from him as a warning. He inches even closer to Phainon, standing protectively between him and the guy with the axe.

Said man simply sighs, eyes narrowing a little as he observes them. “Don’t think too hard on it. It won’t matter much to you once you’re dead anyway.”

“You— you said we’re worthless,” Phainon gets out, hating himself a little for stuttering. It comes out pleading. “We aren’t much, so. Um. It, it shouldn’t be worth the effort.”

“Something is better than nothing, kiddo,” the guy who is still crouching chuckles, scratching his chin. “Besides, you’re pretty stupid either way. Won’t survive long all on your own. Not covering your trail at all, it’s like you’re askin’ to be found. Titans, at least cover the traces of the fires.”

Oh.

Is it his fault after all? He knew he should have taken greater care to keep them hidden. They should have been moving faster, off to any of the cities for new supplies and direction. They still only have one pair of shoes between the two of them. One water flask, one sword, battered clothes, and too thin blankets.

Is there anything Phainon has done right?

Tears well up in his eyes without warning, and Phainon reaches up to rub at them harshly with a sniffle. He should be thinking of ways to escape, not crying.

“We’ve already wasted enough time,” the other man sighs impatiently. “Let’s get it over with.”

Before he can react, the man with the axe closes the distance between them, reaching for Phainon’s friend, face emotionless. Almost bored. He grabs the boy without another word, and Phainon’s body moves on its own, trying to yank his companion away from the danger and closer to himself. Rough

hands settle on his shoulders and squeeze in a warning, keeping him in place.

Phainon can only uselessly attempt to break free as he watches the boy snap his teeth up at the man like a cornered animal. He snarls through clenched teeth when the stranger only snorts at the action and grasps a fistful of long hair with one hand, yanking up to make him bare his neck. The boy doesn’t even wince despite the way it must hurt, but Phainon still lurches forward. The grip on his shoulders only tightens, keeping him rooted in place. He truly is useless.

The golden eyes glint with hatred and defiance as small hands wrap around the man’s forearm, squeezing until the knuckles turn white. The guy grunts in pain, brows knotted in surprise as his hand trembles. His other arm raises with haste, readying the weapon.

“No, please!”

Phainon’s shout echoes through the forest, some birds waking from their slumber and fluttering away with loud squawks. And with it, the axe swings down. Phainon doesn’t look away as it strikes his friend’s neck with a sickening sound.

The silence afterward is deafening, ringing in Phainon’s ears as tears stream down his face. He doesn’t bother wiping them away. The boy’s hands slowly loosen and drop down, hanging motionlessly like a lifeless puppet. The man rips the axe out, and golden blood immediately splutters out of the wound. The body falls to the ground with a thud, gold leaking into a puddle where severed long hair is scattered.

Phainon stares, shaking with the force of his sobbing. He cannot force himself to blink, eyes locked on his friend.

“What the hell,” the guy’s words sound like they come from under the water.

“The head’s still on,” the man holding Phainon’s shoulder points out unhelpfully. Phainon feels his stomach churning painfully, threatening to

spit out whatever he just ate. “That’s unlike you.”

This cannot be happening again.

He thinks of Cyrene’s body, skewered on that dark and uneven blade. Of Livia falling to the ground as she is consumed by the black tide, Piso fruitlessly trying to grab her hand and pull her away from it. His parents being torn apart by the monsters, yelling at him to get away.

And now, his friend—

“Shut up. Thought the little shit was gonna break my arm for a moment.” He kicks lightly at the dead body.

Because there really is no way to survive that.

Is it because of Phainon? Does he bring nothing but pain and death to those around him? Is it just his presence that’s enough to doom them all?

“A small thing like that? Yeah, sure,” comes the response with a light laugh. “He bleeds golden, ain’t he? We never had one of those Chrysos Heirs. Ya think—”

Another person died in front of him. When will it end?

Phainon almost wants to hurry the strangers up to do the same to him. To make sure he doesn’t bring this fate upon anyone else in the future. Phainon thinks he might lose his mind if he somehow survives this.

Not that he wants to survive anymore. He doesn’t deserve to. Maybe if he hadn’t been born, Aedes Elysiae would have still been whole. He should have died there with his family anyway. His companion would have still been stuck at sea, but at least he wouldn’t have been killed so mercilessly.

Phainon’s sobs turn into wheezing, and he falls to his knees when the man decides he no longer needs to hold him back. Phainon lands on his hands, clenching his fingers in the grass. He coughs, barely sees through the tears as he wheezes, trying to get air into his lungs.

His stomach eventually decides to make it easier for him, forcing him to throw up rather than continue panicking and attempting to breathe. It only makes him more distraught, shivering as he still heaves despite there being nothing else to spit out, but at least air finally gets through to his lungs as he gasps.

“Well, that’s disgusting,” the guy mutters and gets up, dragging Phainon away from his vomit by the collar. “But, hey, you’re gonna join your friend soon, yeah? We’re just helping you out.”

Phainon doesn’t answer, taking in hiccuping breaths as he stumbles along until he is shoved closer to the other man.

Is it time? Will they kill him now? He hopes it doesn’t hurt that much. He heard that sometimes death is instant; quick enough that you don’t feel it. But how would anyone know that? It’s not like they experienced it. Maybe it hurts more than anything else.

His friend’s killer positions himself in front of him, reading himself.

Phainon squeezes his eyes shut, trembling.

It’s okay.

He will go to the Nether Realm, and he will meet everyone from the village again. His parents will be proud of him for surviving so long, and he will introduce his new friend to Cyrene, and they will teach him to talk together, and they will have fun without worrying about anything. And no one else will die because of Phainon. Because down there, everyone is already dead.

So, it’s okay.

He takes a steadying breath and waits for the axe to deliver him to the afterlife.

“Phainon!”

His eyes snap open at the voice he only heard once before, yelling his name out fiercely. It’s just in time for Phainon to see the stranger above him

freeze, eyes widening in confusion, before a small body tackles him. Phainon feels a fresh wave of tears, now from sheer relief at seeing his companion up and moving, uncaring of how. The boy is way too small and light to knock the man over. Instead, he lifts himself up until he can lock his legs around the man’s body to keep himself in place, and wraps his hands around the man’s neck.

It happens so fast that Phainon briefly wonders whether he is hallucinating. Or dead already.

His would-be-killer gasps out, dropping the axe and clawing at the boy’s hands in an attempt to get some room to breathe. Amazingly, he isn’t strong enough to succeed. Something red starts forming around their hands, the red markings on his friend’s body glowing brightly for a moment, and then crimson crystals shoot out from between his fingers.

One loud crack of what must be a snapped spine, and the man goes limp. The boy easily jumps to his feet as the body falls to the ground.

A large part of his hair is cut messily just below his chin, where it turns red. It’s matted with gold. Gold splattered all over his skin, blood spilled from a wound that’s no longer there. Slowly, he lifts his head, and his eyes settle on the other man, a few steps behind Phainon. He looks eerily calm; only his lips are tensed a bit, like he wants to flash them in a warning. And when Phainon glances at his eyes, it sends chills down his spine.

Their intensity is unnerving. Inhuman. A predator locking onto its prey. Distantly, Phainon wonders once more how strong the boy might actually be since he survived all alone among the sea beasts created by Phagousa themselves.

“What the fuck are you, brat?” The other man asks gruffly, eventually snapping out of the shock.

Phainon’s friend tilts his head, unblinking. Phainon sees the man visibly swallow, suddenly nervous, and realizes all of his attention is directed at the boy; Phainon momentarily forgotten.

“No matter,” the guy continues, and Phainon slowly inches away from his field of vision. “Just gotta kill you enough times for it to stick, yeah?”

Phainon sees a glint of metal as the man pulls a dagger free from the strap on his thigh and feels his heart speed up in fear. Not again. He makes a run for it just as his friend calmly advances on the stranger. Phainon throws himself to the ground next to his backpack, digging under it to pull his sword out.

When he turns back to them, the man is clutching his stomach, winded. The boy is low on his feet again, glaring up as his arm bleeds sluggishly. The stranger takes another swipe at him with a dagger, and the boy dodges easily, except then the man follows up with a punch to the chest, which connects and sends the boy reeling back, coughing.

Phainon sees the guy smirk from the side.

He takes a breath in and releases it, then runs at him with a sword, making use of the distraction. It’s clumsy, like all technique and muscle memory from his training disappeared at a moment’s notice.

But it’s enough to slide the sword underneath the guy’s ribs and up.

The man shouts in pain, blindly swinging down at Phainon with his dagger. Phainon lets go of the sword, bringing his hand up to shield himself against the blade. The boy is faster, lurching forward and grabbing hold of the arm before it can get close enough to Phainon, stopping it mid-air.

“Fuck,” the man hisses, glaring at both of them. “We both get killed by some stupid kids? This cannot be happening.”

“Why didn’t you let us leave?” Phainon asks quietly. He didn’t want to kill anyone. It’s not as if they did it intentionally. They had to do this. It was just defense. Does it count as killing someone if it’s in defense?

“Was s’posed to be easy,” the man grits out, struggling to take the air in. It might have been his lung that got struck by the sword. He spits red blood at Phainon in anger, trying to yank his hand back.

His friend’s eyes narrow dangerously, and Phainon sees his fingers squeeze even tighter until the man gasps in pain and lets go of the dagger, the blade falling to the ground. Then, the boy reaches with his other hand lower and pulls the sword free. Blood immediately gushes out of the wound as the man collapses to the ground.

It’s quick after that.

The man grows paler by the second, and his eyes turn hazy, breath wheezing. Phainon doesn’t look away until he is certain he is dead and isn’t about to get back up. He figures that his friend might be special in this regard, but doesn’t really want to be surprised if someone else can also defy death somehow.

And just like that, all is suddenly silent.

When nothing happens for another minute or so, Phainon’s head snaps up to his friend, finding him already looking in his direction, visibly relieved that it’s over. Before he can think, Phainon closes the distance and envelops him in a tight hug, making both of them stumble. The boy is stiff in his arms, and Phainon feels tears prickling at his eyes again.

“I’m sorry,” he apologizes, voice cracking. He doesn’t care about the blood he must be getting on himself with the way he is clutching at his friend’s clothes. “It’s all my fault. I, I should have known better. I’m so stupid. They — Of course there would be danger out here. What if you— How would I even—”

The boy’s arms wrap around him and squeeze with a little too much strength, knocking breath out of him and effectively cutting his babbling short. Phainon might have been working himself into some panic. He taps on his companion’s shoulder, and the grip loosens a little.

They stay that way until Phainon’s tears dry up, leaving him tired and feeling disgusted. Washing up sounds like a good idea. They could both use it.

Right now, Phainon is desperate for a moment away from all this. Just a little bit of what became their normalcy so that he can pretend. He can’t break down. They have to clean up so that Phainon can put himself back together, and then they have to move. Phainon cannot mess up like this again, so he will not think about— about anything.

He pulls away, steeling himself to the sight of two dead bodies at their feet. Keeping his gaze low, he grabs the sword just in case. Then, he lights a stray branch with fire to illuminate the way, and takes his friend’s hand, pulling him in the direction he remembers the river being. He leaves all of their belongings behind, not even bothering to spare a thought for them.

They walk silently for what might be ten minutes, maybe more. Or less? Phainon loses track of time a little. He bites his lip when he hears the water rushing forth. As expected, his friend tenses but doesn’t stop just yet, allowing himself to be dragged along. Phainon exhales in relief, tightening his hold on the boy’s hand once, getting a squeeze back. He turns his head and sends him a smile that’s meant to be reassuring, but he’s got no doubt that it falls short.

Quickly enough, they reach the tree line that gives way to a steep riverbank leading down to the river itself. Without the trees obstructing it, the starlight finally makes it possible to see without a torch. Phainon has never loved the sight of the sky as much as at that moment.

But, as expected, the boy halts immediately, digging his heels into the ground with so much strength that Phainon has no illusion he could ever move him if he tried. Not that he wants to force him.

Instead, Phainon turns around to face him, not dropping the hold he’s got on his palm. “Can we please go together?” He asks. Pleads, really. “It’s okay, you know? I get it. I swear I won’t make you go into the water. I just, I don’t want to leave you right now. Please.”

The boy stares at him, peeking over Phainon’s shoulder for a moment, not understanding the words. Phainon’s eyes prickle again, this time in frustration and helplessness. He is getting tired of crying all the time. Why

is he like this? He should have left this childish behavior back at Aedes Elysiae. How is he supposed to grow big and strong if he cries all the time?

“Come with me?” He asks again, scrubbing at his eyes harshly with his other hand. The boy’s brows furrow in concern when Phainon’s hand falls down, probably revealing watery and reddened eyes. Well, maybe it is working in his favor for once. He sniffles and tugs on his friend’s hand one more time with distress. “Please.”

He gestures once for good measure, the simple sign for come.

It takes a few long seconds of studying Phainon’s expression for the boy to reluctantly decide to humor him, taking a cautious step forward.

Phainon immediately brightens up, beaming at him in gratitude. “Thank you,” he rushes out, hurrying them forward again and nearly causing his companion to stumble in the process.

It’s easy enough to climb down until they are at the very edge. The water reaches a bit lower than where the ground cuts off. He could probably dip his feet in there up to his ankles if he dangled his legs from the edge. Phainon makes the boy sit down there, nodding to show that’s good enough and he won’t be pushing for more. He feels an incredible amount of relief wash over him as he watches him immediately relax.

Right. First things first.

Phainon throws the branch into the river to extinguish the fire, then takes his shirt off, wincing at the golden stains covering it. He runs it under the water, scrubbing his fingers against the material to get out as much of it as he can. The shirt is nowhere near the white it started out as; it hasn’t been for a while now. He doesn’t care much at this point, having grown used to the muted grey and brown hues it adopted.

He squeezes the water out of it once he deems it as clean as it can get and puts it aside. He tugs a little on the boy’s own shirt, making a lifting motion with his hand. The boy understands him right away, slipping his own shirt off and handing it over obediently.

“Thank you,” Phainon says, then taps his friend’s knee to get him to pay attention a little more closely.

He flaps the wet shirt in the air as hard as he can a few times to speed up the drying process. Phainon hands it over to the boy and repeats the action with his hands before pointing at him. He gets to it immediately, and Phainon nods to express that he is doing well.

He takes greater care washing the other shirt. It’s more delicate, given how they cut it up before, and is easier to accidentally stretch out or rip. Water swirls in gold and red briefly as he soaks it for the first time, and Phainon finds himself appreciating the fact that the material is red to begin with. The bloodstains from those men aren’t even visible. The gold won’t be as easy to hide, but, well. Maybe if someone doesn’t know the origin of the stains, they will assume it’s supposed to be that way? Very few people have golden blood, so they shouldn’t realize anything is wrong.

Phainon takes his shirt from his friend and hands him the red one, waving his hand in two small circles for repeat. He spreads his damp shirt over the ground as the boy gets to the task again.

Once that’s done, Phainon strips the rest of his clothes, leaving them strewn about on the ground and putting the sword off to the side after rinsing it clear of blood as well. He steps into the water, testing the depth and strength of the current. It’s a little strong, but not enough that he cannot plant his legs firmly enough to not be swept away by it. The water reaches just about to his ribs. He takes one step toward the center of the stream out of curiosity and finds it declining a little bit. Phainon has done this so many times that he doesn’t even flinch at the cold water. He wishes the freezing temperature didn’t affect him as much at night out in the open as well.

He runs his hands over his body, scrubbing the dirt and dried blood off his skin, scratching with his fingernails even when it looks clean, but it doesn’t feel clean enough. It’s only when he notices numerous angry red lines snaking all over his arms that he snaps out of it. Right. He can’t get much cleaner than this without soap. He shakes himself out of it and dips his entire head under the water instead, running his fingers through his hair and

enjoying the rush of the stream against him. The utter silence the water provides, aside from the thrumming of the current.

Phainon gradually lets the air out of his lungs, prolonging it just a bit. He remains that way when his lungs beg for oxygen to be allowed back in, and he forces himself to stay down a little longer when they start hurting.

Something grabs hold of his hair and yanks him up to the surface. Phainon gasps, panting as golden eyes glare down at him, fingers still tightly clutching the white strands. And probably pulling clumps of it out.

“Ouch,” Phainon hisses, his hands reaching up to try to detangle himself from his friend. ”I’m okay! Sorry. Sorry, I know you hate water, but I wasn’t— I don’t know, sorry,” he trails off lamely.

The boy doesn’t relent, staring him down expectantly as he lightly snaps his teeth at Phainon.

Phainon sighs and moves closer until he can heave himself back up onto the riverbank, and only then does the hand slip away from his hair.

He knows they should be getting back on the way already, but he still throws his pants back on and sits next to his friend. There’s one more thing to do, he tells himself. Just one more moment of busying himself with something before they can head back. It’s important to take care of his friend as well, isn’t it?

So he carefully cuts the rest of the long hair off with his sword, leaving it more uneven than he would with a knife or scissors, but he just. He wants the reminder of what happened gone as soon as possible. He doesn’t want to stare at the sharp cut-off where the axe had struck. The boy doesn’t mind, tensing just the tiniest bit when Phainon brings the sword to his neck.

He helps the boy wash his hair. For the first time since they met, he is making a more thorough job of it since they have a steady supply of water at hand. Rinses off as much of his body as he can without getting him in the water. Their shirts aren’t fully dry by the time they’re done, but it’s enough

not to be uncomfortable, even if Phainon briefly worries over catching a cold.

Phainon tempts fate a little and doesn’t try to make a fire to light another branch to see the way in the forest. He hopes it’s close enough that they won’t get lost while trying to navigate blindly. He just doesn’t want to make a fire. The walk back to the camp is entirely silent, only leaves and branches crunching under their feet. His friend seems to have a better sense of direction, correcting their course now and then with a small tug on their connected hands.

Everything is exactly as they left it once they reach the spot, the only difference being the puddle of blood under one of the bodies having grown larger, and the fire that almost went out on its own by now, lighting up the area just enough.

Phainon inhales. Exhales. Inhales again.

And decides that he needs to get used to dead bodies one way or the other. Might as well be now. The sooner the better, right? Right…

His friend has no such qualms, striding to them without a thought and picking the stranger’s dagger up. He looks it over, then wipes it off on the collar of the dead man’s shirt and goes to put it away with the rest of their things. Phainon can’t really argue with it. The dagger will be useful. He glances at the axe, considering it for all of two seconds before deciding he would rather throw it into the river than ever see it again, useful or not.

Very slowly, he crouches down next to the man who killed his friend. Or, well, attempted to. His neck is bent at an unnatural angle, but the red crystals Phainon saw are gone as if they never appeared in the first place. Did he hallucinate them because of shock? But he noticed the markings glow as well, and that was a bit too elaborate to hallucinate. Probably. He doesn’t know how hallucinations work exactly.

They make quick work of gathering their things, and Phainon sneaks enough glances at the two men that, hoping it will desensitize him well enough for the future. He briefly even considers taking their shoes, but

realizes they would be way too big for either of them. His friend does steal the axe-man’s shirt, though, nodding eagerly at it like it’s the best present he’s ever gotten. They take the leather strap from the man’s thigh as well.

They leave with a new torch, going in the same direction as the river runs from, not sparing a glance back.

They walk side by side, so closely that their arms brush together every so often, until Phainon’s legs start shaking from exhaustion. And then a bit further, despite his friend’s concerned looks, until Phainon’s legs actually give out from underneath him.

Only then does Phainon bring out the blankets from his backpack in his spot on the ground, not even bothering to get back up. He knows he won’t be able to stand straight with how much his legs hurt. Phainon pulls out the dagger too, just in case. He places everything where it should be as he shuffles around, a little lost in thought. They’re getting out of this forest as quickly as possible. Are there others in here as well? There could be. What if those two men were in a larger group? Will people come looking for them? Have they left any tracks to follow?

Phainon wishes he had a compass of sorts. They really need to get a lot of things if they want to travel properly. But, to be fair, he thinks traveling without one would be fine anywhere but in a forest of all places.

It’s when he hears the boy trying to set up the fire for the night that he gets yanked out of his thoughts.

“No,” he breathes out and hurries over, nearly falling right on his face as he tries to get there quickly, pulling his companion away. He shakes his head frantically, trying to get the point across.

The boy tilts his head, blinking at him in confusion.

“They saw the fire before,” Phainon explains, a little choked up. “They— They might find us again. Let’s. Let’s leave it today, okay?”

He looks from Phainon to the wood he prepared, then back to Phainon. Then, even though Phainon is sure his friend doesn’t understand the reasoning behind it, he nods. Phainon breathes out in relief. He doesn’t know how he would have explained it if he insisted on setting the fire no matter what.

With nothing else left to do, they settle down for some rest, each wrapped in his own blanket about a step apart from one another. They will be walking a lot from now on, no longer wasting time playing around. They should get as much rest as possible.

Phainon closes his eyes. It takes maybe half a minute before he sees the image of an axe stuck in his friend’s throat, and gold streaming down in a river. His eyes snap open of their own accord, barely making out the outline of the tree in front of him.

So, no closing his eyes, then. Or sleeping.

He doesn’t know how long he stays that way.

He is exhausted to the bone, eyelids heavy but refusing to remain closed at the threat of replaying this day to him. He should sleep. But the cold finally gets to him as well, making him shiver so strongly that he has to grit his teeth together to keep them from clattering.

But it’s okay.

They are both alive, at least. That’s all that matters.

Phainon will lie awake if he can’t sleep, and it should be enough; his body will think it got enough rest so that they can continue.

His friend did die, though. Phainon doesn’t know whether it’s a fluke that he didn’t stay dead, or if he really isn’t human at all. Phainon doesn’t care, and he doesn’t want to know. He is alive, and that’s all that matters.

What— What if he didn’t come back to life? What if he were too late? Phainon would also be dead then. There is no doubt about it. His friend is

strong enough to not only go against Thanatos but also to save Phainon from death himself. And what good is Phainon? He ruined everything. Couldn’t even save his friend first, prevent that one death.

But he can— He will get stronger.

And, and they will get out of this stupid forest, and his friend will need someone to help him communicate once they reach a town, or a village, or something, won’t he? So, Phainon will be useful for something.

And once they do, once they catch enough breath and get enough supplies, they will get stronger together. And nothing like this will happen again.

So, it’s going to be okay.

It already is okay. They got through this day, after all.

It’s okay.

It’s okay.

Itsokayitsokayitsokayitsokayitsokayitsoka—

It’s not okay.

Phainon brings nothing but bad luck and pain, and if this boy can’t die, then just what kind of misery will Phainon bring to him? He should have stayed alone, not gotten involved, the star was wrong, and his wish was so selfish, everywhere he goes, something bad happens, he really is the calam—

“Phainon.”

His name is called quietly, not exactly a whisper but quiet and calm enough to prevent Phainon from springing up in shock. Phainon uncurls himself from the fetal position he somehow ended up in, forcing his body to relax a little bit. Now that he focuses, he sees the outline of his friend kneeling on the ground in front of him. Without a fire, it’s hard to tell what expression he is making as he gazes down at Phainon. And Phainon realizes his teeth are clattering after all.

“S—Sorry,” he stutters out through shivers. “I, I’ll be quieter.”

The boy doesn’t seem reassured, not moving for a long moment. Eventually, he just taps Phainon’s head twice with some hesitation. Is it because there’s no source of light and he can’t gesture properly? Is he just trying to get Phainon’s attention? When he doesn’t react quickly enough, his friend repeats the action again, then brings his palm right in front of Phainon’s eyes so that its outline is visible even in the darkness, and tilts it to the side like he would his head. Ah.

You okay?

“Yeah,” Phainon breathes out, swallowing roughly and doing his best to speak clearly. “I’m. I’m okay.”

Phainon thinks his companion should have a decent grasp of what the word ‘okay’ means, so he doesn’t know what that doubtful noise he lets out is for. Does he not believe him?

Phainon watches as the boy’s silhouette shifts, looking over his shoulder for a moment, considering something. He tries to come up with a way to successfully reassure him that he is fine, really. Or just that there is no need to worry. They don’t have any signs for that. He supposes he can just deny everything when faced with doubt? But it’s clear he—

The boy gets up and walks off, making noise as he shuffles with his blanket.

Well.

That was easy. Phainon didn’t even have to say a word or bring his hands out from beneath the blanket to try and make up a new gesture for some word.

Just as relief bleeds in, another blanket is thrown on top of him, making him jump a little.

“Wh—What?” He asks, watching as the boy tucks one side under Phainon’s body. “What about you? I know you run hot, but you, you will freeze to death. I don’t care if you can’t die or something, you— oh.”

The words die in his throat when the boy carefully unfolds Phainon’s blanket on the other side and worms his way inside, cocooning them both under the fabric and twisting around so that he can cling to Phainon’s body.

Phainon stills entirely.

The boy seems unbothered by it, basically burrowing himself into Phainon’s neck, warm breath fanning over cold skin. Phainon immediately feels the difference, as if someone shoved a furnace under the blankets along with him.

He doesn’t even really care about the temperature at this moment, though.

They hugged for a moment earlier, but this is different. He doesn’t remember the last time he slept by someone’s side. Was it one of his parents after a nightmare? Or Cyrene, napping together under a tree? He forgot how good and safe it felt to be enveloped in someone else’s arms.

Even if they are still out in the open, vulnerable to anything that might decide it wants to kill them right this moment.

It still does an incredible job of calming him down.

Phainon wraps his arms around the slightly smaller figure, holding him protectively. This way, he doesn’t have to worry about something happening to him out of Phainon’s reach.

Subconsciously matching his breathing pattern to that of his friend, he falls asleep before his mind can spiral again.

It’s not a restful night. But it might be okay.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

As they continue on, Phainon doesn’t run his mouth off as much. He even forgoes speaking the words aloud as he used to when he gestures, passing the torch back and forth with the boy to free his hands. His fingers barely leave the sword’s hilt, other than that. His friend doesn’t stray far from him anymore.

And in his haste to lead them out of the forest, Phainon forgets a pretty important detail.

Eating.

He brushes off the way his hands start shaking and the dizziness. He focuses on putting one leg ahead of the other, pushing on. His stomach stops hurting after a while.

It’s around the second day that he thinks he stumbles on something, except he didn’t feel his leg catching on anything. Fingers wrap around his forearm before his face can try to make friends with the ground, pulling him back up and then helping him slowly sit down. It’s a good thing he wasn’t holding the torch at the moment, he would have surely dropped it otherwise. He doesn’t think they would have been able to get out alive from a fire consuming the forest.

Or maybe that would’ve been a good thing. Nothing good in this forest. And Phainon, too.

Phainon blinks a few times, trying to get rid of the swimming vision and mostly succeeding.

His friend crouches in front of him, mouth set in a thin line as he thinks hard about something. Phainon wonders what that might be. There are a lot of things to think about. Eventually, he points to himself, makes a grabbing motion, then a gesture for eating. I will get some food.

Phainon stares at him. Food? Is he hungry? Phainon isn’t; they can walk for a little longer, he thinks. But, well, they should get something together. It’s not good to split up. Phainon doesn’t want to split up.

He attempts to stand back up, only to stagger when he puts weight on his legs, swaying dangerously. The boy immediately presses on his shoulders to keep him firmly on the ground. He leans back, eyes stern. He holds his hand up just to push it downward quickly, then rotates it in a small circle in the ground’s direction, fingers up. Stay here.

“What— No. Let you go alone? No,” Phainon shakes his head vigorously and attempts to get up again.

His friend exhales in frustration. He puts his fists together, then sharply pulls them apart, simultaneously flicking one of them down and forward, and the other up as if gesturing behind himself. Separate.

“We can’t,” Phainon replies urgently, grabbing the boy’s forearm. Dark spots begin to form around his vision. He shakes his head again to get rid of them and to convey refusal, but it only brings him sharp pain at the back of his head. “Let me rest for a second, and we will go together, okay?” He pleads, feeling increasingly lightheaded. He puts his free hand up sharply, fingers spread out to indicate wait, and then swipes over his eyes for sleep. Phainon just needs some rest, and he will be good as new. A low ringing comes from somewhere, but he cannot tell where from. “What if they come back and I—”

He cuts himself off, the amount of dark spots increasing rapidly, and he looks at his friend in panic. He can barely see him, thinks his lips might be moving, but he cannot be sure. Something is wrong.

“I can’t see,” Phainon gasps, his voice muffled. The ringing disappeared, but with it most of his hearing. “I can’t—”

He feels his hand slip from the grip it had on his friend’s forearm as the last of his vision disappears, and with it he falls.

Phainon opens his eyes sluggishly.

“Eat.” A very pointed word, emphasized by something touching his lips insistently.

Phainon blinks, vision adjusting just a little to see his companion bathed in the warm glow of a fire, not taking his eyes off him as he takes a bite himself. Phainon obligingly opens his mouth and munches on the piece of roasted squirrel that’s pushed in. Tastes as bland as ever. He chews slowly, swallowing it once there isn’t much else left to chew.

His friend doesn’t offer him more for a little while. Phainon doesn’t want to think about how he knows that Phainon’s stomach must be twisting painfully, threatening to throw it back up if he eats more. It takes some time to get through the meal, and Phainon falls asleep twice during the process, seemingly lacking all strength. He didn’t realize it got so bad. Can he blame his single-minded focus and self-imposed starvation for not noticing?

The boy seems to know the exact amount of time needed for Phainon’s stomach to get used to food again. At least they stop for water every day now. Maybe the fact that he had some water also added to not realizing he was hungry at all.

This slight setback doesn’t stop Phainon from getting back onto his feet as soon as he regains enough strength within the next few hours. He already messed up once, being unable to accompany his friend. He isn’t pushing his luck with another mistake. He doesn’t want to be separated. They tidy up the area, covering any traces of a fire as best they can, and leave to find a different place to rest. Phainon would love nothing more than to drag his friend as far as they can physically go, but it seems the boy is a little fed up with it. He stops Phainon once he deems them far enough from the fire himself and demands to call it a night.

Phainon bites his lip, considering. It should be far enough. At least his friend allowed him to travel a little bit farther. It’s better than nothing.

They do their routine, and they slip under two blankets together. Phainon hasn’t felt cold in his sleep ever since they started doing this. The

nightmares aren’t so frequent either, and it’s easier to get back to sleep after being woken up by one. The memory of his parents and friends’ corpses, chased away by hands and legs tangled with his. The sight and feeling of the body next to him immediately reassure him whenever he dreams of the axe and golden blood.

“I’m sorry,” he whispers into the boy’s blonde hair. “I will do better.”

Phainon doesn’t forget about eating anymore.

They hunt together, sometimes catching an animal as is, but mostly setting up traps before they head to sleep and checking them after they wake up. Phainon talks a little more. His friend doesn’t try to go off without him again, almost as reluctant to let him out of sight as Phainon is.

Phainon doesn’t want to think about being left on his own, even if it’s for just an hour. The initial stab of panic at trying to consider it is more than enough to tell him he shouldn’t allow that to happen again.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

His companion now consistently tags along with him to the river. Always sitting right at the edge, waiting for Phainon to be done and then allowing him to pour water from the flask over his body to wash away the sweat and dust from their travels.

But it’s only when the riverbank turns into a gentle descent of ground into the water, resembling a small beach rather than a sharp decline cut off into deeper water, that he finally steps into the river.

He is hesitant at first, and Phainon wonders whether it’s because it reminds him of the sea too much. But Phainon grabs him by the hand and doesn’t

even wince when the boy’s grip on it turns too tight and a bit painful.

“It’s alright,” he says instead with a smile, and tugs him gently into the water. “I won’t let anything happen.”

There isn’t any possibility he understands the words, but perhaps something about Phainon’s tone or maybe whatever he finds in his expression speaks to him. His face is set with newfound determination, taking a step into the water even as his hand doesn’t let up. Phainon walks by his side patiently as they slowly reach the point where water laps at their knees. It seems to be the limit for his friend, but that’s perfectly fine. Phainon is already happy with this.

They wash quickly, clothes rinsed and left to dry back by the shore with the rest of their belongings. He helps his friend wash his back and shoulders, the spots being difficult to get water on without either a stream of water coming from above or submerging the body entirely. He is already used to the process either way. He sits down on the ground to relax a little, enjoying the feeling of water swallowing him up to his elbows as he does. He smiles as his friend glares at the center of the river where the water goes much deeper, scrunching his nose as if it personally offended him. It shouldn’t be funny with what led to this reaction, but it kind of is.

Until something slimy brushes past Phainon’s shin, and he flinches back with so much force that he topples over into the shallow water. He resurfaces just as quickly, propping himself up on his elbows, hair drenched with water and plastered to his eyes. What was that?

He swipes his fringe back, just to see his friend crouching a little, now staring into the water with brows furrowed in deep concentration. Phainon can easily imagine a tail frantically swishing back and forth, were he a cat. Before Phainon can question the recent development, the boy lurches forward, one hand submerging into the water without any hesitation, then rising just as quickly to show a fish wiggling in the air, trying to escape the grip.

“Huh?” Phainon rises to his feet, coming closer. “You caught it just like that? I had to stab them with the sword when I was trying on my own!”

This is so unfair.

Well, it is cool. Very cool. But Phainon would appreciate it if he could be better at something for once. He is better at capturing small animals in the traps, but his friend still grasped the skill too quickly for his liking. Although Phainon might be out of his depth when it comes to catching fish, his friend did spend a long time at sea. He has the advantage of knowing how fish think. That must be it.

“Is there anything you’re not good at?” He grumbles, gesturing for give me. The boy hands the fish off without a word, watching as Phainon carefully takes it with two hands to ensure it doesn’t slap its way out of his hands. He learned the hard way just how slippery they are. “Talking, I guess. But that’s fine, I can talk for two.”

He heads back to their supplies and leaves the fish there, far enough from the water, then heads back. Maybe Phainon improved since the last time and just doesn’t know it. He walks back, determined to show that he can also catch fish with his bare hands.

It turns into a competition rather quickly. He should have seen it coming.

The boy catches fifteen and has to release thirteen of them back into the river. Phainon catches three with a technique that resembles wrestling them rather than actually catching. Also, something he should probably have predicted.

He is handed a pretty stone found in the river as a consolation prize, the blue color just one shade lighter than his eyes. Phainon runs his thumb over its surface so often he wonders whether it might affect its shape, and only then does he store it with the rest of the boy’s gifts. Findings.

They eat only fish for the next three days.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Two weeks of obsessively watching every detail around them and jumping at every shadow until the forest finally ends, and Phainon can breathe a little easier.

He doesn’t even realize it at first, not until they are just a few paces from the tree line and some scant light peeks through the branches. Phainon gasps a little, grabbing his friend’s wrist and pulling him forward until they stumble into the open ground, and Phainon’s knees nearly give out at the sheer relief. A tension Phainon became so familiar with throughout the last several days unravels at once. The moons and stars light up everything without a need for a torch. There isn’t any path forward, but buildings span out in the distance. Yellow dots mark them, signaling that they are clearly inhabited.

“We made it out,” Phainon says breathlessly, squeezing his friend’s hand and dragging him further away from that cursed forest. He giggles with exhilaration. “We made it!”

He turns to take one last look at the trees, hoping he will never end up in this place again. The tree line is the exact same as the one they entered through—breaks in a sharp line as if someone planted the seeds with a measuring tape and took great care to keep the trees in such clean order.

Eerie, for such a big forest to be so well maintained.

But it doesn’t matter. They are never going back.

Phainon turns back to face forward, beaming at his friend as he does so. The boy is already looking at him, a soft smile on his face.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 3: and find the path forward
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

“It’s only been a week, but are you sure you don’t want to stay?” She asks, shifting to slump forward and lean her elbows on her knees. “Don’t you wanna make new friends beyond the one you’ve got? There are lots of kids around to play with.”

“Why?” Phainon asks, his brows furrowing. He pinches the skin right next to the red line. Within a moment, one of the legs raises and kicks his shoulder lightly with a displeased huff. “He is more than enough,” he continues with a giggle.

Besides, he wished for just one person to be by his side. He doesn’t want to get greedy. He won’t ask for too much. Just one friend is enough.

Chapter Notes

It takes about half a day to reach the town. Phainon feels giddy at the prospect of the safety that buildings actually provide. He is sick of the trees.

His companion’s gaze doesn’t stray from the constructions as they get nearer, fascinated by the view. Phainon carefully does not think about how it might be the first time he is even seeing a house. As insane as the prospect sounds to him, he doesn’t like how it might be the reality.

The lampposts greet them at the open gates, bathing the streets in a yellowish glow without any effort. The boy stares with wide eyes at everything as they pass the stores, which seem to already be closed, the doors and windows locked tight. It must be nearing the end of the Parting Hour. That’s alright, they can just find a corner to huddle up in and sleep until the Entry Hour comes, when the town will come back alive without a doubt.

Phainon leads them through to where he expects the town square to be, making sure his friend doesn’t lag behind in his quiet astonishment at the architecture. It’s not even that impressive, Phainon thinks. It lacks the warmth of Aedes Elysiae, that’s for sure.

A woman rounds a corner just then, the first person they encounter since coming in. She hums a tune to herself as she walks, not really paying attention until her gaze slides over the two of them, moving past before it snaps back in surprise. She covers it up quickly, altering her course to walk toward them immediately, even as Phainon and his friend stop in their tracks. The boy stiffens at the very sight of her, taking a step forward to get in front of Phainon protectively. His stance is low, and Phainon can easily imagine the intense glare directed at the stranger. Phainon knows it means he will attack first and ask questions later. Well, there would be no questions at all. Not the point.

Phainon forces himself to remain as relaxed as he can manage and grabs his friend’s hand to gently pull him back, keeping him at his side. The boy shoots him a quick look with narrowed eyes before they lock onto the woman again and don’t leave her figure after. He could break free of the grip if he really needed to, but he stays put for now. Even if his muscles still appear so tense that it looks uncomfortable.

Phainon hopes the lady won’t make any threatening movements, or there might be another murder. He doesn’t want a woman who means them no harm to lose her life. He doesn’t want anyone innocent to lose their life. And he isn’t confident they will be able to get out of the town unscathed if that happens.

His grip tightens just a little in what’s meant to be a reassurance. She is maybe two meters away from them when the boy decides it’s too close. He lurches forward a bit, only held back by Phainon’s secure hold on his hand, lips bared as a noise rises from his throat. Like a feral animal. Phainon has no doubt he could break away and attack her if he truly wanted. It’s meant to be merely a warning.

The woman halts immediately, taken aback. Her eyes jump between the two of them, almost like she is trying to find all the puzzle pieces.

Phainon tugs his friend back once more, exhaling in relief when he allows himself to be directed back to Phainon’s side. He grabs the boy’s entire arm and holds it close to his own chest. If he can’t stop him, then at least he will slow him down in case something goes wrong. He wouldn’t harm Phainon on purpose.

“Calm down, please,” he mutters softly. “Everything is fine.” It doesn’t have much effect. Those golden eyes drill into the stranger with intensity that promises danger at one wrong step. “I’m sorry,” he calls louder to the woman.

At that, she simply crouches down to put them on the same eye level, her long dress spread over her knees elegantly. She is keeping her distance, and that’s all that matters. Phainon probably should have seen this coming. Why hasn’t he thought about how his friend would react to meeting people? The fact that he is more than fine with Phainon doesn’t mean he will be with anyone else, especially after the encounter in the forest. Not to mention the adults.

“Don’t worry,” she reassures with a gentle voice and a small smile. “I don’t think I’ve seen you two here before.”

She seems wary of them. Despite it, she still looks very kind. It makes Phainon want to trust her. Dark hair with grey streaks running through it, braided at the back of her head from what he can glimpse, with some loose strands framing her face. He can’t really tell from the distance and low lighting, but her eyes appear rather light; they could be green or blue. There are deep creases at the corners of those eyes and at her mouth. Like she laughs a lot.

“My name is Nysa,” she introduces herself, waving her hand in a friendly manner.

“I’m Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” he offers back easily. It doesn’t matter if his birthplace is gone. He will always carry it with him and let others know of its existence.

She glances at his friend briefly but doesn’t ask his name. Phainon hopes she assumes he doesn’t want to tell her his name, not that he doesn’t have one.

“I think your bedtime should be near, isn’t that right?” She asks with a hum and continues without waiting for an answer. “But I believe you should get something in your stomachs first; you two look like you’ve been living on nothing but squirrels for months. We can talk in the morning.”

Is that— Is it that bad? Enough that she can tell? Phainon feels his cheeks heat a little. He thought they were doing well.

“We don’t have any money,” Phainon feels the need to point out. He would rather she didn’t find out later just to decide they deceived her or something. They cannot afford any trouble. “I’ve got some jewelry I can barter with, but it’s not much. We can work for it, though, we just need a little rest first,” he rushes to reassure.

“Consider it a welcome gift,” she waves him off immediately, chuckling a little. “You two are so small, you’re hardly going to make me go bankrupt. Save that jewelry for something more useful.”

“Oh, thank you,” Phainon agrees readily before she can take the offer back, nodding possibly with a bit too much vigor.

His mouth waters at the mere notion of having a full, properly prepared meal. Not to mention for free. That’s very generous of her. He feels a little bad about the way his friend is still on high alert, watching her and waiting for a moment to strike if she so much as breathes wrong.

“There is a spare room in my house that I can offer you,” she continues. “Can you follow me there?”

“Yeah.” Phainon looks at his friend, unsure of how exactly to proceed with him. What if he lashes out over something?

Nysa stands up, slow and careful, still looking incredibly friendly as she straightens out her dress. The boy tenses up, and the arm that Phainon is

still holding turns rigid. He quickly links their fingers together and taps the boy’s elbow twice. Everything is fine, he tries to convey with his entire being without a proper sign for it.

“It’s safe. She’s going to help us,” he says as calmly and optimistically as he can muster. With that, he starts stepping forward and pulls the boy along with him. He complies, albeit very reluctantly, light on his feet and eyes, breaking away from the woman only once to shoot another confused glance at Phainon. “Could you walk a few steps away from us? Please,” he asks Nysa, smiling awkwardly.

“Of course,” she smiles back effortlessly, moving a little to the side to allow them space.

Phainon breathes out in relief, putting himself between the two of them. This might go well. They will rest, get food, and possibly whatever supplies they need as well. But he will settle for the first two if the rest is too much.

“Is he like this toward everyone?” Nysa asks pleasantly as they start walking, and Phainon cringes internally.

“I don’t know,” he admits a little helplessly. The boy walks alongside him, his hand clutching Phainon’s in a bruising grip as he can no longer look at the woman from this angle. “You are the first person we’ve met since... Uh. In a while.”

Thankfully, she doesn’t prod further than that. She simply accepts the answer, nodding in understanding.

“I’m glad you want to pull your weight, but it might be difficult if he cannot get close to people,” she says, not unkindly. Her tone is still as calm as it was before, like none of this is an issue. “Don’t worry, we will figure something out.”

Just like that, Phainon can breathe a little easier. It’s okay even if she decides it’s too much hassle. He just needs one day to live without worrying about everything that surrounds him, and they can be on their way. That would be more than enough.

“Excuse me,” Phainon begins uncertainly, suddenly realizing he should figure out how much time he has missed in the forest. “What month is it right now?”

The lady glances at him with an unreadable look in her eyes that dissipates after a beat. “We are nearing the end of the Month of Weaving.”

Phainon frowns, mentally doing some math. Not his strongest subject, but this shouldn’t be too hard; he was doing a pretty good job keeping up with days and months before he found the star. He left Aedes Elysiae in the Month of Balance, then got to the first town by the Month of Evernight. He found the star in the Month of Everday, and if now is—

It’s the Month of Weaving?

Phainon nearly stumbles over his own feet, forcibly keeping his posture relaxed so that he won’t alarm his friend.

Logically, he knew a month must have passed while they were in the forest. He remembers thinking about it, realizing he lost the count somewhere along the way. Amid everything, he forgot his own birthday was approaching, not even realizing it must have come and gone by then.

He is ten now. Has been for almost two months.

Still in shock over the realization, Phainon zones out and attempts to redo the math two times as Nysa leads them through the alleyways, making sure she walks off to the side or a few paces in front of them. He snaps out of the daze when she clears her throat, finally noticing they are standing outside the entrance to a small house. The door is wide open as Nysa stands a few steps to the side, waiting for them to go through first.

“Sorry,” he says, and tugs his friend forward.

“Go up the stairs,” Nysa calls after them, closing the door with a quiet thud.

Phainon follows the instructions, finding the staircase right as he walks into what looks like a living room. A cozy one, with a couch and fireplace. They walk up, his friend’s eyes attentively surveying every single object with wide eyes. Their surroundings might be a little overwhelming for him, but at least it takes his mind off the stranger accompanying them. Phainon will take that over, worrying about the hostility.

The stairs lead them to a very small hallway with one door. Phainon figures she wouldn’t have told them to go up if she didn’t want them to go in, so he turns the doorknob and pulls the boy inside. The lamplight shining through the window is enough to reveal the desk set up right in front of it, the bed pushed to the right of the door, a set of dressers, and another door to the left. It’s pretty barren of anything personal.

They step further in, and Phainon tries to let go of the boy’s hand now that they have reached their destination, but his friend refuses to let him, keeping an iron grip on Phainon’s fingers. Well. It’s not like he minds that.

“It used to be my son’s room,” Nysa suddenly says from the doorway and turns the light on, bathing the room in a warm glow. Phainon’s friend immediately goes back to high alert, visibly tensing and glaring at her as he tries to push Phainon behind himself. Is it because she is blocking the exit? Nysa pretends not to see the reaction, continuing with a smile, “The bathroom is right there. Feel free to use it while I go get some food from my friend; he is a much better cook than I am.”

“Thank you,” Phainon nods in gratitude. A bathroom. A real bathroom. Phainon hasn’t felt clean in what feels like years. He completely forgot he might get that luxury again if they find civilization.

“Take your time.” Nysa waves as she leaves, leaving the door open. Phainon doesn’t know whether it’s because she doesn’t trust them or if she wants to ensure they don’t feel trapped in here.

He doesn’t really care.

Eagerly, he heads to the other door and pulls it open, easily finding the light switch and flipping it on. He blinks at the tiny room, his friend looking over

his shoulder with curiosity, once again slightly more relaxed now that it’s just the two of them. Phainon hasn’t seen plumbing in so long. He thought he would have missed it more, but honestly, he has grown used to not having any access to it by now. Though nothing beats taking a proper bath or a shower. He would exchange anything to be able to take one at least once a week on their travels.

The bathroom is tiny with a slightly slanted ceiling. It has a toilet, a sink with a cabinet below, a mirror hung above it, and a bathtub. While the two of them might navigate around each other relatively easily, Phainon has the impression that any adult would struggle not to bang their head or limbs on everything. A bit hesitantly, Phainon pulls the door shut to give them some privacy in case the lady comes back before they’re done.

“We have to take our clothes off,” he says to his friend and sighs when it garners no reaction, their fingers still tightly intertwined with no sign of letting go. Right.

With his free hand, Phainon tugs the collar of his shirt up until he can pull his head out of it, and then awkwardly angles his free arm to wrangle it out of the sleeve, making the shirt rest in a bundled shape on his other shoulder. He shakes it pointedly and looks down at their joined hands before glancing back up to meet the golden eyes. It’s very clear there’s only one way this can work.

Very reluctantly, the boy drops his hand. Phainon quickly lets the shirt fall, and before his friend can grab hold of him again, he tugs his shirt up as well, gesturing for him to take it off. Soon enough, their clothes are lying in a heap by the door, and Phainon is letting warm water fill the bathtub, keeping his hand in it to test the temperature as the boy leans against his side. The way he is supervising the entire ordeal reminds Phainon once more of a cat. He smiles a little at the comparison. The fear of water fits as well.

Once Phainon estimates the water should come up just about to their waists if they sit down, he turns the tap off and steps inside, steadying himself on the boy’s shoulder so that he doesn’t slip on the wet porcelain. It’s a bit hotter than he would usually enjoy, but he figures his companion might

appreciate it more this way. His body temperature has always seemed to be much higher.

Slower and slightly anxious, his friend follows Phainon’s lead. He grabs Phainon’s shoulder roughly when water covers his feet entirely, but he endures it quietly, shuffling away to the other end of the bathtub and sitting down, mirroring Phainon’s position.

It doesn’t escape Phainon’s notice that he is trying to keep some sort of contact between them at any given moment. Even now, his foot nudges against Phainon’s, resting firmly against his ankle. Is it stress? Because they are in a new place, stuck within four walls, unlike ever before? Or because of the prospect of new people, maybe. Is he afraid that something will happen again?

Phainon can understand. Whether it’s any of those reasons or something else entirely. He felt the exact same way in the forest. And a little bit right now as well. Even if he logically knows this town should be safe and no one normally would wish to harm them, he still wants his friend as close to him as physically possible. He doesn’t want him anywhere out of his eyesight. What if they get separated? Would they be able to find each other again? What if the boy decides to leave, and Phainon ends up on his own again? There is so much they can still do and see together, Phainon doesn’t want that to end.

So, yes. He doesn’t mind the touch. Welcomes it, in fact, as it eases his own layered anxiety.

Phainon rakes his eyes over the edge of the bathtub next to the wall, a flat surface on which several bottles are resting. There is some dust on them, but it’s still easy to make out the words on the labels. He hums as he finds the most suitable thing to add to the bath, squeezing out some of it and letting it mix with the hot water.

He allows himself to relax for a moment, feeling his muscles gradually lose the tension. He doesn’t realize his eyes have slipped shut until his friend nudges against his leg, and Phainon hums in question, blinking at him.

The boy swipes his hand over his eyes and tilts his chin a little.

Phainon shakes his head, not bothering to try to stifle the yawn. “Later,” he says. He didn’t even realize he was so tired.

Right, they should get this over with soon. Nysa might come back any moment. Phainon starts washing himself with the water, scrubbing his arms and legs with his hands. Embarrassingly, his skin has already turned pink from the temperature. He isn’t even surprised when he looks over to see that his friend’s skin remains in the same exact shade it always had. So unfair.

His companion copies his movements, running soapy water over his own limbs, and Phainon nods in approval. While the boy is busy with that, Phainon picks up another bottle and pours some shampoo on his head, halfheartedly rubbing it into his scalp before he dunks his head into the bathwater to rinse the foam off.

When he resurfaces and rubs his eyes to get rid of the water before it can get past his eyelids, he sees the boy watching him skeptically. He obviously doesn’t enjoy the idea of submerging his head. And that’s fine. He will just leave his hair for last.

With a tired sigh, Phainon gestures for stay, and turns on the tap on a very low stream. He cups some water in his hand and quickly rinses off the soapy bath water from his arms, hair, and back, then stands up and does the same to his legs, and turns the tap off before the level of water can rise too high and make the boy panic.

It’s only once Phainon steps out of the bathtub, dripping onto the tiles, that he realizes he missed one crucial detail before they started bathing at all. Towels.

Groaning, he crouches down and rummages through the cabinet, glad there isn’t enough space in the bathroom for more cabinets to hide things in. He produces a very large towel and wipes himself off, leaving the towel in the sink when he’s done.

He then calls his friend over to sit down in the tub by the tap and grabs the shampoo bottle, kneeling on the ground. It’s quick work to squeeze out more of the liquid and lather it into his friend’s hair, taking care to angle his head back so that none of the product drips into his eyes. His hair is so soft. It darkens when wet, but the gradual shift from blond to red looks as pretty as ever.

Phainon guides the boy’s head lower and turns on a bigger stream of water to properly rinse out the shampoo, tangling his fingers into the strands to make sure the water runs through the scalp as well. When he is done, he pulls the plug from the tub so that the water can drain from it, and leaves the tap running. He mimics what he was doing earlier and points to the tap, so that his friend will know to also get rid of the soap residue before leaving the bathtub.

Phainon goes to sit down on the toilet to wait there, but a concerned noise from his friend has him backing away and returning to the bathtub, sitting on its edge instead. Same thing, but slightly closer.

He focuses on breathing, head blissfully empty of any thoughts for once. Just heavy exhaustion. He gets up only when the boy steps out of the tub, grasping the towel and grinning a little as he throws it over his head. It slips down a little, and golden eyes glare at him weakly before he gets to drying himself off as well.

That taken care of, Phainon leans down to pick up their discarded clothes, feeling a bit dizzy as he does so. They aren’t the dirtiest they’ve ever been, but they have only been washed in the river water so far. It feels wrong to wear them after getting so thoroughly clean, but Phainon is honestly beyond caring right now. He dresses sluggishly, missing the hole meant to fit his head about three times before he finally pulls through with a yawn.

Two minutes later, they are ready to leave the bathroom, dressed and mostly dry, the wet towel left behind to hang on the pipes. Sleepily, Phainon opens the bathroom door and slowly steps out, his friend’s shoulder brushing against his back.

And then, they both notice Nysa standing at the door, smiling pleasantly and pointing across the room to the desk.

Phainon almost smiles back as he looks over and finds two plates resting there, his stomach rumbling.

But his friend stumbles back in shock before he can head over to the food, apparently having forgotten that they are currently in an unknown territory with strangers milling around. Phainon turns around to face him just in time to see him bare his teeth at the woman, eyes wild and scared. Phainon shushes him gently and takes hold of his hand again, waiting until he calms down to pull him out of the room again.

Nysa only watches on with concern, but thankfully doesn’t comment. Phainon isn’t sure whether he can provide a convincing answer were she to ask. So, it’s a bit of a relief she leaves it be.

Phainon closes the door behind them with his foot and walks with his friend to the desk, picking the plate up and sitting on the desk’s surface with it on his lap to eat more comfortably. He would rather his companion sat on the chair, but he is definitely too high-strung and won’t turn his back on the woman watching them. So the chair is left empty, the boy not even sitting down like Phainon is, and instead staying on his feet as he takes the other plate.

He blinks at it sluggishly, noting the fried meat and potatoes. It’s basic. It makes Phainon’s mouth water within a second.

His friend makes a surprised noise off to his side, and Phainon watches as he chews, then glances up at Phainon with wide, shocked eyes before earnestly digging in. With the speed he is going, it looks like he is afraid someone might take the food away from him at any moment. Phainon is glad he could finally experience proper food. He hopes it won’t ruin their very bland options out in the wild for him, though.

Tiredly, Phainon sticks his fork into a potato and unceremoniously pops it into his mouth. Oh. Oh, he forgot how everything is supposed to taste.

“This is so good,” Phainon groans out with his mouth full. It’s been months since he last ate something seasoned, and the taste almost makes him want to cry.

“I will be sure to tell the chef you’ve enjoyed the meal,” she chuckles and only observes as they eat their fill. She looks like she wants to take a step forward to take the plates once they are done, but seems to think better of it, only shrugging to herself. “Don’t worry about the dishes. They won’t run away, will they? You boys should definitely get some rest now.”

“Thank you,” Phainon says for what feels like the hundredth time as he sits down on the bed, his friend following suit even as his eyes don’t leave Nysa. He doesn’t look openly hostile now, at least. “Have a nice night as well.”

“Oh, thank you. That’s sweet of you,” she gushes and finally turns the light off before exiting the room, closing the door behind herself this time.

The bedroom falls into complete darkness, the lamppost outside the window turned off as the Parting Hour must have gone past. The only source of light is a dim, pale shade thrown their way by the moons.

Phainon slumps onto the small bed and lets out a long exhale. Slowly, he rearranges himself so that he can lie down properly, and feels his friend climb up a little higher, too.

Now they can finally sleep in peace.

Well, not exactly.

Some hours later, Phainon gives up the idea of being well-rested for the first time in ages.

The boy is overly vigilant, sitting stiffly in bed with his back pressed firmly against the wall and staring tirelessly into the door. Phainon’s exhausted brain supplies that he is definitely feeling cornered, stuck in the room. The

sea didn’t have a single thing obstructing his field of vision. The forest was open enough, easy to hear and spot a threat once it was approaching. The bedroom has four walls that lock them away from the world, but deprive them of seeing or hearing anyone who could come to them.

His behavior, in turn, makes Phainon way too anxious to fall into a deeper sleep. He dozes off a few times for the scant few minutes, always waking up and turning restlessly before the process repeats. It’s even more tiring.

For a moment, Phainon wishes he could live like this.
