“Agh. Forget I said anything,” Euterpe mutters under her breath, lifting her hand up to rest it against her forehead tiredly. “Not my business unless you stay.”

Phainon only shrugs. She is a little weird, but at least she’s kind. And not boring. She played a game with them just the other day, revolving around hand gestures. It didn’t go perfectly since none of the rules could be easily explained to the boy, but it was still fun. She asks a lot of questions, though.

But Phainon appreciates any conversation he can be a part of. As amazing as his friend is, he won’t be of much help once they move on.

“You’re not thirty anymore, Euterpe,” another by-now-familiar voice reaches them, and Phainon looks to the left to see Gavriil approaching them, hands in his pockets. “Get up from the ground.”

“Excuse me, I feel twenty and not a day older,” Euterpe protests, performatively brushing her hand through the dark locks and sticking her nose high in the air.

“It’s almost like you never grew up,” Gavriil says, letting out a short laugh as he comes to a stop.

He reaches out to her with his hand, which she accepts after rolling her eyes briefly. “I’m young in spirit.”

Without warning, she is quickly pulled up to her feet and then unexpectedly twirled around. She yelps in surprise as she is spun, but it grows into a louder, pearly laugh until Gavriil stills them both, and she rests against his chest.

“Not thirty anymore, huh?” She asks a little breathlessly, looking up at him with a grin.

Gavriil hums noncommittally. “Never said it was a bad thing.”

Euterpe shakes her head and pulls away, brushing dust and dirt from her clothes. “What are you doing here?”

“Nysa asked me to fetch the children and walk them home. She won’t make it tonight, something about appeasing a Lord of sorts.”

“Those types are always so entitled,” Euterpe exhales deeply, her demeanor dimming a little. She shakes herself out of it quickly, clapping her hands in Phainon and his friend’s direction. “You heard the man, boys. Stop daydreaming and get going. We’re gonna grab some food on the way.”

Phainon just barely stops himself from whining about staying for a little while longer. It’s so entertaining to watch them interact. The only thing Phainon and his companion can do in Nysa’s house that adds some novelty is to take a super-long bath. As relaxing as it is, it’s nowhere near as interesting. And his skin gets pruny.

He squeezes briefly around the boy’s ankle and then gestures to him once he looks up at him, Let’s go.

His friend nods once, and they both slip off the bench, ready to make their way back.

“Are you sure it’s okay that we won’t be able to pay you back for everything?” Phainon asks at the mention of food. He’s been thinking about it for the last few days. His mom definitely wouldn’t have approved of taking advantage of someone’s hospitality without returning the favor. He

wouldn’t want to disappoint her. “It’s not much, but I can at least give you the—”

“Don’t worry about it,” Gavriil says, sending them a small smile. “We can afford it for two weeks. Nysa’s own kid is all grown up and off to make a name for himself in the big world. The two of us don’t have any children of our own, so it’s easy to pitch in, see what we missed out on.”

“I would have adopted you two if I could,” Euterpe nods along with a very serious expression.

Phainon cannot stop the grimace from forming on his face. “Um. I appreciate it?”

Gavriil bursts out laughing while Euterpe gapes at him in shock.

What? She is fun and all, but— he just doesn’t see it. Maybe if Nysa said it. If they weren’t set on course.

“At least pretend you’d like the idea!”

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

“But I don’t have anything else to exchange for it,” Phainon repeats for probably the eighth time, and it’s almost petulant by now.

Almost. He is not whining.

But it must have been an hour since they found the little store selling relics, as the small sign above the door proudly proclaimed. Phainon was already interested through that word alone, captivated by the idea of an item that survived through the hardships of its era. All of the things set out on the tables and shelves look sparkly and incredibly old at the same time. There

must be so many histories connected to them, and Phainon could spend day after day listening to all of them.

“Nothing I can do for you.” The man shrugs without any concern, leaning on the table that serves as a counter. “Either you get me two hundred balance coins, or you dig through your little backpack for something pricier to barter with.”

Phainon groans. He has another bracelet, but he can’t just pay with both of them and leave himself with no means to pay for anything else in the future.

“It’s not a set. It’s just one armguard,” he argues back, latching onto any detail that might bring the price down. “Shouldn’t the cost be halved?”

He wasn’t intending to buy anything, but it’s the only item his friend seemed to show any interest in. It wasn’t a tough choice to purchase it. After so many small gifts collected and carefully stashed between their bags, he finally has a way to get something for him in return. He won’t just pass on it without giving it his all.

“Halved?” The man repeats incredulously, shaking his head in disbelief. “This comes from the nation of most glorious warriors. The craftsmanship of their armor and weapons is unparalleled across all of Amphoreus. I cannot just sell it at any price; it would be an insult to—”

“Why are you so stingy, Peros?” Gavriil’s tired voice rings through the small shop, and Phainon glances up to see him stepping closer to them until he stands right at his friend’s side. Phainon looks away once he makes sure the boy isn’t tensing up due to proximity. “They are just children. Shame on you, truly.”

The shopkeeper clicks his tongue and looks away. “I have to earn money somehow, don’t I?” He mutters under his breath. “Maybe my prices would be lower if the rest of you weren’t so uncultured and decided to buy things every now and then.”

“Maybe if you didn’t try to shove some bull—” Gavriil coughs suddenly, the words sharply cut off. Did he choke on spit when speaking?

“I’m telling the truth,” Petros defends himself, gesturing to the armguard in question with fervor. “Any relic appraiser would tell you there is no doubt about its origin. I am certain collectors would pay quite a hefty amount to obtain it.”

“Even if,” Gavriil says after a brief pause to inspect it. He appears not to necessarily believe that last sentence. “It’s small, intended for a kid. And, like Phainon said, just one of the two. Collectors won’t be interested in an incomplete set.”

Phainon nods eagerly, wholeheartedly agreeing.

The boy yawns, leaning against the table and possibly dying of boredom. Phainon can’t really blame him. He can’t even really follow the conversation, stuck waiting without any idea of what’s going on.

When Petros still doesn’t agree to lower the price, simply huffing in their direction, Gavriil sighs and looks down at them. “I can pay for you.”

“No,” Phainon shakes his head, not even having to think twice about it. “You are all already being very generous to us. This isn’t something we require, unlike the supplies. Besides, it’s a gift. I want to be the one to get it.”

It’s silent for a moment, and Phainon feels a flush spreading across his cheeks. Did he say something dumb?

“Such a noble heart,” Gavriil comments eventually, reaching out to ruffle Phainon’s hair. Phainon sees from the corner of his eye as his friend loses all traces of sleepiness and tracks the movement with full attention. Gavriil either doesn’t notice the wariness or doesn’t care. “And yet your own heart isn’t moved, Petros?”

“I can pay with that bracelet,” Phainon offers again, hoping maybe this time it will work. It hasn’t so far, but he is rather persistent.

Another moment of quiet as Petros seemingly tries to scrutinize them and figure out whether it’s worth it at all in one look.

“Oh, fine.” The man says through gritted teeth, staring at Gavriil pointedly until the man nods. “Give me that bracelet.”

“Thank you so much, Mister!” Phainon gushes with a grin, emptying his bag to dig through it and bring out the item.

He doesn’t feel any particular sense of sentiment toward it. It wasn’t his dad’s, or even his mom’s. He doesn’t remember Cyrene wearing anything like that either, so he couldn’t have taken it from her. It might have been one of the very few pieces of jewelry he owned.

It’s fine; he rarely wore them anyway. It was pure chance that he had them on when the village was attacked.

Maybe one day it will also become a relic. Some of the last remnants of Aedes Elysiae.

Then again, it couldn’t have been made there, so maybe not. It’s just something a person who left the village and came back to visit brought with them. It’s nothing significant. So, Phainon can part with it without having any regrets. It doesn’t have any real ties to Aedes Elysiae.

He looks away as he quickly slides it across the table’s surface.

There. It’s done now. He can’t get it back, and he will have a shiny armguard in exchange. It’s a fair deal. Actually, the armguard is probably worth much more than his bracelet if what they’ve been saying is true. That means he made a good decision. It could come in handy one day.

And if it’s really from the nation of warriors, then maybe it will bring them some much-needed luck with training to get stronger.

“It won’t be comfortable to sleep in it,” Phainon repeats for probably the sixth time, and it’s just pure exasperation by now.

The boy pretends not to hear him, not that it makes much of a difference when he doesn’t know what ‘comfortable’ is. Among some other things in

that sentence. The future tense, for one. His friend stubbornly gazes toward the ceiling, his arm stretched out away from Phainon.

It should be fine for one night. He didn’t want to take it off for the bath either. Tomorrow, though, Phainon will have to do something about it. He can’t just never take it off again. What if it grows attached to his skin?

Just for the sake of annoying him a little more, Phainon leans over his body and reaches for the armguard one last time. He only manages to brush his fingers against the golden surface of it before a thin arm snakes around his body with an incredibly tight hold, rendering him unable to move up in the slightest. Sort of like the world’s most forceful hug.

“Fine, fine,” Phainon mumbles with an eye roll, slumping on top of his friend. The boy huffs, keeping his arm still angled very much so away.

Phainon eyes the pattern etched into the metal, some symbols that resemble the sun. He saw similar ones in a textbook once. It’s pretty. And gold seems to suit his friend very well, adding some light to his usually dark attire and going well with his pale skin. The gold of the garment pales in comparison to his eyes, though. He would have looked good in that bracelet Phainon gave away as well.

Phainon feels a pang of regret in his chest, but chases it away as quickly as it comes. He got the armguard, and his companion is so happy with it that he refuses to take it off at all. It was worth it, and he would’ve done it again. Everything is worth it to see his friend so excited and happy about owning something.

When the arm around him loosens its hold a little bit, he rolls over to the other side completely, settling in between the wall and his friend, settling in to sleep. When he wakes up in the morning, the dawn pattern is printed into his shoulder where the boy must have pressed against with his forearm.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

“You really don’t want to stay, huh?” Nysa says softly as she crouches down beside them at the open gates. It’s the correct side of town, the one people usually arrive from.

She isn’t even a few meters away. Not even leaving one step’s worth of space between her and them. She is right beside them.

And the fact that his friend is as calm as ever fills Phainon with giddiness.

It was a very slow process, one which Phainon tried his best to help with. Nysa’s patience, understanding, and her warm presence held true even when the boy snarled at her when she got too close too quickly. She never once got angry or fed up. Always quick to back off and apologize, keeping her body language relaxed.

Phainon thinks one of the reasons he allowed Nysa within touching range so quickly was that she was always the one to put the plate filled with food on their table. The progress slowed down after that, and it took eight days before he allowed his guard to lower just a little, letting his eyes wander away from her figure even when she got close to them. No longer tracking every minuscule shift of her body. Two more days until he tugged on her robes and pointed at something with a tilted head and one gesture. Phainon translated it breathlessly, the boy completely unaware that Nysa wasn’t privy to their way of communication.

After that, he even let Gavriil and Euterpe considerably closer than before. He is still cautious but no longer so skittish, only giving them a warning glare instead of snapping his teeth if they get too close.

Small steps.

Still bigger ones than Phainon could have hoped for. He hopefully won’t have to worry too much once they reach their next destination. Wherever that might be.

Even for that reason alone, going forward sounds like a good idea. Once they leave, they will see more of the world and meet new people. His companion will realize that not all of them are bad, and that buildings mean protection rather than blindness, as he still seemingly itches to get outside as soon as he can.

Phainon looks at Nysa, adjusting the strap of his backpack.

She let her hair down today, grey streaks blending with the black strands seamlessly. Her eyes are regretful, like she wishes she could’ve done more. Concerned and asking them to reconsider.

“It’s not that we don’t want to…” Phainon trails off, glancing beyond the gates at the well-traveled path.

It would be good for them here, actually. For his friend. What’s one more week or two? Maybe a month? They would have a more stable schedule, and they could learn a lot as well. Phainon saw the town’s school, much bigger than the small schoolhouse they had in Aedes Elysiae. They could teach his friend to talk in there. And their food wouldn’t be bland anymore.

But Phainon has a goal that he must accomplish, and the sooner he starts on it, the faster he will be able to put it to rest. Once he is done, they can stay in some small and slow town, doing nothing but meaningless work and talking to locals. But there’s no time for that now.

He wishes he could ask the boy for an opinion. That he could give him a choice at all. If that’s what he wanted, Phainon would leave him behind in this small town even if it hurt a lot. Maybe they would have met again someday, bound by that prophecy. But without the ability to talk to each other, it would look like Phainon was abandoning him. He would never do that.

But instead, he is the only one who can make a choice. Either leave or stay.

And, selfishly, Phainon’s very core burns with the desperate need to get stronger and avenge his hometown. It’s his one goal that keeps him going,

the reason he is still alive. If he doesn’t do it, no one will. No one will remember his village, and no one will bring the cloaked figure to justice.

The town might be peaceful, but it won’t provide them with the means to achieve Phainon’s goal. And even without a thorough way to communicate, he has a feeling his friend also wouldn’t really wish to stay. He is restless as it is, always wanting to move, and with his eyes silently cataloguing their surroundings at any given moment. He wouldn’t have found enjoyment here.

They need to find a well-suited place, and maybe then they will stay.

Perhaps they should try heading to Okhema.

“It’s that you cannot be tied down to this place,” Nysa completes his sentence with an understanding, although somewhat sad smile. “There aren’t that many opportunities for you to improve as much as you want to, are there?”

Phainon smiles back easily. “We need the best training,” he says happily, “So that we can become the strongest.”

“Can’t you really stay even for a year?” Nysa asks again, though Phainon can see from her expression that she’s already expecting yet another refusal. “The way you’re going, you will deprive yourselves of any semblance of childhood. Would the world really end if you allowed yourself one year of respite?”

“We can’t,” Phainon replies. It comes out a little reluctantly, but he knows he won’t give in, as tempting as it is. He can’t.

“I cannot force you,” Nysa says as she inhales deeply. “At least you accepted both of the new backpacks without any fuss, along with the supplies. Come visit if you’re ever passing by, you hear me?”

“We definitely will,” Phainon promises easily. He doesn’t intend to ever be anywhere near the Sea of Souls again, but if they somehow end up in the

area, he will drag his friend over again. “Thank you so much for everything you’ve done for us.”

“It’s no trouble,” Nysa waves him off with a warm grin. She gets up and presses her hand against the top of Phainon’s head, then does the same to his friend before she shoos them away. “Now, get going before Euterpe gets here and decides to kidnap you. I’m afraid Gavriil would aid her with it, and there wouldn’t be much I could do.”

Maybe it wouldn’t be the worst to have the choice taken from him.

But Phainon just laughs as he takes his companion’s hand and tugs him forward and out of the town through the large gates and onto the well-traveled road. Many people must come in and out of this place.

Phainon glances back now and then as they walk, and each time he glimpses the figure of the woman still standing in that place, watching as they move away from the safety of Nysa’s town. She gets smaller and smaller until she’s just a tiny dot, and Phainon cannot be sure whether it’s actually her or if she has already left to attend to her duties.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

And so, they continue traveling.

With great relief, Phainon finds the open wilderness to be much less stressful than the dense forest. Less chance of someone sneaking up on you. And not as dark, with all the stars shining directly above. The food Nysa forced into their backpacks until they were almost bursting open lasts them for about two weeks, carefully rationed by Phainon. And then it’s back to the bland meats with berries in between. If they find any. He is glad Euterpe took the time to help him memorize which ones are edible.

During the next two months or so, they make their way through two villages.

They stay for a week in the first one, old ladies fawning over them and how brave they must be to venture out on their own like this. They give them food and get angry at any attempts of refusal or repayment, claiming young boys need their stomachs filled to grow tall and strong. Some men give him advice on catching prey and teach both of them how to throw knives properly. Phainon has to work hard to convince them that yes, they definitely aren’t too young and no, they aren’t going to hurt themselves.

They leave with two new throwing knives in their possession. And if Phainon slices his finger open trying to spin one of them right after they resume their journey and needs to keep it wrapped in a strap of cloth for a little while, that’s none of their business.

People aren’t as friendly in the second village. They watch their every move with wariness, barely speaking a word to them, even as Phainon tries his best to grin at them and make harmless conversation. They don’t offer any food, and when Phainon offers to work for it, they turn him down. Almost out of spite, Phainon plans to stay a little longer and try to make them warm up to him. The plan falls through when one person threateningly raises their hand against his friend when he bumps into something, and Phainon barely manages to restrain him in time from retaliating. Suffice to say, the boy doesn’t allow for there to be less than ten steps of distance between him and any person in the village after that.

In the end, they leave after just four days with empty stomachs. That is, until his companion produces an entire roll of bread out of his backpack, a few minutes' walk from the village. Phainon doesn’t even try questioning how he got it. Maybe when Phainon was trying to argue his way into using a bathroom with a stall owner at one of the houses.

But even with that unpleasant experience, it’s still nice. Peaceful.

He tries to ignore how the last time he felt settled, reality ruthlessly crashed down on their heads.

Phainon still refuses to sleep with a fire burning beside them. The only reason he never ends up staying awake for the better part of the night to keep watch is that his friend seems to spring awake at the tiniest of sounds. They develop more gestures as time goes by, and Phainon teaches the boy how to pronounce some of the simpler words. It’s a slow process. Thankfully, they aren’t in a hurry. The boy rarely speaks unprompted, but Phainon finds that he seems to have figured out how to say some words on his own.

“What if we just,” Phainon muses, mindlessly tearing the cooked bird into pieces, “Gave up? Find a corner somewhere and stay. Like that first town, or the friendly village. Or somewhere completely remote? We could hunt nearby and maybe plant some stuff.” He pops a part of the thigh into his mouth and chews loudly. “I could teach you to talk in sentences. And write. Read, too. We could get some books? My mom used to read a lot to me. I could read to you as well.”

Phainon daydreams about the idea a lot. Picturing all the things they could do and learn together. Wondering if, with time, he would have forgotten about getting revenge, if maybe it would stop hurting after a while.

He looks up, and the golden eyes are already set on him. The boy lies on his stomach, chin propped on his forearms as he blinks at Phainon lazily. He still listens attentively to every word, like he is trying to figure out the meaning, regardless of everything.

His friend is strong. Phainon finds himself admiring him, just a little. Everything they went through, everything he must have gone through on his own before Phainon came along, and yet he doesn’t even seem to mind. Sure, he is also tormented by nightmares, thrashing in his sleep and choking on empty air until Phainon gently wakes him up. But he doesn’t seem anxious, not like Phainon is. Doesn’t carry whatever scarred him so thoroughly in every step he takes.

Or maybe it’s ingrained in him so deeply that it just seems normal to him. It’s not any better. Worse, even.

“It would be nice, wouldn’t it?” Phainon trails off with a small smile. He sighs and allows himself to fall onto his back, staring up at the stars. He remembers exactly one constellation and cannot even locate it. “Pity we can’t do that.”

If they decided to stay in a place like that, they would never get stronger.

And it would be fine, probably. Phainon thinks he could get used to it with time. To the idea of living for the sake of living, and doing his best to forget the bloodied past. He could do it if he had someone to help him through. And, and his parents would have probably wanted him to have a peaceful life. As supportive as his mom was of his dreams, she always tried to convince him to choose something safer. What if Nysa was right?

But then, Phainon wouldn’t be able to get his revenge for the demise of Aedes Elysiae. That’s the only reason he is moving forward at all. Why he hasn’t gone back to that village and let the monsters take him back to his family. He cannot let everyone’s deaths be for nothing, forgotten. He cannot.

And they would never find out about the boy’s origins. There might be a person who knows more about him, somewhere. If they keep going, they might stumble on them. If not, then there will surely be someone who could help once they reach Okhema.

So, they cannot give up. For both of their sakes.

“You sleep?” A quiet question coming from his side.

Phainon’s eyes snap open, not having even noticed when they slipped shut. He blinks at his friend in confusion, finding him staring expectantly.

The verb’s form isn’t correct, but—

Phainon never even tried teaching him ‘you’ since it seemed a bit complicated to explain without words. How was he supposed to say it refers to his friend, but also any other person, and even Phainon himself, depending on the perspective?

Apparently, the boy picked up on it regardless. Probably from listening to Phainon’s endless talking and the conversations in settlements. Once again, he is strong. Smart.

“Not yet,” Phainon says back with a grin, shaking his head a little. He bites down on the meat still clutched in his fingers, now gone cold.

The boy nods, shuffling a little closer to Phainon and flopping onto his back as well.

Maybe they will get their peaceful life after it’s all over. But that’s still so far away that Phainon doesn’t think it’s even worth thinking about that much.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Of course, they are bound to reach another forest sooner or later. Phainon would have preferred to opt for the ‘never’ end of the ‘later’ option. Unfortunately, he is forced to face such an obstacle on the ‘sooner’ side of things.

As they stand at the tree line, stalling instead of going in, Phainon is tempted to just go around it instead. He does not want to be surrounded by trees again.

But the path that leads into the forest looks well-traveled, and the trees aren’t so close together. It appears that they will still be able to see their surroundings without a fire. They need to follow the road as best they can, because eventually, it will lead them to a city-state. There should be a lot of opportunities in a place like that. For work, learning, training, everything. Phainon is already almost eleven, just eight more months until then. They shouldn’t be wasting time like this anymore.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon picks the leaves off the trap they set up the day before, some bird cooing in protest of being held captive. Tough luck, they have to eat something other than the few kinds of berries Phainon knows to be edible. Birds are more work than they’re worth with how small they are, though, he hopes that the other tra—

“Who are you?”

The words are spoken with genuine curiosity. Nothing hostile or threatening, or anything that would warrant concern. But the way the voice sounds from right behind Phainon has him startled, like he hasn’t been in a while. He didn’t hear anyone coming up to him, not to mention it should only be him and his friend around here.

He whirls around, unsheathing his sword and swinging it widely with his body’s momentum. He sees the person smoothly jump out of its way, blinking down at the weapon in surprise. It’s just some girl, giggling as she places her hands behind her back and leans forward with amusement.

“You barely know how to use that, don’t you?” She asks cheekily.

Over her shoulder, Phainon notices his friend stepping quietly in their direction, his eyes narrowed as he surveys the situation. He’s probably been watching since the start, deeming her not dangerous enough to immediately step in. Phainon has never been more glad that someone isn’t an adult.

Phainon gets up from the crouch, almost half a head taller than she is when he stands straight. She is thin, and her features are still very childish. “And how would you know?” He asks, some irritation at the words bleeding through. “You don’t look like you’ve ever even held a sword.”

The girl bursts out laughing at that, the sound high-pitched. She is a strange one. Phainon looks at his friend, finding him just as perplexed as he is. Though he is more likely wondering what they’re talking about.

“Sure,” she says with a snort once she calms down. Her eyes are glinting when she looks up at him, not one bit intimidated by their size difference. “Wanna find out?”

Huh?

Phainon tilts his head at her in confusion. “You want to... fight me?”

“Yep,” she grins, popping the ‘p’. “It’s gonna be funny.”

She looks kind of frail, like she would break in half if Phainon miscalculated and hit her a little too hard. He doesn’t think it would be very funny. She doesn’t seem like she wants to do them any harm either.

“I don’t want to hurt you,” he tells her, a little concerned. “Do you even have a weapon?”

She giggles again and shakes her head, barely able to contain herself, as if it’s the funniest thing she’s heard in months. “Maybe worry about yourself,” she replies, and her eyes are sharp when she glances at him again.

Well...

It should be fine, right? She seemed quick enough on her feet, and Phainon will just pull back if it seems like she’s out of her depth or something. It’s not like it’s a duel to the death. If she’s here all by herself, it means there must be a settlement nearby. Even if she gets hurt a little by accident, help shouldn’t be too far away.

“If you are sure...” He trails off, still uncertain. He resigns himself to this when she only nods eagerly in response.

Fine, then.

Phainon’s eyes meet his friend’s once more. He is a little tense, watching the exchange with focus and ready to follow Phainon’s lead. The girl’s behavior might not betray anything hostile so far, but the boy remains cautious as he always does.

With golden eyes pinned on Phainon and waiting for a sign, Phainon ignores the way the girl steps to the side and turns to watch them curiously. He quickly points between himself and the girl, taps the hilt of his sword twice, then brings his palm up and pushes it to the ground. We’re going to fight, stay there. He follows it with a smile, trying to convey it’s a friendly fight.

The boy looks the girl up and down, then raises his eyebrows at Phainon. He glances at the girl one more time, and his gaze only turns all the more doubtful. You sure?

Phainon rolls his eyes. What’s there to be worried about? Still, for good measure, he points to his friend, then taps the sword again and shakes his head firmly. Don’t fight.

He gets a slightly uncertain look at that, but the boy only makes a quick circle next to his right eye. I’ll watch. Then he slouches down, less alert and ready to get involved at a moment’s notice than before. His eyes are still keen, though, signaling he will insert himself into the situation if he spots one wrong move.

“Okay,” Phainon says aloud, directing his attention back to the girl. “We can fight now if you still want to.”

“What was that?” She asks, her eyes jumping between the two of them with interest.

Well, uh, Phainon assumes she could understand most of it. The gestures are pretty self-explanatory, in his opinion. By now, though, he is so used to them that he forgets people don’t actually communicate in such a roundabout way daily.

“I just told him not to attack you when we fight,” Phainon explains, scratching the back of his head. Probably saved her life with it, too. If his companion didn’t know what was going on and saw her attack him, Phainon suspects the crimson crystals would make a reappearance.

“Couldn’t you just, I don’t know, talk?” She prods further, squinting at the boy as if she could find what’s wrong with him through that alone. “Is he mute or something? Deaf?”

“Doesn’t know Common,” Phainon elaborates with a sigh. Well, he knows a few words and has a good grasp of the tone, but that doesn’t matter much. There is nothing wrong with him physically as far as Phainon is aware, except for the inability to die.

“So you communicate with, uh, hand signs? That’s actually cool,” she puts her weight on the heels of her feet, a little lost in thought. “Where is he from? Must be pretty secluded not to know Common.”

A star led me to him.

He was stranded in the Sea of Souls.

Both are true, but Phainon has a sneaking suspicion that if he said either of those to her, it would only lead to some uncomfortable questions he isn’t willing to answer. And ones he doesn’t even have answers to.

“Dunno, we met randomly out in the wild,” he settles on with a shrug. “It was a little rough at first, but eventually we figured it out.”

She nods like that’s exactly what she thought. She looks his friend up and down as well, similar to how the boy searched her with his gaze before, and purses her lips. After a few seconds, she turns with her back to Phainon’s companion and grins at him again, even more determined than before.

“So, can we fight now?”

Phainon exhales with mild disappointment. At the back of his mind, he hoped she would get distracted enough to forget.

Instead of responding verbally, he assumes the proper stance. The girl nods in satisfaction. And then, without a warning. She moves.

It’s over embarrassingly fast.

Phainon will insist it took an entire minute at the very least, even though it feels like it couldn’t be more than thirty seconds before he hit the ground, the sword knocked out of his hand.

The boy makes his way over as well, so now two heads are looking down at him and biting their lips to not smile or laugh as he stares blankly at the dark sky peeking through the treetops. Great.

The girl’s lips part to say something, but her face scrunches up immediately, and a rough cough comes out instead. She bends over a little, covering her mouth as her body trembles with the force of it.

His friend reaches down with his hand, offering it to Phainon. With a sigh, Phainon takes it and lets himself be pulled to his feet. The hand squeezes lightly before letting go, and Phainon is treated to a very amused gaze and raised eyebrows. Really?

Phainon huffs and juts his chin out a bit. Leave it.

He does get a small smile for that, so he cannot be too angry or embarrassed at being bested like that. What is it, about the sixth time he saw his friend smile at all? He will gladly fall back down onto his butt again if it means he smiles more. It’s a nice smile.

The girl’s coughing fit ends then, and she breathes heavily for a few more seconds before she straightens up, eyes a little reddened from the force of it.

“You alright?” Phainon asks, a little worried. He didn’t get a single hit on her, but is she perhaps sick? Should they walk her back home?

She clears her throat, placing one hand on her chest and rubbing it lightly. “Yeah, I’m fine.” Her gaze turns back to teasing after a beat, as if nothing happened. “Still worried about hurting me?”

“Where did you learn to fight like that?” He grumbles at her, stepping away to pick up his sword. It is still a little humiliating. He is willing to bet his friend would have won that fight by sheer determination and brute force,

finesse or not. His reflexes are crazy fast. He would have avoided her quick attacks. Although it would have also definitely resulted in injuries. Or maybe she would have found a way to bring him down? She seems skilled.

“I’m Kremnoan,” she says, in a tone someone would say ‘duh.’ “My first toy was a sword. It would be shameful if some foreign boy could best me.”

“Kremnoan?” Phainon repeats, interest piqued. With sword in hand, he comes back to his friend’s side, thoughts racing.

Those warriors following the Titan of Strife that Cyrene used to tell him about—they were from Castrum Kremnos, weren’t they? The fortress that overflows with soldiers and signifies victory. It must also say something about their capability to train anyone if a fragile-looking girl like her can fight so well at such a young age.

A memory comes back to him of discussing that city-state in class. Phainon idly making plans to travel there for training once he is all grown up, only to completely forget about them.

Maybe... Maybe the two of them could stay there for a little while? Take a break from traveling and learn how to fight from experienced people. It would be a good start to get stronger. Even among fighters, there should be an adult who could help with his friend’s Common. Just a few months would be good for them.

“Can you take us with you?” He asks, making the decision. Yet again, he cannot ask his companion for an opinion. But he has a feeling he will like it there as well. He likes movement, and if Kremnoans agree to train them, there will be lots of it. Worst-case scenario, they will leave after a few days.

The girl is caught off guard by the question, but seems to recover fairly quickly. She considers them both much more carefully than she did before, and Phainon sends her a small smile while the boy stares back impassively.

Eventually, she only shrugs. “Sure.”

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 4: and settle there
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

“You invented your own language?” Ptolemy asks, eyes snapping between Phainon and Mydei. His knee jumps up and down a little, barely hidden by the low table they are sitting at.

“I wouldn’t go that far,” Phainon replies with an awkward chuckle. It’s hardly anything, a set of very simple gestures. There are so many things he has wished to say for months now, and couldn't.

Ptolemy levels him with a flat stare. “Language is the principal method of human communication. Ordinarily, it is assumed language is synonymous with speech, but that isn’t necessarily the case.” His fingers drum on the wooden surface. “Can you convey your thoughts and ideas to him?”

Chapter Notes

“Isn’t Castrum Kremnos a movable fortress?” Phainon asks as they walk, the girl leading them through the path visible only to her. “Why is it here?”

Is there anything of worth in the area? Phainon hasn’t bothered to inquire about that when asking for directions to the nearest city-state. From what he gathered during classes with Pythias, Kremnoans move only to wage wars. And, as far as Phainon knows, there shouldn’t be much beyond regular villages around.

“Oh. No. We, uh,” the girl scratches her head, not turning to face him. She is a few paces ahead, her steps almost as silent as his companion’s. “We aren’t really a part of Castrum Kremnos anymore. I barely even remember it. We are— it’s just a settlement, I guess. But we’ve been here for a while now, don’t worry.”

So, these people are not from Castrum Kremnos?

Is there a point in going, then? All he knows about Kremnoans is their fighting prowess. If the girl and her people aren’t that, then it might be a brief stay for Phainon and his friend.

Well, they could be training on their own, right? No need for the fortress with that. The girl is strong after all. Even if Phainon wishes to learn from the best. Maybe they could point them to the fortress then?

Alright, Phainon isn’t very keen on calling two people ‘the boy’ and ‘the girl’ in his head. One is already one too many. “Hey, what’s your name?” He asks, breaking the silence.

Quickly, she spins around on her heels to face them with a wide grin. “Hephaestion,” she replies, making an exaggerated bow without missing a step as she walks backward, left hand resting against her chest gracefully.

Her long hair flows dramatically in the air. The color is a very light brown, almost blond, highlighting the slightly darker shade of her glimmering eyes. Phainon never thought much of the brown color. It just seems a little boring to him. He always favored blue. It’s the color of his own eyes, which he inherited from his father, and the sky above the Dawn Device. It’s something peaceful and known to him, comfortable. The rich gold and red have been growing on him lately, making him think of fun, companionship, and safety. But the girl wears brown incredibly well, making it appear remarkable.

“I’m Phainon,” he offers back with a grin of his own.

Her eyes move to his friend with curiosity, only to be met with a blank stare. “Right,” she says flatly, gazing back at Phainon. “No name for him?”

Phainon fiercely misses the way Nysa pointedly did not ask.

“Well, he can’t exactly tell me his name,” he retaliates defensively. It’s not his fault that the boy probably doesn’t even have a name in the first place. Thankfully, Hephaestion doesn’t dwell on the details of it for long, or she

would have realized it means there isn’t another language the boy can speak.

“Then what have you been calling him?” She asks instead, avoiding walking into a tree with her back at the last second. Can she somehow see behind herself?

“Nothing,” Phainon admits quietly, looking off to the side.

Hephaestion’s eyebrows rise in something that might be judgment. “And you’ve been traveling together for how long?”

Phainon looks at his friend.

His hair is down to his shoulders now, red tips uneven and sticking up in places. He grew a little taller since they first met, reaching somewhere near Phainon’s forehead. He isn’t so thin that his limbs resemble sticks anymore, having gained some light muscle. They are the same build now, he and Phainon. With so much happening, it feels like it’s been ages. But no, a full year ago, Phainon was still running around Aedes Elysiae with his wooden sword, helping with some tasks and stealing pastries from his mom.

“Six months? More or less.”

“You two are so strange,” Hephaestion says under her breath and decides she’s had enough of looking at them, turning back to face the right way. Before Phainon can question what that’s supposed to mean, she continues, “What if he thinks his name is ‘hey’ or something now?”

“I don’t even say ‘hey’ to get his attention much!” Phainon protests, affronted.

“Do you whistle, then?” She calls over her shoulder with a barely suppressed giggle. “Is he a dog?”

“I did that, like, maybe twice—”

The conversation continues on for a little while until they eventually grow silent again. Hephaestion hums a quiet tune as she leads them forward. It

takes maybe fifteen minutes before they step out of the forest and see the houses scattered not so far away. Ten more to actually reach the settlement.

It’s larger than Phainon thought it would be, possibly bigger than the last village they went through. Aedes Elysiae was definitely smaller than this. There aren’t many people outside, and those who mill around the houses seem to be minding their own business, wrapping up their chores for the day. Weapons and shields are scattered at every step, with makeshift training dummies placed on fences and walls, set up at the center of the crossroads. They walk past what looks like a hornswine pen; the animals eating eagerly from their feeders.

It feels like a normal village, were it not for all the weaponry giving off an impression that an army may have passed through.

In the end, they follow the girl into one of the houses deeper into the center, the door creaking loudly as they step through. There is a short corridor with two doors on the right, and it gives into an open space that appears to be a small resting space connected to the kitchen. In the corner, a man sits on a chair that has seen better days, leaning forward with his eyes set firmly on a sword in his hands. He cleans it with practiced motions. As Phainon watches, he concludes that this man could, without a doubt, perform these motions deep in sleep.

“Dad,” Hephaestion calls with a smile in her voice, rushing to his side and poking him in the shoulder. “I brought guests. I found them in the forest,” she titters excitedly, almost jumping on her heels.

Her father frowns at the words, eyes rising and finding them across the room within a fraction of a second. Phainon smiles awkwardly and nods in greeting when the intense gaze settles on him, looking up and down as if trying to spot a threat.

Then, once it deems him harmless, it moves to his friend.

Phainon finds himself counting his own breaths to keep calm when the boy gets the same treatment, staring back attentively and slightly tense. He gets to three before the man’s grip on the sword changes. Hephaestion’s father

suddenly clutches at it so tightly his knuckles grow white, eyes widening significantly, and jaw slackening.

Phainon’s heartbeat quickens. Not again.

“Guests?” The man repeats after his daughter incredulously. “This boy just might—” He watches Phainon’s companion intently and, without taking his eyes off him, he cuts the sentence before it can go any further. Then he calls much louder, “Love, come here quickly!”

Hephaestion glances back at them with uncertainty, no longer so trustful and carefree, then addresses her dad. “Is something wrong?”

Phainon really, really doesn’t like where this is going.

He thought they would be welcomed, going by Hephaestion’s behavior. Maybe tolerated until they can prove themselves, going by what he’s heard about Kremnoan warriors.

Phainon isn’t the only one; his friend is also on high alert at the change in atmosphere. He takes one step closer to him, making their shoulders brush. I’m here. The boy’s furrowed brows soften just slightly, but he remains tense even as he leans back against Phainon.

Another set of doors groans as they are swung open, probably the back door, and a woman comes through the kitchen, wiping her hands on a stained shirt. “What is it?” She asks impatiently. She stops mid-step when she notices her partner’s expression and follows his line of sight. Then, she takes a step back as her eyes land on the boy. “This, could that be the— Did the Queen have any relatives?”

What?

Alarm bells go off in Phainon’s brain. What kind of question is that supposed to be? The Queen?

But before he can question it further and out loud, the woman begins moving toward them quickly. He instinctively pulls his friend back, placing

himself between him and the rest of the room. The boy might be more tolerant of people by now, but even he can sense something is off about this situation. Phainon doesn’t want to risk anything bad happening.

Hephaestion’s mom stops about two steps in front of them, crouching down. She doesn’t look as soft and kind as Nysa did. Her hair is bound tightly for practicality rather than style. And where Nysa’s wrinkles pointed at humor and laughter, this woman has a thin scar running from her nose and down her left cheek. And another one across her neck, as if someone tried to—

She simply looks intimidating, is what Phainon thinks.

“I don’t think so,” the man responds behind her with a slight shake of his head, even though his partner cannot see him. “Master Krateros was all she had, as I recall.”

One good thing is that the exit is right behind them. Just a short corridor and a closed door away. They can make a run for it if things go wrong, and they would probably be able to get away safely, all things considered. Phainon still remembers the way they came from. In fact, they could leave right now.

But it seems like those people might know something about the boy’s origins, and if it’s—

“What are you talking about?” Hephaestion asks before he can form a question in his head, irritated at being left out.

Her father looks at her with a conflicted expression, like he is unsure whether he wants to answer. Whatever it is, it cannot be that bad, can it? The boy is young; he couldn’t have done anything wrong to get them to hate him or something. Is it about what his parents might have done? It shouldn’t matter, then, should it?

“I think,” the woman starts slowly, gazing over Phainon’s shoulder and surveying his companion’s face with scrutiny. “I think this is late Queen Gorgo’s son, Crown Prince Mydeimos.”

Phainon almost reels back in shock when the words register in his brain. He does take one small step back, bumping into his friend.

His friend.

The Queen’s son.

Is Phainon friends with a prince?

For a moment, excitement runs through him like an electric shock. A prince? And now he has a name to finally call him by. Mydeimos. It’s a little long, and Phainon will have to get used to it, but he doesn’t care. It’s better than anything he could have ever thought of to call him by. It means someone took care to name him. That he won’t have to do it himself one day.

He always thought his friend was cool. He had survived all on his own in the sea for a long while, probably, and he learns so quickly. He is strong and tries to protect Phainon in his own way, and it feels like he would face the Titans and stare them down without fear, despite being so small. Phainon didn’t think he could become even cooler.

He doesn’t realize he’s started grinning in happiness until it falls with the realization that people might want to take Mydeimos away from him because of this. Being a prince must be a big deal, right? He is important to many more people now, not just Phainon. And they will all want to spend time with him, and they will probably take him to a castle or something. Where Phainon might not be able to follow.

And here Phainon thought he might have finally found someone who wouldn’t just leave.

“Where did you meet him?” The question is directed at Phainon, snapping him out of his thoughts.

Selfishly, he wants to turn back around and walk out. Keep the boy to himself and try to face the world together. It’s not like he understands what

they’ve been talking about. And Phainon finally has something to call him by, too. It— it wouldn’t be so bad.

“Um,” Phainon looks at his friend, finding him already staring back anxiously. Waiting for a decision to be made, a flight-or-flight response delayed until Phainon makes a sign of any sort. He, Mydeimos, deserves better. Doesn’t he? He should have more people taking care of him, keeping him safe, and teaching him things Phainon would never be able to. Maybe they will allow Phainon to stay for a while, too. “The Sea of Souls.”

A quiet gasp from the mother. Phainon sees something like pity in her eyes when he shifts to face them all again. As much pity as those hardened eyes can allow for.

“Hephaestion,” the father calls, “Go fetch Lady Archidamia and tell her of this. Make sure she brings Lord Dametrius and Lord Savvas. Quickly.”

“But—”

“Now.” He doesn’t raise his voice, but the authoritative tone has her complying immediately regardless, all traces of protest gone like a switch flicked.

She runs out of the house on quiet feet, the door left cracked open.

If he grabbed his friend’s arm and they—

No.

“Guess we’re staying for a while,” Phainon sighs, shaking his head a little. He still isn’t entirely sure about this, but he supposes they can always sneak out when no one is looking. Probably. “Um, could you tell me a bit more?”

The man finally gets up from his seat and gestures to the chairs. “Come sit; we will try to shine some light on the situation for you. It’s going to take a while once those three get here.”

With only a moment of hesitation, Phainon nudges Mydeimos and inclines his chin a little. The boy nods, and they move toward the chairs, setting

their belongings down beside the furniture. His friend immediately pushes one of them closer to the other before anything else. The seats are a little high, forcing them to jump up to get on, feet dangling in the air as they settle. They sit close together, leaning against one another without a thought.

“He hasn’t spoken a word since you arrived,” Hephaestion’s mom observes, eyeing where their arms brush together. “Is something wrong?”

“He doesn’t know Common.” Phainon brings one of his legs up onto the seat to get more comfortable. “He understands some words by now, though. Why doesn’t he know Common?” He asks the question that has been bugging him for months now.

Because even toddlers learn it rather quickly. Parts of it, at the very least. He remembers Piso babbling incoherently for a bit, the sounds forming into some of the easier words rather quickly. Meanwhile, his friend didn’t have any knowledge whatsoever. There must be a specific reason.

“We did tell you we would elaborate on certain things.” The father looks to the ceiling briefly, already tired. When his eyes meet Phainon’s, they are filled with regret. “Prince Mydeimos was thrown into the very sea you found him in, no later than a week after his birth. Everyone thought him dead until now. If he hadn’t escaped its clutches before meeting you, I imagine there simply wasn’t anyone to teach him Common. Or anything else, for that matter.”

Phainon’s breath catches in his chest. He did think it might be a case, briefly. When he let his mind run wild as they sat together at the fire, making scenarios of his friend making the sea his own home. It was only out of boredom, really. He dismissed the idea right after, thinking it would be impossible for someone to spend their entire life all alone in the water. Too cruel. He clung to the idea that his companion might have been simply lost, fallen from a ship, and unable to get back to his family. Not discarded.

They say he is the Crown Prince. That means Mydeimos is important. Did no one intervene? Or look for him at the Sea of Souls? It’s a creepy place, but surely someone could have gone out immediately to get him back out?

“Why did no one save him?” He frowns at them, and now both adults look uncomfortable.

“We were forbidden to,” Hephaestion’s mother replies quietly, eyes downcast. “It would have been considered treason. No one dared to disobey the order. Much good it did us, exiled from Castrum Kremnos as we are, in the end.”

“But we will make it right,” the man continues in her stead, sounding determined. “Queen Gorgo was an excellent ruler, caring for us all equally, and prosperity came along with her ascension to the throne. We owe it to her to ensure her son grows up adequately. Lady Archidamia will know what to do.”

Too little, too late, Phainon wants to tell them. It won’t make up for the years spent in the sea. In the same way that Phainon won’t ever get his family back. No matter how hard he tries to improve and avenge them.

“How old is Mydeimos?” He asks instead.

Hephaestion’s father frowns a little, taking a minute to recall the old date. “He was born on the last day of the Month of Strife. He should have turned ten by now.”

So, there are only three months between them. And here Phainon thought his friend would be younger by years. Two, at least. He did grow quite a bit after he began eating regularly, no longer so thin and small. But the initial impression got cemented in Phainon’s brain despite the changes.

Phainon doesn’t ask any other questions. He knows the two most important things: his friend’s name and age. Anything else can wait for now. There should be time to ask more things later, right? If he comes up with some good questions. There’s been a bit too much information to try learning more right now without becoming confused.

He still cannot get over the fact that the boy is a Crown Prince. Phainon would have never thought of that. What sort of nation loses its own prince? In all the stories he’s heard and read, people who are that important are

always guarded. Why was he thrown into the sea in the first place? Did his parents not care?

Phainon thinks back to his mom and dad. The laughter flowing through their house and the love in their eyes, warm hugs and kisses to his forehead, despite how he tried to duck away from them each time. His mom halfheartedly trying to convince him to choose a safer future, perhaps one where he doesn’t stray from home too far and for too long. His dad patiently teaching him new skills, always closely watching so he doesn’t accidentally hurt himself.

And what about Mydeimos? Did neither of his parents fight for him, wanted to keep him close? As the King and Queen, they definitely could have done something. It’s Castrum Kremnos, too. They must have been powerful.

On the spot, he decides he hates his friend’s parents.

Just as the thought forms, Phainon hears the door banging against the wall as it’s forcefully opened. Three people stride in with haste, Hephaestion silently following behind them.

The woman leading them has a presence like nothing Phainon has seen before. Hephaestion’s mother’s appearance suddenly seems gentle in comparison to hers.

She looks to be the oldest of the three as well; her hair dark grey and bound in a rigid bun, face littered with more scars than wrinkles. There is golden armor covering her forearms, shins, and stomach. Like she’s prepared to fight at any moment, rather than wind down in the late hours of the day. Her eyes narrow in calculation as she looks Mydeimos over, completely disregarding Phainon.

The man next to her, maybe just slightly younger than his companion, takes one look at them, expression faltering just slightly, and moves to talk with Hephaestion’s parents immediately.

The third person, a much younger man in glasses, isn’t as callous. His gaze jumps between Phainon and Mydei, more like he is assessing them with a

vague degree of concern rather than blatant disinterest in their well-being.

Phainon sends him a thin smile, knocking his ankle into that of his friend as he observes Hephaestion migrating to the very corner of the room when no one pays any attention to her. She sits down by the wall with her legs crossed, eyes sliding over every person in the room with concentration. She listens to every word as the adults start talking among themselves, not even trying to ask them questions. Phainon can guess why.

He tries to follow her lead at first. What they are talking about is important; it concerns his friend’s future.

Unfortunately, as they argue about what to do with their freshly recovered prince, and consequently ignore Mydeimos and Phainon’s presence at all, his mind starts to wander. They don’t seem curious about where they came from, not like Hephaestion’s parents. There is no relief or happiness. Just cold facts on who Mydeimos is and how that changes everything.

“—curse of immortality, it can be of—”

Phainon hums at the words, kicking one leg back and forth in the air. He almost wants to thank the Titans for that curse. It sounds more like a blessing to him, actually. Neither of them would be sitting here now if it weren’t for it. His friend being unable to die means he shouldn’t be affected by Phainon sort of bringing disasters along with him, right? He won’t leave Phainon.

If, at the very end, they are the last two standing, Phainon would be alright with that. Probably. As long as the cloaked figure is killed, he will be happy. And if his friend is there with him.

He hopes Mydeimos will decide to help him in that quest once the time comes. But even if not, Phainon will definitely be able to do it by himself at that point. And then he will come back to his friend, and maybe they will live peacefully after that.

Phainon would like that very much.

“—needs education. We ought—”

Will they teach him to talk in full sentences? Phainon cannot wait to converse with him properly. Well, he doesn’t exactly mind what they have right now. They can read each other; words aren’t so necessary. And they can still use the signs. They could even make more of them once his friend learns, and Phainon won’t have to struggle so much to convey the meaning.

They will teach him even more than just speaking, won’t they? Maybe Phainon will be allowed to ask some questions as well. He needs to find out more about the Titans and Chrysos Heirs.

“Come off it, Dametrius. Sufficient training will—”

Perhaps going along with Hephaestion was the best decision Phainon could have made. They will be cared for here—or at least Mydeimos will be—and there must be capable people around. If Phainon convinces them he should stay around, they could both improve together. Learn to fight side by side, be unstoppable.

It’s an exciting prospect.

Who better to train them than the Kremnoan army? They follow the Titan of War. There is no way they aren’t the best at fighting and teaching how to fight. Even if they’re not in Castrum Kremnos itself, that one lady looks like the strongest person to ever exist. They will want their prince to be the best of the best, and Phainon will make sure to keep up. Surpass him, even.

“—a kid, what about King Eurypon and—”

The older man points at them aggressively without even looking over. Phainon rests his head on his friend’s shoulder and closes his eyes just for a moment. It’s all so boring. They don’t seem to care whether he has any opinions anyhow.

He quits attempting to think, the words turning into white noise. He falls asleep without meaning to.

Phainon jolts upright, his arm jerked roughly to pull him back into consciousness. He blinks his eyes open sluggishly, immediately landing on the boy’s face. He must have been the one who woke him up, fingers still loosely wrapped above Phainon’s elbow. He doesn’t spare a look at Phainon. Instead, he is staring straight ahead at the people surrounding them. His gaze flutters between the adults with caution, never settling on one figure for too long.

Anxious with all their attention on them, waiting for Phainon to take charge.

“What?” Phainon asks through a yawn, directing it to no one in particular.

“We will resume tomorrow,” the scary woman informs him in a voice so stern that it tells him any interruption will result in punishment. That tone almost fires up the instinct to open his mouth and argue with her regardless. His gut tells him to keep quiet, though. “Young Lord cannot speak, can he? Starting tomorrow, there will be lessons to remedy that. There isn’t any time to waste.” The man in glasses nods beside her, clearly invested in their prince’s education. “We extend our gratitude to you for discovering him and guiding him to us. You may stay as long as you wish. You are welcome to sleep here, but we ought to take Lord Mydeimos to appropriate quarters, which will belong to him from now on.”

So, they are already separating them?

Phainon bites his lip, looking back at his friend. The golden gaze now meets his steadily, fingers squeezing his arm once before letting go. A reassurance of sorts. He can probably sense Phainon doesn’t exactly enjoy where this is going.

What should he do?
