chapters.title: Chapter 6: and stain them crimson
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

"Was this worth your entire pay for the last three assignments?" Mydei asks flatly, eyeing the precious relic held in Phainon's arms. "We don't even get paid that much."

"You're a prince, they would buy the whole store if you asked," Phainon shoots back.

"Archidamia would sooner bury me alive herself," Mydei rolls his eyes.

Chapter Notes

Peucesta hums a soft melody as he gently directs Mydei around the kitchen. Phainon likes watching them cook. What he enjoys about the activity even more is the fact that Mydei cannot over-salt anything when he is mildly annoyed at Phainon. Not with Peucesta watching, or he might risk getting that silent, disapproving look.

Hephaestion fidgets next to Phainon, swiping hair back from his forehead with irritation.

It’s short now. Phainon initially felt a pang of regret at the sight, suddenly reminded of how Mydei’s hair was forcibly cut off a while ago.

Except this was done entirely at Hephaestion’s choice, apparently. The haircut now resembles Phainon’s in length. But where Phainon’s falls right into his eyes, Hephaestion’s parts in the middle, swept to the sides. If not for the fact that the loose light brown strands constantly attempt to stubbornly cling to his forehead. He had Peucesta cut it for him on the very day Perdikkas gave him that new medicine.

Both Mydei and Hephaestion have faces that are so pretty that any hairstyle would suit them. Mydei just a little more so, Phainon thinks, but Hephaestion hasn’t lost any charm due to this change either. Still pretty. Boy, girl, whatever. Does it matter?

It took an entire month to finally stop slipping up when talking about him. Perdikkas reassured Phainon and Mydei that it was perfectly normal and Hephaestion wouldn’t hold it against them, however long it might take to completely switch to using the correct pronouns.

By week two, Phainon found himself getting increasingly angry at every ‘she’ that fell from his own lips. He wasn’t doing it intentionally. Mydei clicked his tongue at himself each time, clearly just as frustrated. But they got there in the end. Thankfully.

Phainon glances across the table at Ptolemy, the teen engrossed in his book. He swipes his thumb over the corner every other second, feeling along the sharp edge. Phainon could try annoying him into chucking the book at them. But then Peucesta would be disappointed, and he doesn’t want that.

Phainon shifts in his chair to sit sideways, leaning against the table. Hephaestion has his legs bent and cradled close to his chest with one arm, eyes almost crossed as he continues to fight with his hair. He exhales harshly, tugging on it roughly. Phainon doesn’t like the expression on his face.

“How much longer do we have to wait?” Phainon whines, propping his elbow up on the surface and resting his chin on his palm.

Mydei glares over his shoulder at him. His eyes jump to Hephaestion as if on sheer instinct, and then back to Phainon. No longer glaring. He blinks twice. Phainon shrugs helplessly.

“About ten minutes,” he replies and turns back to the pan, nudging Peucesta.

“Don’t be ungrateful,” Ptolemy scolds halfheartedly, turning a page.

Phainon rolls his eyes, huffing. “I’m not,” he says, and stretches his leg out to kick at Hephaestion’s chair. “We had to eat the worst things ever back in the forest. I’m always happy with any food,” he mutters, digging his heel into Hephaestion’s hip and jostling him until he gets a glare much more annoyed than the one Mydei directed at him moments ago.

“Really?” Hephaestion asks with a sigh, clearly humoring him. “What did you eat, then?”

“Mostly birds, mice, and rabbits,” Phainon responds. He tried to eat a worm once or twice. Not the best experience.

“How is that bad?” Hephaestion asks with a small frown. “Rabbits are delicious.”

“Not unseasoned,” he replies, sticking his tongue out in disgust. He grew somewhat used to them in the end. He would no longer notice the taste. Or lack thereof.

“Rabbits?” Ptolemy repeats, and his eyes are fixed on Phainon when he looks over. “In the forest?”

“Yes?” Phainon tilts his head at him.

Ptolemy stares for a few more seconds. “Those were hares,” he says slowly.

Hares? What?

“Isn’t that the same thing?” He asks with confusion. They are, aren’t they? Phainon thought it was just a synonym.

Ptolemy inhales very deeply without taking his eyes off Phainon. He holds it in for a moment and releases it in a rush. “No,” he replies wholeheartedly.

It’s quiet for a few beats. Then, Hephaestion giggles. Success.

“You are so stupid,” Hephaestion says, changing his position to fold his legs underneath himself.

Phainon takes it back. All that effort just to be insulted.

“Hey,” he protests, now outright kicking his thigh. “You definitely didn’t know either!”

“Stop kicking me,” Hephaestion tells him, grabbing Phainon’s ankle and pulling on it. Phainon takes hold of the table in the very last moment, able to keep himself seated. Ptolemy quickly places his hand on the table as well, keeping it balanced when it starts shaking. “I did know.”

“Yeah?” Phainon yanks his leg back, and Hephaestion sways on the chair, letting go to steady himself as well. “What’s the difference then?”

“Of course I know the difference,” he says, raising his chin in an attempt to look down on Phainon. It only works because he is sitting on his legs. “It would be stupid not to know.”

Phainon wants to punch him, just a little bit. In a spar. “Well, maybe it’s yo —”

The large pot makes a thud as it’s placed in the center of the table, shutting him up. Phainon and Hephaestion instantly straighten up, glancing nervously at Peucesta. Unexpectedly, the incredibly unimpressed gaze is directed at Ptolemy.

“Oh, come on,” Ptolemy says immediately, a little sheepish as he finally puts his book away. “I couldn’t have stopped them. They were having fun.”

Mydei slips into the seat on Phainon’s other side, chair screeching for a second when he shuffles closer and then starts loading food onto their two plates.

Peucesta doesn’t talk much. Even less than Mydei—for now, because Phainon will get Mydei talking more if that’s the last thing he does—but he makes up for it with his ability to convey quite a lot of things with his eyes alone. It’s impressive. And effective.

Phainon picks up his fork and starts eating as Ptolemy attempts to give a more sufficient explanation of why he would let Hephaestion and Phainon fight when it’s not the time for sparring. Peucesta dislikes it when they keep arguing while eating.

Mydei leans forward a little to glance at Hephaestion around Phainon’s body. “You look good with this hairstyle,” he tells him with the plain sincerity of someone who only ever speaks the very thing that’s on his mind. Phainon, still chewing, points at him with his fork and nods in agreement.

He openly stares as Hephaestion freezes with his eyes wide, and some pink dusts his otherwise pale cheeks. Was he really this embarrassed by the haircut? Phainon doesn’t see why he would be.

“Thanks,” Hephaestion mutters and looks away, reaching out toward the pot to signal that’s the end of the subject.

Now, with a shy smile on his face.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

“You are so stubborn,” Mydei says, grappling with Phainon to keep him in place. “Can’t you just admit it?”

Ptolemy clicks his tongue, and Phainon can bet he is rubbing his forehead in frustration. “I am once again requesting that you cease the—”

“You are the one who started it,” Phainon hisses over Ptolemy’s voice, kicking Mydei’s shin away.

“Boys,” Ptolemy tries again, the word barely escaping through his gritted teeth. Hephaestion sighs somewhere at the back. “We have three chapters of history to cover today.”

“Do you want me to end it, too?” Mydei’s hand grips his jaw painfully, the cold metal of his gauntlet digging into the skin.

A worrying crack echoes as Ptolemy seems to have had enough. Mydei and Phainon raise their heads simultaneously to see the splintered wood of the nearby fence, stilling in their positions. Did he kick it?

“Sit down and hold your tongue as I bid you,” Ptolemy seethes, flush high on his cheeks from anger. It looks funny with his otherwise pale skin and blond hair. Like a tomato. Phainon feels satisfaction at witnessing someone else blush as thoroughly as he always does. “For if I once begin to lay my hands about you, though all heaven were on your side it would profit you nothing.”

It takes a beat, and then Mydei and Phainon are staring at one another blankly. Frozen as their argument is, momentarily forgotten in favor of expressing their utter confusion. What?

Phainon is one hundred percent certain that he and Mydei could actually take Ptolemy down in a fight. He knows the teen isn’t as useless as he claims to be, but he looks the opposite of threatening. Physically, at least.

He is about to say it, but Hephaestion’s loud groan interrupts him. “What have you done?” He puts his head in his hands in clear resignation. “Not the long quotes again.”

“What quotes?” Phainon asks and regrets it immediately when the upside-down image of Ptolemy gapes at him in bafflement. If it’s another long-winded lecture, he will be better off antagonizing Mydei until he knocks Phainon out. He wouldn’t do it if that meant he had to deal with Ptolemy alone, though, so that’s a lost cause.

“You didn’t even notice?” Hephaestion asks with disbelief. “It’s been years.”

“You haven’t read—” Ptolemy sputters out, then stops himself and grips his blond hair in frustration. “Cerces have mercy, I need to start assigning you

two some reading materials outside of what you are doing with me. I cannot believe I haven’t yet.”

“Uh. I can’t read,” Mydei says in an attempt to get out of it. It’s a lie; he is undeniably able to read. It takes him longer and requires more effort, but he can.

Ptolemy isn’t very impressed with the excuse. “You won’t get better unless you practice. This is a wonderful idea, actually.”

Is it too late to apologize and start behaving? Chances are that Ptolemy might forget about it once they dive into the material for the day. They are too busy to have to read books in their scant free time as well. They already come home just to wash very quickly and collapse in bed within minutes.

“Ptolemy, I was just going over to yours,” Perdikkas’ voice sounds from behind the teen, and Phainon breathes out in relief. Amazing timing. He comes around, stopping to blink down at Phainon and Mydei on the ground. “You’re all here?”

Ptolemy scoffs, kicking lightly at the dirt. “Guess who has the extraordinary pleasure of being assigned the babysitting duty to the dumbass trio over here?” He rolls his eyes, sullen. “Not Peucesta, let me tell you that. Lucky bastard.”

“Don’t lump me in with them,” Hephaestion protests, like he doesn’t instigate just as often.

“We don’t need babysitting,” Phainon says at the same time, words muffled as Mydei’s hand smashes his head into the ground, resuming their fight now that Ptolemy is distracted. Phainon almost bites down on the dirt by accident.

“Peucesta is too young to handle them,” Perdikkas says with amusement. Then, his voice grows into a more serious tone, “Hephaestion, no exertions for one week. You have three days left, don’t ruin it.”

“Why do you think I’m just sitting here?” Hephaestion replies sulkily and exhales dramatically. His voice sounds a little hoarse from how much he’s been coughing lately.

“Peucesta is just one year younger than us,” is Ptolemy’s retort. Phainon would be offended by how much he wants to get rid of them, but he might be partially to blame this time.

Phainon and Mydei watch Perdikkas approach Hephaestion and pat him on the shoulder. And along with that, Phainon finally manages to spin Mydei around to be on top of him, straddling his thighs. Ha, take that. Mydei jabs his fingers in between his ribs, and Phainon just barely manages to lock his legs to prevent them from being flipped around again.

“Lady Archidamia deigned to inform me about this splendid change in my schedule this morning,” Ptolemy continues, frustration bubbling back up. “Something about a council meeting and an evaluation with the trainers, so their session got postponed. I’m beginning to think I should have accepted the invitation to the meeting as well. You try getting two brats to sit still for a lesson when they are full of energy and itching for a fight.”

“Judging by the way you are clutching a book which certainly doesn’t belong to their curriculum, you weren’t trying very hard,” Perdikkas points out, knocking on the hardcover as Ptolemy raises it.

“It’s a good read. I indulged myself for all of half an hour before giving my all to put those two back on track to no avail,” Ptolemy defends himself with an almost offended tone at the mere implication that he’s been slacking off.

“You cannot stand Lady Archidamia,” Perdikkas reminds him, observing Phainon and Mydei with keen eyes. There is a bruise blooming on Phainon’s left cheek, he knows. Phainon looks back at Mydei, finding no obvious signs of harm except for dirt smudged all over. It’s a good thing they aren’t standing because Mydei would be limping. “She would have raised your blood pressure even higher than the kids.”

Ptolemy grumbles something under his breath, and Phainon can easily imagine him crossing his arms. He glances up from Mydei’s face to find him doing just that. Predictable. Phainon is pretty sure he wouldn’t last five minutes in a fight against either of them. Hephaestion included.

“You said you were coming over for something?” Ptolemy recalls, not even looking at the two of them.

Mydei’s hand makes contact with Phainon’s chin again, painfully pushing it further away. Phainon retaliates by shoving hard on Mydei’s shoulders, pinning him to the ground as securely as he can. He has basically won already. Mydei’s glare says he realizes, too.

“There’s a medical book I want to borrow,” Perdikkas explains. “Although I’m uncertain whether you even possess one such as this.”

Ptolemy hums in consideration. “I’m afraid I won’t be of much help if the book in question consists of medical procedures,” he says eventually with regret. It’s clear he wishes he had unlimited access to every book in existence.

“No, no,” Perdikkas rushes to reassure. “I simply require a classification of a specific illness, nothing much else. Lord Dametrius mentioned he may have read something similar to what I’m searching for in one of your books a while back.”

Mydei bucks his hips, attempting to throw Phainon off. He isn’t very successful, as Phainon manages to keep his balance and only tightens the grip on his shoulders. He grins triumphantly.

“If it’s of a theoretical nature, there might be something in my collection,” Ptolemy ponders, Phainon and Mydei’s misbehavior entirely forgotten. Phainon has never been more glad that the teen is so easily distracted. “Chances that it’s exactly what you are searching for are low, but you could find something else that might point you in the right direction at the very least.”

“Worth a try,” Perdikkas sighs. “I will take anything at this point.”

Mydei snaps his teeth at Phainon in annoyance. There isn’t any heat to it, just pure exasperation. Despite being in the winning position, Phainon feels warm as the golden eyes pin him in place.

“I’ve got three shelves dedicated to medical textbooks. There must be something of value in them,” Ptolemy continues with a huff. Phainon is very glad for the timing of him and Mydei being locked in a sort of stalemate, because next his stern gaze settles on them. “You three. Behave. By the time I’m back, there will be consequences if I don’t find you calm and ready to learn, you hear me? And, under absolutely no circumstances are any of you allowed to die when I’m not looking. Do you understand me?”

He waits a second, gives a sharp nod to himself, and then walks off in the direction of his house. Perdikkas only shakes his head and follows after his friend, throwing them one last amused glance.

“I cannot die,” Mydei calls after them, because Phainon being a smartass— Ptolemy’s words—is rubbing off on him just a little.

Phainon huffs out a chuckle and sees Hephaestion roll his eyes.

“You can die,” Ptolemy turns around to yell angrily, “You just don’t stay dead!”

“Same thing,” Mydei mutters, and thankfully, Ptolemy can no longer hear him. He rotates his shoulders, Phainon’s hands rolling with the movement as he’s no longer actively pushing him into the ground. “Will you get off me?”

“Oh. Oh, yeah, sorry,” Phainon laughs and slips off his thighs, settling on the ground next to him. Mydei pulls himself up into a sitting position, turning his head in all directions to stretch the muscles.

It’s easy to pass the time in companionship.

Hephaestion makes some remark that serves to effortlessly rile Phainon up, and they bicker for a while until a coughing fit overtakes their friend. They

wait it out and get right back into the conversation as if nothing happened, even if Hephaestion’s breathing is labored and he subtly rubs one hand against his chest occasionally. He doesn’t like it when attention is brought to his illness.

Ptolemy and Perdikkas return eventually, two incredibly thick books held carefully in the latter’s hands as he bids them farewell. Ptolemy takes one look at them and must realize that the only reason they all aren’t actively fighting in that very moment is because Hephaestion can’t.

He only rubs his forehead in resignation before he decides to change today’s subject to something that never fails to bring Phainon’s attention into focus. Namely, the analysis of ancient relics. Mydei settles at Phainon’s side quickly, knowing that’s something he finds a genuine interest in.

Hephaestion only groans at the prospect of three hours of pure boredom that await him. Phainon thinks he simply doesn’t have any taste.

The bed seems strangely empty when Phainon jerks awake, a strangled yell dying on his lips. It gets easier to calm down from a nightmare after experiencing them so often. Breathe in, breathe out. Think of what he did yesterday, and what he’s supposed to do in the morning. Try to override any thought that tries to touch any subject that even remotely relates to whatever he tends to have nightmares about.

Turn to Mydei, take in his scent, and try to match their breathing. Sometimes, Phainon searches for the pulse point and counts in his head, measuring the beats per minute the way Perdikkas taught them, until he slowly drifts off again.

He swipes his hand around, trying to find the human furnace that doubles as his friend, but has no luck with it. He turns to the other side and repeats the

process. Still nothing. He could have gone to the bathroom; it had happened before. But Phainon doesn’t hear water rushing or any other sort of shuffling around.

Now thoroughly alarmed, he pushes himself to his elbows and cracks his eyes open, blinking a bit to try and see through the darkness, accented only by the dim moonlight from the outside. And right in front of the bed, there is a slumped silhouette. Phainon doesn’t scream, but he does violently flinch back, his heartbeat skyrocketing. The adrenaline wakes him up to the core, the training about to kick in to try to defend himself, when he notices it’s a very familiar silhouette.

He gets a glimpse of moonlit blond hair and pale skin covered in red markings, and he falls back onto the mattress as if someone cut his strings. “By Kephale, don’t scare me like that,” he mumbles, rubbing his eyes. “Why aren’t you in bed? Come on, it’s cold.”

“I’m sorry,” Mydei whispers, not moving one bit.

“Why are you apologizing?” Phainon asks incredulously, raising the blanket. It’s not that serious. They both did weird things right after waking up from too realistic nightmares or memories. It’s rare, but sometimes you just have to get away and make yourself small. Hide under the table, maybe. It’s fine. “Just get in here.”

“Phainon.” His name is spoken louder, and something about the tone causes the alarm bells to go off again.

Phainon opens his eyes and takes a closer look, willing away the exhaustion as best he can.

The moonlight paints Mydei in pale shades, ones Phainon is used to from their time in the wild. It makes the gold splatters on his skin and clothes stick out, some even smudged on his face.

“What?” Phainon’s breath escapes him, knees hitting the floor painfully as he rushes to get closer until he can grab Mydei’s shoulders. “What

happened? Why are you covered in blood? Why didn’t you wake me up? Who did this?”

“I’m not telling you,” Mydei says, eyes set with stubbornness. “You’re just going to be angry.”

“I’m not,” Phainon protests, even if he already feels panic merging with anxiety into a bubble of anger. It’s a very familiar emotion. Phainon used to lose himself in it just a little bit, back when it felt like it was just him against the entire world, before he found Mydei. It still simmers under his skin. But not as loudly, and it’s easier to ignore.

Mydei exhales slowly, his gaze entirely flat. He is tired. Not the sleepiness kind. “You are.”

“I won’t be angry, I promise,” he still insists. He glances lower, to the thick golden stain at the very center of Mydei’s chest. His hold on Mydei tightens without any input from his brain. It doesn’t exactly help his case. “Just— Why didn’t you wake me up?” He asks instead, voice cracking.

Before whatever happened occurred. After he returned in such a state. Does he, does he not trust Phainon?

Mydei closes his eyes, probably able to read through Phainon’s slow descent into spiraling. Well, what else is Phainon supposed to think? They spend every waking moment side by side, and then something happens, and Phainon isn’t even privy to it? What if Mydei—

“I thought I would be fine without you for an hour after you fell asleep,” Mydei finally admits quietly, and cuts through the mess in Phainon’s mind, golden eyes swimming with regret once he opens them. And guilt. “I started panicking about five minutes after stepping out. It didn’t matter at that point. And I got back in half an hour, even.”

Phainon tenses at the words. It feels like betrayal, in some sense. Phainon wouldn’t willingly leave Mydei, not even for a minute. But that’s… That’s Phainon. And it doesn’t matter what he would or wouldn’t do. What matters right now is that something evidently went wrong. Phainon feels a sick

thought creep in at the back of his head, that this is precisely why they shouldn’t be apart. Bad things happen when they’re not together.

“Mydei,” he calls, letting his hands fall and trying to focus on the situation at hand instead. “What happened?”

Mydei shakes his head, his fringe falling into his eyes. “It will affect you, and you will do something stupid. I don’t want that,” he states firmly. “Phainon, I gave my full consent to do this, and I was fully aware of what they would do. It’s fine, it doesn’t matter anymore. It’s only the fact you weren’t there that messed with me. And then I felt bad about it, and I didn’t want to wake you, and— I just, I need, uh.”

He trails off, clicking his tongue in annoyance at himself. He either forgot a word or doesn’t exactly know what he wants. Phainon would bet on the latter, he rarely forgets words anymore. Mydei raises his hand and then slowly curls it into a fist, looking up at Phainon helplessly.

Yeah.

Phainon sighs softly, pitching himself forward and hugging his friend. Mydei’s hands wrap around his middle, a little unsure as they always are when it comes to deliberate affection. It’s alright, Phainon doesn’t mind. After what can’t be more than two minutes, Phainon rises and pulls Mydei along with him into the bathroom to wash off. They are staying in until at least Lucid Hour tomorrow, and he doesn’t care what their trainers might think of it.

Mydei stays true to his word and doesn’t reveal any details of what transpired despite the incessant begging that ensues for the next hour, even as Phainon guides Mydei into the bed by his hand, still making childish bargains to exchange for information. It’s mostly for show, and he revels in the small smile it gets him when they lie side by side, and Phainon offers to take over cooking. Mydei huffs. They both know it’d be nothing other than a downgrade from Mydei’s dishes.

Mydei even falls asleep eventually—quicker than Phainon expected him to —sprawled out on his back with his head turned toward Phainon, their legs

tangled together underneath the sheet.

Phainon doesn’t have the same luxury, not with his mind racing as it does.

He isn’t stupid. They learn the same things, and Phainon quietly remains on Mydei’s right during those special meetings with the self-appointed Council, listening to any and all advice the leaders have for the Crown Prince. Their plans.

Some weeks ago, Archidamia told them about how the settlement acquires enough supplies to get by, and then some more. Kremnoans offer their services in exchange for goods, money, or favors. It helps that the settlement is situated five days’ worth of light travel to reach one of the city-states, Milios, where information flows easily. Groups of people chosen personally by Archidamia and Savvas travel, sometimes gone for even two months, in order to participate in combat. The success rate is very high. And it shows in the way the settlement prospers.

They don’t reveal they hail from Castrum Kremnos, for some reason, but no one seems to care about the warriors’ origins when the job is done well.

She told them that the youngest to participate in any expeditions tend to be fourteen. Phainon and Mydei are special, she said, apparently of the mind that if they were raised among the Kremnoans from the beginning, they would have been ready by twelve. Even by the sole fact that they are Chrysos Heirs. Despite the fact that Phainon is one month away from being thirteen himself. A few days ago, she deemed them stronger than even those fourteen years old already, and offered them a spot on the team that will be sent to defend a nearby village. It’s going to be five people total, including the two of them. Supposed to be one of the easiest missions.

They are meant to go over the strategy this weekend, three days before they are set to move out.

It’s easy to figure out what today might be about. In less than a week, they will participate in their first proper battle. Not in a controlled environment, and with opponents that aren’t guaranteed to stop even if you yield. Not that any self-respecting Kremnoan would yield outside of a spar at all.

The significance of covering their weaknesses had been drilled into them every single day until they grew to be able to watch their blind spots without a stutter. Even if Phainon and Mydei are additionally trained to function as a flawless unit, it wouldn’t do well if the Kremnoans let their Crown Prince out onto the battlefield just for him to die. Mydei is immortal. But the extent of it isn’t known to the Kremnoans. Now that Phainon thinks about it, not even Mydei knows whether there’s a time limit on it. If there is a spot that might be a weakness, or if it’s just specific kinds of death he can recover from.

Maybe they don’t trust Phainon to ensure his friend remains unharmed. Perhaps they are right to.

He notices the almost faded bruises on Mydei’s neck, in addition to the thin line on his chest. Both will be gone by the Entry Hour. Maybe they wanted to check if there were any limitations to his immortality, with a healer at hand just in case. Phainon hopes there was one. Archidamia could have quietly requested that of Mydei when Phainon was distracted with something else, painting it as a necessity to allow them to fight. Kremnoans can be pretty extreme, as he’s heard of their multiple downright scary customs. And punishments.

Phainon doesn’t think that’s fair, whatever reason they had.

It doesn’t help that Mydei said he changed his mind right after he stepped out of their house. Phainon lies awake, staring as the yellowish prints of fingers slowly fade into Mydei’s regular skin tone on his neck, and imagines guards dragging him away by force. Keeping him still as whoever was in charge of the experimentation kills their Crown Prince.

He hates the person who brought destruction to Aedes Elysiae. He hates Mydei’s parents for not keeping him safe. And he is starting to hate the people who take care of them now, just a little.

Phainon isn’t dumb, but he still stupidly challenges Archidamia to combat on the very next day. No one else in the whole settlement has enough

authority to carry out something of that sort. Phainon is extremely defiant at his very core toward things he disagrees with. Both he and Mydei, they will fight with their teeth if they have to until the last breath. And he—

He cannot just sit back, not when the person most important to him is made to suffer.

Some small part of him entertains the prospect of winning against her, displaying his growth over the last two years. Even if logically he is aware that there is no chance of that happening. Mydei only ever got a hit on her because she was caught off guard that time, when everyone was still attempting to separate them. Neither of them has managed to repeat that just yet.

Thankfully, the confrontation happens away from prying eyes. Just one set of them, belonging to Mydei. Phainon can feel the glare and anger directed at his back all the while. Phainon doesn’t even get to go on offense, as Archidamia treats the duel as seriously as she would any other. She immediately tries to overpower him, and his defense manages to last for maybe fifteen minutes before he is laid out on the ground. Which is impressive enough. He has no way of knowing whether she took pity on him and indulged him for that long, or if he really improved enough to push back to such an extent.

Archidamia doesn’t dignify the fight with any comment, simply walking away. She is neutral. Not even smug or pitying. Phainon doesn’t know if that’s worse, to be deemed so beneath her care.

Mydei pulls him up to his feet roughly and shoves him toward Perdikkas’ house, trailing two steps behind him as they walk without a word. Phainon sustains a bruised rib and slightly damaged pride, but at least he held up his own convictions. He didn’t just sit down and do nothing.

Mydei doesn’t speak to him for two whole days, only reluctantly allowing touch when they’re falling asleep.

He only cracks when Phainon talks himself hoarse, desperately trying to fill in the stony silence between the two of them. Mydei tiredly calls him a

dumbass before sitting so close their thighs brush together, and Phainon simply laughs in relief. He knows Mydei is angry that Phainon did something reckless despite claiming he wouldn’t. It doesn’t hurt any less to bear the consequences.

But it’s better than thinking he did something wrong that resulted in Mydei not confiding in him when making a choice to voluntarily die at someone’s hands.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Traveling again is fun. He nearly forgot all the enjoyable aspects of it while cooped up in the settlement for so long.

Phainon and Mydei run around a bit, high on the energy of being back in the wild. They race back and forth, try to trip one another up, and point at every single detail that grabs their attention. One of the adults always keeps watch while the rest sleeps, and Phainon doesn’t feel that anxious over the flames crackling away at the center of their small camp.

The rules are simple.

Don’t get hurt. Kill as many assailants as you can.

Valorous death before glorious return.

Phainon knows their temporary companions are meant to be keeping an eye on them, making sure they don’t actually die. Mydei, because he is the Crown Prince. Phainon, because it would make Mydei revert to being feral. Or at least he assumes so. They might as well not really care about Phainon’s safety, but he’d like to think otherwise.

It takes just under five days to reach their destination, and the battle is already ongoing. Their group rushes in, weapons at the ready, and Phainon

feels the adrenaline rush through his veins.

He’s got his favorite sword and a shield that he already thinks of abandoning. He is faster without it. Mydei doesn’t use one either, so Phainon isn’t going to be any worse.

There are people clad in crude armor, screaming as they attack the villagers who try to fend them off with pitchforks, sickles, and the like. At least it’s easy to distinguish between them.

Phainon feels the muscle memory kick in as some stranger attempts to get a hit on him, dodging and parrying flawlessly. It’s sort of fun, even. The Kremnoan training truly seems to be superior. It’s not even difficult. Phainon still doesn’t have to exert himself as another man joins in, trying to overpower him. It’s easy to sidestep them, his footwork carrying him and confusing the opponents, as he uses his small size against them.

It’s only when Mydei runs past him, Phainon’s eyes following the quick movement as he crouches to avoid a strike from a spear, that he remembers what they’re here for. Mydei jumps up into the air, throwing himself at the enemy and tearing through their throat with his gauntlet before moving past without a second glance at the corpse at his feet.

Phainon’s blood runs cold in an instant. Right. He is supposed to kill these people.

He doesn’t know what the exact reasons for this conflict are. But those villagers, they seem rather defenseless. What would even warrant an attack on such a village? Could it even be justified in any way? Phainon wouldn’t have thought twice about this if this were Aedes Elysiae. It’s the very reason he is on the quest to become stronger.

And these people in armor, they are attacking Phainon at this very moment.

This is just self-defense, isn’t it?

Phainon has done it once before, he can do it again. The circumstances aren’t so different.

And if he wants to stay by Mydei’s side, he has to keep up.

Exhaling sharply, he lets muscle memory take over and briefly closes his eyes after positioning to strike the man closest to him. There is a wet gargling sound, forcing Phainon to look again. The man clutches his neck, pulling away from the sword. Crimson red spurts out from between his fingers as he chokes on his own blood. Phainon feels rooted the spot, eyes stuck on the injury he just delivered. These people, they— They aren’t really trained, are they? What if it’s—

The second assailant recovers from being knocked down to the ground and makes a move to get revenge on Phainon, charging with a spear. Mind completely blank, Phainon’s body moves on its own, dodging the wide strike and countering. All that suffering poured into hours that bled into days of training paid off for something. Mydei is much better at handling a spear than this guy, barely giving Phainon any space to move when they spar. Phainon could defend himself against such a weak assault in his sleep.

The armor is of poor quality. It doesn’t protect all the vital spots, not like the Kremnoan variety. It’s easy to get close, it’s quick to slip his blade between the clasps and dig it up.

The man screams, louder than the clanks of weapons all around them. It’s a sound that Phainon knows will ring in his ears hours later. And Phainon—

Phainon feels numb as the body drops to the ground, his sword clutched tightly in his hand. He doesn’t think of anything as his feet carry him away and into another fight. He ignores his stomach twisting on itself as he slices through another person’s leg, watching them tumble to the ground. He leaves that one be, figuring they are harmless. A Kremnoan warrior finishes the job for him, eyes briefly sliding over Phainon before settling on a new opponent.

And Phainon swallows the lump in his throat, gaze raking over the flat ground and finding Mydei engaged in combat not too far away. He breathes a bit more easily at the sight and makes his way over.

The villagers are exhausted and relieved in equal measure. There is no tension in the way they hold themselves, as if an immense weight has just been removed from their shoulders. But their faces are closed off, entirely detached from the whole ordeal. A few women have shown up by now, one with a small child cradled close, their face protectively hidden in her chest.

They pay well, and they are grateful for the help. But it’s clear they don’t want these foreign warriors anywhere near anymore. They give Phainon and Mydei a wide berth in particular, for some reason. Maybe because they’re the same age as their children. Fighting. Killing. There is obvious judgment in their cold stares, but none of them speaks up.

The Kremnoans remain good-natured, uncaring of the attitude directed their way. Phainon is glad they don’t unnecessarily prolong the whole thing, wrapping it up within an hour before the five of them are back on their way home.

Phainon doesn’t speak all the way to the same spot they set camp in just this morning. He still feels numb. He doesn’t even want to think, not really.

The adults chat with each other aimlessly, like it’s just another regular day for them. Do they really not care one bit? Do they not wonder whether the person who perished under their blades had any family? Friends? Lovers? What about their dreams and wishes that will never come true? Does it really not matter?

Mydei’s foot nudging him breaks him out of his thoughts. He moves his gaze away from the fire, only now registering the smell of cooked and seasoned meat. The food must be almost ready.

Mydei stares at him when he looks over, body angled toward Phainon. Do you want to talk? He gestures quickly. Phainon hears the conversation on the other side of the fire trail off, and knows the three must be watching with varying degrees of curiosity and amusement. People who don’t know them always do.

Phainon shakes his head.

He doesn’t want to talk. He doesn’t know what exactly he wants. To sleep and to pretend he spent this day differently. That he won’t have to do what he did today again, and again, and again. Until he reaches his end goal. And then, he will be able to stop. It’s a very hopeless thought. How many years until then?

You okay? Another sign, now coupled with a concerned glance.

Phainon nods and tries to give him a thin smile. He is sure it falls short, definitely not conveying his usual optimism. The subject is dropped, and Phainon doesn’t even notice the time passing until food is pressed into his hands, and he automatically shovels it into his mouth, chewing without tasting much and swallowing.

He has to do this. It’s the only path for him.

They will come home, and he will figure out how to deal with it.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

The door to their bedroom opens silently, the hinges recently oiled to operate smoothly. Phainon leans into the corridor, angling his head to look toward the living area attached to the kitchen, noting the empty table that’s pushed to the wall. Yet dim light comes from around the corner that hides two old armchairs. Phainon glances a bit lower and finds two legs stretched out into the corridor. Ptolemy must still be up, reading one of the books he keeps scattered around Phainon and Mydei’s house.

Phainon inhales. Does he want to dive into this right now? It can wait. They just came back from their very first mission with permission to take tomorrow off in celebration of their success. But sleep eludes him, so it might be the perfect opportunity to get it over with now.

Mydei can spring up from deep sleep at the tiniest of sounds. Phainon is the only one who can get away with shifting around him without having to deal with a crimson crystal forming at his throat. His voice doesn’t seem to wake him up either, as long as he doesn’t speak too loudly.

Phainon hopes that even if he wakes up once the other teen starts talking, he will be able to peacefully drift between sleep and wakefulness rather than completely abandon resting.

“Ptolemy,” Phainon calls quietly from the doorway, not stepping out into the corridor himself.

Ptolemy’s head surfaces from behind the wall, blond hair swishing in the air with the motion. He doesn’t look surprised to see Phainon up, despite it being well into the Curtain-Fall Hour.

“Everything alright?” He asks, in a tone possibly even quieter than Phainon’s.

“Yeah, I’m okay,” Phainon nods, hand gripping the doorframe tightly. “Can we talk?”

“Sure. Come here.”

Phainon glances back into their bedroom, along the wall closest to him. Mydei still sleeps peacefully in their bed, his chest rising up and down in a regular motion. He might be pretending, Phainon is too far to tell. His feet feel rooted to the floor, refusing to step over the thin line separating the room from the corridor.

“Could we, uh.” He stops and looks back at Ptolemy, finding him staring at him patiently. “Do it here?”

“That’s fine,” Ptolemy responds and gets up from his seat without a complaint.

Phainon hears him set the book down somewhere, but he doesn’t turn the light off. As he makes his way over, Phainon sits down on the ground,

angling his body in such a way that allows him to have a clear view into the bedroom. It’s not really necessary. But it makes him a little calmer when he can see.

Ptolemy follows Phainon’s lead, choosing to sit opposite Phainon with his back to the other door, which leads into the guest room. He looks slightly above Phainon at the entrance he’s almost guarding, then to Phainon himself, but doesn’t speak up.

“Don’t wanna wake him up,” Phainon offers up as an explanation.

He ignores the way it makes no sense, considering they should’ve moved further away if that was really the only thing he cared about. Ptolemy doesn’t seem to mind the flimsy excuse, only nodding once to accept the answer. It successfully makes Phainon feel relieved. Ptolemy is safe. He can and will talk to either of them about anything in the world without judgment.

“Does it ever get easier?” Phainon asks after a few minutes, bringing his knees up to lean his chin on them.

Ptolemy’s lips set in a thin line. “You mean the killing, don’t you?” He clarifies, voice just one step above whispering.

It’s not surprising anymore, the way he can come to the right conclusion with so little information. He is smarter than everyone in the settlement combined, Phainon’s sure.

“I. I killed some people,” Phainon finally admits out loud, mostly to himself than anyone else. But once the words start flowing, he cannot stop them. “No one in the battle seemed to care about ending another person’s life. But I can’t stop thinking about it. And I told Archidamia it wouldn’t be a problem, I cannot go back on this. But what if, what if I don’t stop feeling like this? How do I stop it? Why am I the only one having issues?”

Ptolemy hums, tapping his fingers on the floor in thought.

“You shouldn’t worry too much about that. Your reaction is perfectly normal,” he reassures softly, eyes full of understanding. “Any civilian outside of this place would be rightfully horrified at hearing about, witnessing, or participating in what happened on your expedition. I’m truly sorry you have to grow up in these conditions, where it’s so normalized.” A small, resigned smile is offered to Phainon. “I think there is something a little skewed in us Kremnoans. Maybe we’re just programmed this way, to kill our enemies freely with no remorse. The way we’re brought up, generation after generation, might be to blame for it.”

So… Is it just because Phainon is an outsider here? Would he have been able to accept his duties more easily if he had been born Kremnoan? Phainon isn’t a civilian. He has a prophecy to uphold, and if he wishes to stand by Mydei’s side, he has to pull his weight.

He cannot afford to agonize over this. Not that he let himself think about it in the first place. He knows his mind sometimes gets away from him, prone to spiraling. He’s done enough of that. Especially in the forest. He hasn’t allowed himself to revert to that state of panic ever since, and if he has to shut down any thought that might lead to it, then so be it.

And maybe, just maybe, he will get used to it enough with time that he won’t even have any thoughts about it to shut down anymore.

“Have you ever killed?” He still asks, even though he can figure the answer out from Ptolemy’s words so far.

“Yes. Quite a few people,” he replies with a nod.

It doesn’t appear like he wishes to elaborate. He seems to reconsider that decision with a long, resigned sigh when Phainon’s gaze turns expectant, clearly conveying that he will not go back to bed until he at least gets an explanation.

“My parents have always been highly reputed scholars in Castrum Kremnos. Right before I left the fortress, I tagged along with them to participate in negotiations with a Lord of sorts,” he reminisces with a quiet hum. He doesn’t seem to like those memories very much. “In hindsight, I

don’t imagine either party intended to truly form an alliance. Sometimes, I think I was allowed to come along for that reason alone, to check if I’m truly so hopeless in combat as I always refused to take part in such things. Needless to say, the conversation escalated to the point of a fight breaking out. I killed four people trying to get out with my parents.”

Phainon’s head makes a quiet thud as he rests it against the doorframe, his back already leaning against it. Mydei still hasn’t moved one bit. He definitely should’ve woken up by now with all the talking on Ptolemy’s part.

Phainon exhales, glancing back at Ptolemy. “Did you feel wrong at all about it?”

“Not really.” He shrugs and looks up at the ceiling. There are slight shadows under his eyes. Phainon should… probably thank Ptolemy for indulging him and let him go rest. He really should. “It’s either you or them, you know?” Ptolemy continues, eyes slipping shut. “And no one who steps onto the battlefield is innocent. As a wise man once said: It’s human, we all put self-interest first. I’m sure people on the other side of the battlefield are also trying to justify the violence to themselves as best they can.

“You know what else is very interesting about humans?” Ptolemy looks back at him tiredly, but he still smiles to try to put Phainon at ease. “We can adapt to just about anything. You are a strong and resilient kid, Phainon. You will overcome this if you set your mind to it.”

Phainon thinks so, too. There isn’t really much of a choice anyway. He has to get over it. In these fights, he’s defending himself and the people around him. Someone has to be strong enough to deal with bad people, right? And bad people rarely stop at anything, so sometimes drastic measures are needed. Phainon might be needed.

“Thank you for talking to me,” Phainon says with gratitude, straightening his legs out along the floor. He still isn’t very sleepy, but he thinks he can lie in bed without the risk of getting lost in his thoughts now.

“Anytime,” Ptolemy waves him off with a grin. He gets up with a quiet grunt, rising on his toes and bringing his arms above his head to stretch with a yawn. “Remember that even if you ultimately change your mind and decide this path isn’t for you, we will all support you. Mydei would be the first one to cheer you on, you know.”

And he does know.

It’s the same way Phainon is willing to stay among the Kremnoans as long as necessary, and the way he would drop everything at a moment’s notice if Mydei expressed the desire to leave everything behind. He would try to convince him to take Ptolemy, Perdikkas, Peucesta, and Hephaestion along, but he thinks they’d follow suit without even being asked.

“Yeah, but I think I am on the right path,” Phainon says with a wide smile of his own, getting to his feet as well. “I think I should get back, or Mydei will be cranky in the morning that I didn’t let him sleep.”

Ptolemy huffs in amusement just as a very doubtful noise comes from the bed.

“You’re the one who can never get up in the morning,” comes the muffled reply, words barely distinguishable as they seem to be spoken right into a pillow.

Phainon huffs. So what if Phainon likes to sleep in? “Well, I’m still up faster than you.”

“In those dreams you’ve got while you still sleep past the waking hour?” Is the response full of a mocking tone.

“There is a time for many words, and there is also a time for sleep,” Ptolemy cuts in before Phainon can think of a retort, walking back to the living area to turn the lamplight off. He comes back through the dark corridor, his silhouette moving along the wall. “Perdikkas expressed willingness to come visit tomorrow, so I would advise both of you to quit squabbling and sleep.”

“Yeah, yeah,” Phainon grumbles, already mourning the hours of sleep he won’t get back. Maybe he will nap in the afternoon? That is if Hephaestion doesn’t decide to bother them. “Sleep well.”

“You, too,” Ptolemy chuckles. Phainon closes the door to their bedroom just as Ptolemy opens the one leading into the guest room.

Mydei still doesn’t move a single muscle even as Phainon makes his way toward the bed, face burrowed into the pillow, when Phainon climbs over him and settles in between his warm body and the wall.

He exhales deeply and closes his eyes, lying on his side with his hand resting on Mydei’s hip. There is no shirt to tangle his fingers in, so he settles on just tracing his thumb in circles on the skin. He already knows it’s more likely he will experience nightmares of the interesting variety once he manages to doze off. There’s not much he can do about it, except to hope his friend will chase them away somehow if they get too bad.

It will get better with time. Just as he will become better at… handling his duty. There is no other way.

He feels Mydei shift and opens his eyes. Golden ones blink at him from up close, wide awake and determined. Ah. He really must have been listening all along. Or at least to most of it.

Phainon waits him out. His eyes cross when he looks lower and notes that their noses are almost touching. It’s nice, literally feeling him breathe against Phainon, in and out.

“I can kill anyone for you,” Mydei offers quietly, matter-of-factly. Phainon freezes. “You don’t have to do it.”

It’s… sweet. As morbid as it sounds. Three or four years ago, he would have been horrified to hear words like these. Now, he only feels relief to be cared for by someone to such an extent.

“Thank you,” Phainon says, allowing for a tired smile. “But I’ll be okay. We are supposed to be equal, aren’t we?”

Mydei only nods in acknowledgement, not pushing for anything else. Phainon delights in the way Mydei unquestioningly believes in Phainon.

It makes him want to believe in himself as well.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

“Deliverer?” Hephaestion repeats, his brows furrowed. “What a weird thing to call it. Are you meant to be an errand boy?”

“Not in the sense of bringing something, but the state of being saved, set free,” Ptolemy explains as he surveys the card over Hephaestion’s shoulder. “Deliverance, as in salvation.”

Phainon itches to retrieve the card, not exactly trusting them not to damage it. It’s beyond important. It’s the one and only memento he has of Cyrene. He wouldn’t forgive them easily if it were damaged. Even if they are friends. He forces himself to keep still, though, relaxing only when Mydei leans over and plucks it from Hephaestion’s fingers.

“Well, the guy has white hair like you do,” Hephaestion continues, brows furrowed. “Did you start cutting it that way because of it?”

Phainon is almost certain that his haircut predates the card. Or at least predates his knowledge of the card’s existence. He doesn’t know how old the cards are or where they came from. Cyrene just had them, and he never questioned it. “No,” he says flatly.

Peucesta strums the lyre absentmindedly, watching them with interest rather than trying to actually play something. “They are for divination, you said. Do you remember this one’s meaning?” Perdikkas asks for him. He does it sometimes, when it’s clear Peucesta isn’t having a day where he feels up for talking. Perdikkas doesn’t understand Peucesta in the same way Phainon understands Mydei, so he always just ends up asking for elaboration.

Phainon still hasn’t figured out what Peucesta’s willingness to talk depends on. Hephaestion says it’s just the way he is, and there might not be much else to it.

“My friend, she said that, uh, according to some prophecy?” Phainon doesn’t remember the term anymore. She mentioned it so many times, and only the ‘tri—’ part of it remained in his brain. “It’s about absolute harmony and perfection.” And not having a dark side. He drew it so many times, he cannot forget. “In all the years, I’ve only ever drawn that card out of twelve.”

He smiles, a little bitterly. He doesn’t relate much to the card that he couldn’t seem to shake for the last few years of his life in Aedes Elysiae. Always the Deliverer card, day in and day out. He stopped feeling disappointment after a month, looking down dispassionately at the card in his hands during each draw. Piso was always jealous. Cyrene would look at him with compassion, trying to bring his attention to the positives.

“That’s statistically impossible,” Ptolemy says, and his leg jumps up and down in excitement. “Your friend must have been exceptionally talented in divination for it to occur so consistently.”

Phainon nods eagerly, happy to move on with the subject. “Aedes Elysiae fell under Oronyx’s domain. There was even a large statue dedicated to them where we prayed and left offerings.” Phainon remembers mouthing along but not really saying any words when he was very little and too stubborn to participate, his mom reprimanding him later. “My best friend, she wanted to study with the priests in the Abyss of Fate.” And Phainon wanted to go learn to fight in the Castrum Kremnos, he vaguely recalls. He swallows past the guilt of being the only one whose dreams are being realized, even if partially. “She was gifted,” he gushes instead. “Had those dreams about prophecies. And she would do daily pulls out of her set of oracle cards for any of the other kids.”

“She sounds bright,” Perdikkas says after a few minutes of silence, when it becomes clear Phainon may have stumbled onto a slightly too emotional subject. “It makes me wonder what cards the rest of us would’ve pulled.”

Ah. Phainon deeply regrets not putting all of them in his backpack for safekeeping when they were hanging out on that cursed day.

“Sorry, I don’t remember many others,” he apologizes sheepishly. He really should’ve paid some more attention to her passion. “Oh, but there were a Healer and Scholar cards. I can’t tell if the meanings fit either of you, though.”

Ptolemy makes a noise of agreement. “There are a lot of people working in every field. Not all of them fit into the set archetype, and I imagine cards used for divination might have quite unorthodox interpretations assigned to them.”

Phainon isn’t sure what exactly ‘unorthodox’ means, but it sounds accurate enough.

“You say it’s not about errands, but you do help around a lot,” Hephaestion muses, smirking as he glances at the card again before meeting Phainon’s eyes. His hair is long enough to reach his jaw now, framing his face sharply. “You even brought Mydei to us. Aren’t you the Deliverer, then?”

“I’m not an errand boy,” Phainon defends himself, annoyance at Hephaestion already spiking up. Titans, it’s been three years, and he still finds ways to get under Phainon’s skin flawlessly. It must be considered a talent by now. “See if I ever do any favors for you again.”

“Well, given your actions,” Ptolemy picks the subject up with a teasing smile, and Phainon wants to groan, “You just might deliver us to salvation alongside our dear Crown Prince. Accept the things to which fate binds you, and love the people with whom fate brings you together, but do so with all your heart.”

“Yeah, you might as well get used to the new title if Ptolemy brought out a quote in relation to it,” Perdikkas snorts. It evolves into a short laugh when Ptolemy jabs him in the arm.

Phainon isn’t that confident about outright accepting it. He doesn’t think it fits him very well, and he is far from perfect. Not suitable to be associated

with a fate that hasn’t got a dark side when his driving force boils down to growing strong enough to kill one person. He isn’t worthy of it.

He looks at Mydei, hoping to gain some support against those treacherous people he calls friends.

“It doesn’t sound too bad,” he decides eventually and stomps all over Phainon’s last traces of hope. Mydei’s lips quirk up a little bit, and his eyes crinkle with humor when he regards Phainon. “Deliverer.”

And—

And maybe the title isn’t so bad, actually? Maybe Phainon could live with it if Mydei is the one to call him by it. Doesn’t feel as heavy, almost light.

“Peucesta is my new favorite,” Phainon still declares in defeat.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

The laces barely hold together, but Phainon still attempts to wrestle them into compliance, sitting on the cold stairs leading up to some bookstore. They bought a random book for Ptolemy, knowing he would appreciate it regardless of its contents. Mydei watches over his hands like a hawk, protective of the garment as he is. Back in that no-name town, Phainon did not expect the importance of the trade he had bargained for.

“That armguard is barely holding on,” he states the obvious. Phainon thinks it should’ve already retired a few months ago, but Mydei is as stubborn about it as he had been when it came to taking it off the very first time. Some things don’t change.

“It fits perfectly fine,” Mydei predictably insists. The way his hand twitches makes it evident he wants to pull his arm back to safety, where his precious armguard won’t be treated to offensive comments anymore.

Phainon briefly glances up to raise his eyebrows at Mydei to convey just how nonsensical he finds that statement. Then he pointedly looks back at the armguard. The battered laces can be replaced rather easily. They can find anyone capable of doing that on every corner of the settlement.

Not much can be done about the way it only covers about the upper part of Mydei’s forearm, where it used to firmly wrap almost entirely around it. Or the fact that it no longer stretches from wrist to elbow, now undersized after multiple growth spurts.

“Clearly,” he says drily. “You know you will have to stop wearing it eventually, right?”

Mydei doesn’t dignify the statement with any response, only staring down at said armguard as if he is trying to will it into becoming a better piece of equipment. Wouldn’t it be nice if things like that grew along with them? Or that swords sharpened by themselves. Phainon felt sick looking at his own weapon for a week after being assigned as a punishment to do maintenance on a thousand of them along with Mydei. As mild a punishment as it might be by Kremnoan standards, it almost made him abandon his weapon of choice.

They could probably find someone who would melt the metal and make it into something new entirely. He has a feeling Mydei wouldn’t like the idea very much. The armguard will probably end up among Phainon’s collection of trinkets found by Mydei over the first year of their friendship. He is a little sad his companion seems to have abandoned the tradition, but that’s fine. Phainon can just take it up himself instead.

Speaking of—

“Milios is huge; there has to be some antique store in here,” he says, finally finishing the laces. He drops Mydei’s hand and gets to his feet, stretching his arms out high above his head. “We’ve still got some time to kill. Wanna go look for one?”

Mydei moves his arm around, pronating and supinating, to check whether the armguard holds. Once he is satisfied, he gets up as well, sending

Phainon an unimpressed look. “You know that our retinue will start hunting us down in about an hour if we’re not by the gates.”

“If you put it like that, it makes me want to actively hide from them,” Phainon hums with a grin and sets off into the street, Mydei following with a huff.

“Was this worth your entire pay for the last three assignments?” Mydei asks flatly, eyeing the precious relic held in Phainon’s arms. “We don’t even get paid that much.”

“You are a prince, they would buy the whole store if you asked,” Phainon shoots back.

“Archidamia would sooner bury me alive herself,” Mydei rolls his eyes.

Then, Phainon adds more defensively, “This is the Red-Crowned Vase with Single Handle. I’ve seen it in one of the books about Kremnoan relics Ptolemy showed us. It’s worth every Balance Coin,” he insists, carefully holding the vase up to offer a better view.

The lady at the store claimed the bottle’s neck is supposed to resemble the Kremnos Guardian’s helmet. Phainon wouldn’t know, he’s never seen the Kremnoan Titankin. It doesn’t look very much like the regular helmets in the settlement, though. But it does have the characteristic crimson shade wrapping around it, highlighted by the golden detailing. Phainon is confident that’s precisely the antique it’s supposed to be.

“I should have figured your taste would be questionable at best when you were overjoyed to be gifted a stick by me,” Mydei replies, rolling his eyes when Phainon lets out an offended gasp.

What does it say about you since I like you so much? He almost says.

“Now you’re finding fault with the sticks?” Phainon asks with performative disbelief. “Next, you’re going to tell me you hate my eye color.”

“I like it a lot, actually.” It’s said like the most casual sentence to ever be uttered. Phainon still almost misses a step and frantically cradles the vase close to his chest in fear of destroying it should he actually trip up. Which he doesn’t. Because it’s a very casual thing to say, and Phainon is casual about it.

Mydei likes his eyes? Phainon likes Mydei’s eyes as well. It’s a very pretty and vibrant color. And Phainon likes his own eyes too. Reminds him of the sky he could still see stretching toward the Dawn Device back in Aedes Elysiae. He didn’t think Mydei would like it much, though, since his go-to appears to be the Kremnoan scarlet. Isn’t that the opposite of bright blue?

But he does like Phainon’s eyes. Cool. It’s—

Phainon is happy to hear that.

He is saved from coming up with an answer by one of the Kremnoans spotting them and calling out to get their attention. Phainon thinks they might be even five minutes before the appointed time. It’s alright, they can play hide-and-seek next time and see how good the Kremnoans are at hunting. Phainon is certain that he and Mydei could hide so well that no one would ever find them.

He smiles and returns their greetings, already thinking about showing it off to Ptolemy and where to store it. It could be the start of a bigger collection, Phainon hopes.

“What’s that ugly thing you’ve got there?” The last guard asks, utterly perplexed.

Before Phainon can retaliate, Mydei laughs. And Phainon’s irritation at his relic being disrespected yet again dissipates just a little bit in the same exact moment. He cannot bring himself to be overly annoyed, not when it results in an occurrence as rare as Mydei’s laughter. Something that goes further than a grin or even a chuckle.

Somewhere deep inside, some puzzle pieces slot together as Phainon looks at Mydei, who grins as he bumps their shoulders, careful not to jostle

Phainon too much, lest he drop the precious cargo. He doesn’t really understand the incomplete picture those puzzles attempt to portray, but it’s warm and just a little bit scary.
