chapters.title: Chapter 7: and lead them to the origin
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei grabs the helmet and forcefully starts pulling it off Phainon's head without a word of warning.

"Ow," Phainon exclaims, hands shooting up to grab Mydei's to prevent his head from being torn clean off. "Leave it!"

He hears Mydei huff, but the too-rough motion ceases. He carefully slips the garment off and glares at his friend, rubbing the back of his head where the metal dug in. Mydei doesn't appear guilty in the slightest,

"You looked foolish in it," Hephaestion pipes up unhelpfully.

Chapter Notes

The man whose name Phainon refuses to learn glares at him, teeth gritted. “We cannot afford any weaknesses,” he says slowly, as if he were speaking to someone three years of age, not thirteen. “Not out on the battlefield, and certainly not by the Crown Prince’s side.”

“I still kill them when they pose any real danger to either me or others,” Phainon argues back, having shifted to the edge of his seat in his anger. “The ones I don’t are already unarmed and hurt, unable to move. They are defenseless. Why not deal with them after the fight is over?”

“Kremnos takes no pointless prisoners,” a woman scoffs this time, her arms crossed. “Only political ones, and that’s in unique circumstances.”

“We aren’t in Kremnos,” Mydei points out bluntly, speaking up for the first time since the whole debate started half an hour ago when Phainon was reprimanded for not killing his opponents. Which was entirely unrelated to

another point he was trying to make in the first place. He has gotten better at the whole killing thing since their first mission. But he still cannot bring himself to strike a person who looks at him with fear in their eyes, shielding their body as best as they can after being defeated.

Dametrius breathes in loudly, and it stops whatever retort the other two may have had before it can even take root. “My Lord, these are still Kremnoan traditions which you cannot forsake.”

Mydei frowns but remains silent otherwise.

And Phainon wants to scoff. What traditions? Murdering people who cannot even defend themselves anymore? Is it due to the Kremnoans glorifying the death sustained in combat?

“Phainon. You never know what they might scheme up if they stay alive,” Archidamia explains, still patient. “People are resourceful, especially when they sense Thanatos approaching. Killing them is an act of mercy, saving them the terror that comes with the unknown of what might happen to them as captives of Kremnos, was that a practice we cultivated to begin with.”

Phainon doesn’t think it makes sense. Who wouldn’t prefer an option of being kept prisoner while alive compared to being dead forever?

“You take such great pride in being the best warriors Amphoreus has to offer, yet you cannot handle a hostage?” Phainon demands, fully aware he is pushing his luck. “What’s prideful about that?”

Right on cue, the man’s fist connects with the table. Phainon takes satisfaction in not flinching at the loud bang, just like the rest of the room’s occupants. “Watch it, boy,” the guy warns. “Don’t forget your place. If you think you are more than a mere—”

“Isn’t Phainon right?” Mydei talks over him, and the man’s mouth snaps shut in a fraction of a second, chastised even more thoroughly than when Dametrius intervened. Phainon has to bite the inside of his cheek to keep the laughter in. It never fails to amuse him how everyone falls over their feet when Mydei so much as breathes. It allows Phainon to get away with

many things. “Upon reflection, I don’t see any value in wasting the lives of people who have already acknowledged their defeat.” He leans back in his seat, ankle propped up on one knee, when Phainon glances his way. His posture is relaxed, but his gaze remains harsh, daring the man to continue arguing with him in the same way he did with Phainon.

Phainon feels a surge of something resurface from deep inside as he inhales, unable to stop the grin from stretching his lips. It feels good. Like they are truly on equal standing, and Mydei will make sure everyone knows it.

“It may seem this way now when the conflicts you are providing aid in are small, Young Lord, but when you are facing a greater enemy, any and all numbers count.” Archidamia takes it upon herself to explain when it becomes clear no one else is willing to do so. The withering stare she sends all of them for their cowardice feels almost just as good. “You cannot afford a single threat to persist. Even the smallest chances of turning the situation can come to pass on either side of the battle. It’s best to grind those odds to zero.”

It’s quiet as both of them take the words in, turning them over to try to understand what she means.

Phainon hates to admit that, in the end, there might be some sense in it. Kremnoans are extensively taught how to escape captivity before being deployed. They have gone through that specific training themselves. All the ways to slip off any bindings, what to say, and what not to say to your captors. Tactics of diversion and how to potentially mobilize any other prisoners to help with an escape. The more help, the better. One more body between you and death as well.

If they know how to do it, the people they defeat may as well. It is a risk.

Even if Phainon still thinks the Kremnoan army—or the smaller equivalent in the settlement—should be powerful enough to neutralize it. With all their fame and after everything Phainon has seen himself, he’s supposed to believe they wouldn’t be able to come up with something?

He sees it in Mydei’s eyes, too. Doubt about her words and willingness to push. Phainon knows Mydei isn’t nearly as affected as he is. He could definitely go on without an issue. Perhaps a single thought spared for the dead before moving. It’s what is expected of him, and he certainly doesn’t shy away from death. Be it his own or the enemy’s. Yet he still would fight for this if Phainon dug his heels in about this.

And Phainon would love to do just that. But he can’t have everything, and at this point, he’d rather win just the one battle this argument evolved from. He exhales and shakes his head, hoping this won’t be taken as him agreeing with their statements.

“All of our assignments have been completed without a hitch. Even you are satisfied with the pace we’re going at with our improvement. Titans, two weeks ago, you had Mydei participate in devising a strategy to push back against the siege on Megara, which we are not even participating in.” Phainon decides to round back to their original subject. They’ve already been at it for two hours, and he isn’t ready to let go just yet. “I don’t see how the matter of not killing everyone in sight relates to not letting us out into the more serious battles facing armies.”

The two who keep attempting to shut him down roll their eyes, and even Savvas sighs loudly. The woman shakes her head in displeasure. “And that’s precisely why—”

“That is only one reason,” Archidamia cuts her off immediately. He’s been bringing it up with varying degrees of insistence every single week for the last two months. He gets the idea she might be tired of his persistence to let them out for bigger expeditions. Ptolemy’s tactics truly work wonders. “Our settlement has a wide range of incredibly talented people: fighters, generals, engineers, smiths, and many more. Unfortunately, we have had no luck in finding or training a messenger capable enough to be assigned to the Crown Prince.”

“There are plenty of excellent runners around,” Phainon still argues. In some of the very first of these weekly meetings, they learned that there are numerous people constantly sent out to scout and search for potential work.

“I’m not saying they aren’t adequate. I’m saying they aren’t the best,” Archidamia shoots back steadily. “Children this young participating in wars are bound to garner unwanted attention, and I’m not taking any chances. Not only that, but most of our high-end expeditions consist of providing aid in pushing back the black tide from the towns and cities. That’s no ordinary opponent. Even with Young Lord’s regeneration rate and the curse he bears, the possibility of permanent death is too high. There needs to be a highly skilled runner present who can immediately gather reinforcements. There is no time to be wasted.”

And that finally makes Phainon slump down in his seat, defeated. He cannot argue with that if it’s about Mydei’s safety, can he? He has seen the abominations rising from the black tide. The way it spread through Aedes Elysiae was frighteningly rapid. He cannot fault Archidamia and Savvas for refusing to let them out on those missions if that’s their concern. Even if they had no qualms about taking the risk of killing Mydei just to check, a year ago or so. He doesn’t care that it’d be impossible for them to do so.

Phainon glances at Mydei helplessly.

The Council estimates they can be let out on more difficult missions at fifteen. It doesn’t align with Phainon’s plan to go back to Aedes Elysiae before they can plan for a more concrete future. He has to go and see the ruins, just once. Find out what’s left of his childhood and put it to rest, allowing himself to focus on his goal with one less regret of never looking back. Check if there are any clues on where to find the person responsible and plan accordingly.

Ptolemy says that the settlement’s aim is to return to Castrum Kremnos and take their rightful place. Give Mydei a chance to slay King Eurypon. Mydei himself doesn’t have any firm idea about what he wishes to do, be it with his birthright or his future in general. He is going along with everything, perhaps partly because there’s no better alternative, but also because he grew to care for his people. Phainon ultimately wants to kill that one person. It hasn’t changed, and it never will.

But before he can do that, he needs to get stronger and help Mydei figure out what he truly wants to do along the way. So that they can have a place

in each other’s lives, no matter what. So that there’s something to come back to once Phainon’s revenge is completed.

He thinks he will be able to focus on that once he at least glimpses what’s left of that catastrophe.

Two more years until they are fifteen… It doesn’t sound like much, does it? Except it does to Phainon, who detests the feeling of stagnancy.

With Mydei’s eyes on him, Phainon waves his palm, mimicking a flag’s movements. Of a white one in particular, though that’s just in his mind. Then, he inclines his chin just the slightest amount. Give up?

Mydei makes a few circles with his hand before curling it up into a fist and swiping it from left to right, flicking his fingers at the end. Try later.

Alright, so they’re not completely giving up.

Phainon looks back at the adults and steadily ignores the annoyed and impatient expressions. At least Archidamia and Savvas are used to Mydei and Phainon’s behavior by now. As much as he still doesn’t necessarily like them, he thinks he would have hated it even more if others were to take the position of leaders. Lesser evil and all that.

“Well, can’t you just… train one?” Phainon asks, careful not to sound whiny as he gestures widely in the air. Kremnoans have a regimen for every classification of soldier under the sky. Phainon refuses to believe a capable runner cannot be brought up. Although it might take a while to train one, too…

“If only it were so easy,” she lets out a low laugh. At least it isn’t mocking. “Tell you what. If you find me a suitable one, I will reconsider your request in a much more favorable light, whether I like it or not. If not, you will have to patiently wait another two years.”

Well. Without one, they’d have to wait the same amount of time either way. And who knows, maybe they will manage to stumble upon a suitable candidate. The chances are very low, as Archidamia surely would’ve

already found one if such a person resided in the settlement, but things less likely than that happened before. Like Phainon finding Mydei by the sea at all.

“We will find one,” Phainon vows, seeing Mydei nod from the corner of his eye.

“Best of luck,” Dametrius says drily from the spot at the back where he’s taking notes.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

“Hephaestion, have you ever thought about becoming a messenger?” Phainon asks, no longer caring about how desperate he sounds. It took two weeks to entirely abandon the idea of finding someone new.

Mydei lies on his back at Phainon’s side, hands fiddling with the blue fabric draped over Phainon’s shoulder that flows all the way to the ground as he rests against the large tree. He started out with a purple one he unearthed from the wardrobe. Peucesta took one glance at it and didn’t accept any protests as he switched it out. Phainon suspects that once he stops paying attention, the cape-like thing will be tied into a large bow.

“Why would I do that?” Hephaestion asks with obvious distaste.

“You’re already pretty fast,” Phainon says casually, shrugging like it’s not important. “It wouldn’t take much to turn you into the best runner, right?”

“Archidamia told us we cannot go any further if we don’t have a messenger she approves of,” Mydei explains without being asked to, ruining Phainon’s thinly veiled plans to recruit Hephaestion into the role.

Not that he thought he’d have had much success in it. It became apparent that Hephaestion’s entire existence revolves around eventually being able to

shine across the battlefields within only a few days of knowing him. Phainon has been friends with him for three years now. He overheard Proteas talking about it with Archidamia, too. How he and Mydei are shaping up to be the strongest warriors Kremnos has to offer, with their raw power and nearly limitless potential. But Hephaestion aspires to have a more precise and refined style of fighting. Something invaluable and unpredictable. Though Phainon has no clue why Archidamia would even care about Hephaestion’s progress in the first place.

“I want to fight people, make them run circles around me,” Hephaestion says and rolls his eyes. “Not be the one mindlessly running back and forth to carry messages.”

“It’s for the greater good,” Phainon insists, and Ptolemy snorts to the side.

“You are the Deliverer, shouldn’t you be the one doing the deliveries?” Hephaestion taunts with a self-satisfied smirk. Phainon bristles. It’s not even that good of a comeback. It’s been overused too many times since he showed them the card. Nothing to be so proud of, that’s for sure. Unfortunately, it doesn’t stop him from being irritated.

“Hephaestion is annoyed because his requests to be allowed to join in on the simple assignments, such as those you started out with, are being denied as well.” Ptolemy pipes up before Phainon can retaliate, not even looking up from where he is scribbling notes on his lap. Hephaestion twists to the side to look at him, betrayed. It goes unnoticed. “Have you considered he might be scared you two will get too far for him to follow?”

“Ptolemy,” Hephaestion hisses, fingers fisted in the grass they’re all sitting on. “I am not scared.”

“If you don’t talk, the seeds of resentment will take root,” Ptolemy muses quietly, unbothered about exposing him. Peucesta watches helplessly, only offering a sympathetic look when Hephaestion’s cheeks bloom with pink.

Truth be told, Phainon didn’t even really consider the possibility. To him, it’s obvious that Hephaestion will follow in their footsteps once he grows

up. Even if the two of them get slightly ahead, they will make sure to pave the way for him at least.

“You are a prodigy,” Mydei says, sitting up properly. He leans one elbow on Phainon’s raised knees and rests his chin against his palm. “You have nothing to worry about.”

“I’m a prodigy by mortal standards,” Hephaestion scoffs, picking individual grass blades out of the ground. “I don’t have that fancy blood of yours. Just regular strength and speed. How am I supposed to compare?”

“Hephaestion,” Phainon calls slowly, slightly in disbelief. “You’re constantly forcing us into a draw because we cannot catch and pin you if we spar individually, even if we bleed with ichor. How is that not impressive already?”

“We will fight on the same battlefield one day,” Mydei follows up with a decisive nod. “I am of the mind it will happen sooner rather than later.”

Hephaestion visibly calms down, just a little bit. He doesn’t look entirely convinced, but he doesn’t protest further, still picking at the ground. Phainon doesn’t think anything else will get through to him right now. Should they fight more together? …They do spar with Hephaestion, but not very frequently as of late, now that he thinks about it.

It’s quiet for a long moment, everyone lost in their own thoughts, until Peucesta speaks up quietly. “I believe my childhood friend would qualify for Lady Archidamia’s extensive criteria.”

Phainon immediately perks up. “Why haven’t you said so?”

There’s someone? It’s a real possibility that they could get a proper runner? Phainon needs to meet them right this moment. Why are they still sitting around and not heading over to meet them?

He attempts to get up to his feet, but Mydei leans more heavily on his knees, forcefully keeping him seated. He looks exasperated when their eyes meet. Phainon tilts his head at him in question.

Mydei gestures with one hand, the other still on Phainon’s knee. Stop rushing.

“Because, as far as I’m aware, he remains in Castrum Kremnos,” Peucesta elaborates as he watches the exchange.

Hephaestion only glances between all of them, not really caring about the conversation as it doesn’t affect him, but Ptolemy’s head snaps up to stare at Peucesta with full attention. The end of his pen hits his notebook repeatedly, fingers fidgeting with it up and down.

“His name is Leonnius.”

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Archidamia is incredibly unimpressed when she unlocks the door, and the three of them storm past her without a word.

“We found a messenger!” Phainon announces excitedly, leading their little group to the living area and taking his usual place on the two-seater, with Mydei right by his side within seconds. Ptolemy chooses to stand next to them, arms crossed.

Archidamia sighs and closes her eyes briefly. Phainon thinks she might be fighting off a headache. It’s good that she’s really skilled in combat. “Did you, now.”

“A boy two years my junior, so he would be well within the age range to operate as the official runner for the Crown Prince,” Ptolemy explains with a blank face. He doesn’t like Archidamia very much, possibly even less than Phainon. “He resides in the fortress, but we have it on good authority that he could outrun some of the experienced messengers at the age of twelve already. I imagine he may have surpassed the best of the best you are searching for by now.”

Archidamia’s silence is very pointed, a quiet kind of incredulity evoked by what she’s hearing. “Has it escaped your notice that we’re not cordial with Castrum Kremnos? How do you imagine anyone reaching him, even if he happens to be as good as you’re suggesting?”

A sharp smile spreads across Ptolemy’s face, and Archidamia immediately narrows her eyes. “I am of age, and I’m one of the very few that aren’t formally exiled,” he says with great satisfaction. “I can guide Phainon and Mydei through the fortress to find the boy.”

“Why, by all Titans almighty, would you take Lord Mydeimos to the very place that wishes to slaughter him on sight?” Archidamia questions, her voice strained.

It’s something they discussed before coming over, after they got every single detail out of Peucesta and formed a plan. Mydei and Phainon have to participate in this retrieval mission, and it’s non-negotiable. Phainon pushed for it adamantly. Even if they ever make their way back to Castrum Kremnos years later, Mydei deserves to see it as soon as possible. He should have at least some good memories of it. Phainon lost his homeland before he was ready; he wants his friend to experience it before it’s too late.

“It’s Mydei’s birthplace. Don’t you think he deserves to witness for himself how his homeland functions?” Ptolemy shoots back without hesitation, humming as he pretends to think it over. “Isn’t this the perfect opportunity to show they’re ready for a larger scale of operations, if they are to successfully return without giving anything away? Besides, who knows if that boy will agree to leave Castrum Kremnos unless I have ironclad proof, which would be Mydei himself.” Those are perfect arguments. Phainon doesn’t think they can be disputed even if Archidamia tries. Ptolemy looks her dead in the eye as he continues, “I know you’ve been eyeing Aidonia for a while now, Lady Archidamia. Wouldn’t it be in your interest to get your soon-to-be mightiest soldiers prepared as quickly as possible?”

There is a long moment of silence as Archidamia digests his words. “The fortress is constantly on the move, always by the site of conflict soon to be born,” she says eventually, and Phainon cheers internally when she doesn’t rebut anything Ptolemy has said. “There is no guarantee we will find its

precise location anytime soon. Or that it will be close enough to even attempt traveling. I cannot begin to describe just how much luck you’d need to possess for this to occur.”

“Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity,” Ptolemy quotes shamelessly.

Phainon is having the time of his life witnessing this battle unfold. It’s fascinating to watch. Ptolemy might not be the greatest of warriors, but he sure is a formidable opponent in verbal spars. Archidamia, meanwhile, is as knowledgeable in strategy as she is headstrong. If she doesn’t agree with an idea, she will go to great lengths to stand her ground.

“Well. We have quite a lot of time to spare until the time limit you have set runs out, wouldn’t you say, Lady Archidamia?” Ptolemy shrugs without a shred of concern. “I have no doubt our skilled scouts possess the ability to find its coordinates rather quickly. And who knows, perhaps it is written in fate, and the fortress will appear close enough just in time.”

Archidamia sighs, pinching the bridge of her nose. “What motive do you have in this, scholar?” She asks bluntly. “You are an annoying pest at the best of times. I find it hard to believe you suddenly gained the courage to offer yourself in such a way.”

“I am immensely flattered you hold me in high regard, Lady Archidamia,” Ptolemy replies in an overly sweet tone. “What if I said I simply wish to accompany the Crown Prince in the crucial step on this grand path of his life?”

“I know the eyes of a schemer, child. You may hold more intelligence than even an above-average person, but you cannot shed the skin of an opportunist.” Archidamia’s harsh words make Ptolemy’s eye twitch in a funny way, but he doesn’t refute her either. As she continues, it doesn’t seem like she cares that much for his reasoning. “But I shall entertain your request. I will discuss it with the Council at the soonest opportunity. Should we come to an agreement and allow you to make your journey, we will appoint scouts to locate the fortress’s whereabouts. You three should pray to all Titans that it’s revealed to be somewhere close.”

“Yes,” Phainon hisses quietly in victory, pumping his fist in the air. He finally takes his eyes away from the two and meets Mydei’s gaze. He sends Phainon a wide smile, slightly more subdued in his excitement.

Ptolemy sounds extremely self-satisfied when he speaks next, his own smile bordering on smug. “I am relieved to see even you can recognize reason—”

“I haven’t said the conversation is over,” Archidamia speaks over him, settling her intense stare on the two of them instead, and Phainon’s excitement vanishes within a second. Archidamia could make a career out of killing any positive mood instead of people. “There is another pressing issue with your endeavor. If you are so insistent on heading to Castrum Kremnos, it’s important to remember that your father, King Eurypon, will be right there, Lord Mydeimos.”

Alright. This seems more like she wishes for them to be cautious rather than having a problem with something. Phainon will take what he can.

“I am well aware,” Mydei replies, not particularly caring.

Phainon knows he doesn’t have an opinion on the prophecy or his people’s expectations about his highly anticipated involvement in Eurypon’s death. He never expressed willingness to talk about it at length, even as Phainon offered his ear. Personally, Phainon thinks Eurypon should be thrown into the Sea of Souls at the soonest convenience. Over and over again, preferably. He isn’t very sure about Queen Gorgo, as everyone around appears to possess a great amount of respect for her and what she’s done for the Kremnoan people. It has to mean something, right? That she wasn’t entirely selfish to leave her son to such a cruel fate.

“I hear you never inquired about the past, Young Lord,” Archidamia continues, stepping closer to lean her hip against the drawers placed near the wall. Phainon doesn’t know how she’d ever find out whether they asked every single person in the settlement or not. Or maybe she is assuming that if Mydei wished to know, he would have asked one of the few people in charge of him. “Be it regarding what transpired right after your birth, or the lives of your parents preceding that event. Why might that be?”

It’s a reasonable question. Phainon himself wondered about it at first, curiosity burning inside him to know more about his friend’s origins. And most of all, to understand why his parents would ever forsake him in such a way. Although eventually, he came to the conclusion that it’s not his place to outright ask. Perhaps if he hadn’t been by Mydei’s side at all times, he would have caved. But as it is, if Mydei is content, then so is he.

Phainon can certainly understand not wanting to converse about a tragedy in one’s life. Over the first few weeks after their arrival in the settlement, people would ask about his origins, curious about the boy who found their lost prince. He always simply responded that his homeland was long gone before derailing the conversation with something else or excusing himself. With all the chaos and excitement brought by the Crown Prince’s return, as well as figuring out what that means for everyone, Phainon’s sudden appearance got swept under the radar fairly quickly. By now, he has become a permanent fixture that isn’t questioned anymore. He just is, as is Hephaestion, and as are any other kids running around the settlement. Only that he is also the prince’s shadow, as none of the others are. That, too, is no longer questioned much after that altercation on one of the roads. One good thing that came from it.

He is content with that. He isn’t sure he can handle retelling the tale of Aedes Elysiae over and over again. It’s one thing to mention a slight detail or a memory, even if a pang of grief threatens to pull him under if he isn’t careful. It’s another to admit to everything that happened in there to anyone that isn’t Mydei or Ptolemy. Maybe the rest of his friends, one day, before he sets out to visit his homeland one last time.

“It already happened, and nothing will change it,” Mydei says matter-of-factly, and Phainon’s thoughts halt. “If it were important, someone would have told me by now. They didn’t want me, so they threw me away. What’s there to think about?”

Archidamia’s mouth clicks shut audibly, disregarding whatever else she wanted to say when Mydei didn’t respond immediately. Ptolemy’s, meanwhile, parts in shock. Phainon just stares at him.

It’s… a fair conclusion, he thinks. But he cannot imagine any other kid thinking in such a way. Phainon should have expected it, shouldn’t he? Mydei embodies the very concept of how Kremnoans are painfully blunt and straight to the point. It’s his way of being. He would imagine there’s no other reason for his fate other than being unwanted, since he’s done nothing to warrant it.

Archidamia exhales slowly, eyes closing briefly. She looks pained. “I think it’s time you learned more about your family,” she decides eventually, walking off to grab a chair and drag it close to them. Then, she addresses Ptolemy, “You may leave, scholar. A meeting will be held tomorrow regarding this matter, and on the day after, I will outline the parameters of this supposed expedition to Castrum Kremnos for you.”

Ptolemy nods to show that he understands. “Do you want me to stay?” He directs at the two of them, unconcerned with Archidamia’s opinion.

Phainon looks at Mydei in question. It’s entirely up to him, considering the subject.

His friend only shrugs, face expressionless. Phainon can tell he is trying to come off as disinterested, but Mydei cannot hide the curiosity lurking in his eyes from him. So, nothing negative.

“We will be alright,” he says eventually.

Ptolemy nods again, somehow managing to look more agreeable this time around. “I will wait at your house.”

He doesn’t wait for an acknowledgment, spinning on his heels and walking out without another word. That leaves the three of them in the large living room, completely silent. Archidamia only shakes her head in exasperation and finally takes the seat, resting her elbows on her knees as she leans forward.

She breathes in and out to steady herself, then looks straight into Mydei’s eyes with such seriousness that it rattles Phainon a little bit.

“Even if you never actively searched for answers, I am certain you have heard about your mother’s achievements and rule from people around,” she says, hands clasped together. “There will never be another ruler like her. For a person who didn’t come from the royal bloodline herself, she was flawless in her position as the Queen of Kremnos. I will look up to her for the rest of eternity, grateful I could experience her brilliance firsthand.”

Mydei kicks his legs back and forth a few times before he catches himself and stills the motion, clearly interested in every word falling from Archidamia’s mouth. For once, Phainon also cannot help but listen along without the instinctual need to go against her.

“Have you ever wondered the reason for my exile?” She asks and leans back in her seat.

“I figured it would be better not to know,” Phainon interjects before he can stop himself. Knowing Archidamia, it must be something grand and bloody.

And with that, Archidamia chuckles genuinely at the comment, leaving Phainon stunned. It’s the first time he’s witnessed her express humor beyond a smirk or simple smile, an amused laugh that’s more for show than anything else. He didn’t think she was capable of that. Once he gets over the surreal aspect of this experience, he feels a weird pang of satisfaction at having achieved this feat.

“It’s rather simple, I’m afraid.” She says, and a faraway look appears in her eyes, her expression turning melancholic. “I hadn’t been notified of what transpired in Castrum Kremnos during the small-scale war I was assigned to lead. It’s only on the way back that I found out about Queen Gorgo’s death, and consequently about your fate, Lord Mydeimos. Overcome by sorrow, I challenged King Eurypon to combat.” She smiles ruefully. “As one might expect, I lost.”

Expect? Phainon stares at her, taken aback by her words. Who would expect Archidamia to ever lose against a mortal man? This just might be the most difficult thing he has had to imagine in his life so far.

“For a while, I served directly under Queen Gorgo. A mirror to Master Krateros’ position, possibly one rank lower on the grounds of his unparalleled accomplishments and the duty appointed to him.” Her eyes shift between Mydei and Phainon, slightly resigned. “Normally, I would say you cannot comprehend the unwavering devotion I held for her in my brittle heart. But, perhaps out of everyone else, you two may understand it, and then some.

“To say I was furious upon my arrival at the fortress would be a gross understatement. It felt like someone ripped away a part of my very soul. She was the reason for the direction my life took. All my achievements, all my scars, and all the lives taken by my blades—all given to her on a platter, in exchange for something so simple as being her most trusted general and her friendship,” her eyes grow hardened as she traces a deep scar on her forearm, healed in an uneven and ugly pattern. “Just to find out not a single one of those cowards deigned to stand their ground and aid her against the King’s madness,” she says through gritted teeth. “The biggest regret of my life, for which I will have to crawl to the Nether Realm and beg for Queen Gorgo’s mercy. It was my duty to protect her. Had I come back a few days earlier, perhaps she would have escaped with her son from the clutches of her treacherous husband.”

When they barged into her house, Phainon expected to endure hours of arguing with Archidamia for the chance to be allowed to travel to Castrum Kremnos. He wasn’t prepared to be faced with so much new information. Not only regarding Archidamia, but also Mydei’s parents.

Phainon glances at his friend. Mydei sits with his back straight, expression carefully blank. They taught him well over the years. Never show discomfort. Yet his mouth is slightly thinner, and his brows are furrowed just so. He is conflicted about what he’s hearing. Although Phainon doubts anyone but him would have realized.

“I expected to be swiftly delivered into Thanatos’ embrace upon my failure to avenge Queen Gorgo,” Archidamia continues on. “Though perhaps some shreds of decency still remained in him after what he’s done to his wife and Lord Mydeimos, for he declined his right to take my life. Even so, that meant exile. Despite the shame now resting on my shoulders for not only

being unable to protect my Queen, but also failing the gladiator’s combat, most of my troops followed me out of the Castrum Kremnos’ gates. They still remain by my side in this settlement. I could never repay their faithfulness.”

A heavy silence falls when she’s done speaking. She looks softer than usual, and the fact alone makes Phainon’s head spin. Soft and Archidamia should never go together in the same sentence, and yet. It’s so painfully obvious that Queen Gorgo was important to her.

But most of all, Phainon finds himself relieved to hear Mydei’s mother didn’t take part in sentencing him to such a cruel fate.

“Was my mother kind?” Mydei chooses to ask, of all things. Phainon doesn’t really understand why. They know she was; they heard it countless times from various offhand comments.

Archidamia nods without a second of delay. “I haven’t met a person kinder than her. Her aspiration had always been to gift her people the best lives they could lead.”

Mydei also nods, seemingly satisfied with that answer. Well. If that’s what he needed to hear, then who is Phainon to question it?

“I realize I am exceptionally harsh on you,” Archidamia tells Mydei earnestly, almost regretfully. “I simply wish to guide you to become a man your mother would have wanted you to be, by any means necessary. One day, you will become one of the greatest Kings of Kremnos, known throughout all of Amphoreus. I know it.”

In its own slightly twisted way, it’s relieving to hear. The fact that Archidamia places so much faith in Mydei to reach greatness. It’s a better notion than doing it for the sake of appearances or for much more selfish reasons. She still isn’t a good person in Phainon’s books. But this paints her as more human than he’s seen her over the years. No longer an inaccessible, intimidating figure that’s above something as simple as caring for another person.

Even if Phainon doesn’t think this is very fair. What about Mydei being his own person? And it doesn’t change that the way she may show her care is absurd to Phainon at most times, as extreme as her decisions are.

Ultimately, his opinion doesn’t matter, so he keeps his mouth shut. It’s not the right moment to argue about such things. And it’s just as well, because Archidamia proceeds to reveal more details about Mydei’s parents, words about the past memories, the king’s madness, and the prophecy, spilling forward as if she has been waiting for the right time to share them.

As they step out of Archidamia’s three hours later, Phainon is still reeling.

Mydei’s eyes remain sharp, and he walks home with steady steps, but Phainon can see that his thoughts are somewhere else entirely.

For about three years, Phainon has hated Mydei’s parents with a staggering force. Even when he heard people reminiscing about the past and bringing up the late Queen and her noble deeds. The emotion burned even brighter when King Eurypon was brought up, rarely ever portrayed in a good light. He feels guilty for jumping to conclusions about Mydei’s mother.

She was genuinely a good person, never wavering. He feels joy at the knowledge that she loved Mydei all the while, and that she was determined to fight for him until the very end, willing to throw her life away for a mere chance to save her son. Not hesitating even as no one else backed her up, when it was all doomed from the very start.

Mydei was loved from the very beginning.

And Phainon will make sure he still is, no matter how many years pass. He deserves it. For people to see him as the kind person he is, just as his mother was. On top of becoming a renowned warrior, not because of it.

As they near their house, Phainon distantly wishes Queen Gorgo and Mydei were exiled instead of the grim fates that awaited them. Or escaped with Archidamia’s help. That maybe his mother ended up stumbling into Aedes

Elysiae one day with a toddler on her hip. And maybe he and Mydei would’ve grown up together from an even younger age, and Mydei wouldn’t have grown up not knowing what love and caring meant.

Maybe the village wouldn’t have been so defenseless against the black tide and that cloaked person if Queen Gorgo was there. Maybe at least a few people would’ve escaped with their lives intact, not just Phainon.

Quietly in his head, he apologizes to Mydei’s mother for all the bad things he may have thought about her so far. Half of that hatred he harbored for his friend’s parents disappears, just to be shifted more firmly onto Eurypon himself.

Selfishly, he hopes Mydei will fulfill that prophecy, which led to him being thrown into the Sea of Souls. It would serve the old man right to be killed in such a way.

“How was it?” Ptolemy asks cautiously the very moment they step through the front door.

“Archidamia loved my mother,” Mydei announces, halting any thought processes running through both Ptolemy and Phainon’s minds. He walks to the kitchen for something to eat, leaving Phainon to scramble after him.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Eventually, a scout returns with the coordinates for Castrum Kremnos’ whereabouts. Astonishingly, it’s two weeks’ worth of travel away from the settlement, as the woman relates. Perhaps Ptolemy is right, and this is happening by a stroke of fate. Phainon doesn’t particularly care, not as long as it aids him in furthering his goal.

Then, it’s one more day of the Council talking it over one last time, and the three of them are given strict instructions on what they are to do and what

they cannot do under any circumstances. Again. Ptolemy nods along with a smile so artificial that there is no doubt he has no intention of adhering to the rules. The next day, they are finally allowed to step out of the settlement’s grounds.

Traveling with Ptolemy is just as fun and effortless as Phainon imagined it would be. He keeps a strict schedule, but he knows all poisonous weeds and berries, and has countless tips to make survival just a little easier. He is shockingly good at tracking animals. Unlike when it was just the two of them, now a deer is enough to keep them all fed for two days, rather than most of it being wasted. They are still growing, after all.

It helps that Mydei is now slowly mastering the art of cooking, and they did bring along some seasoning. There are also the weeds and roots Ptolemy picks up on the way to add to the variety. Everything actually tastes good. And Ptolemy engages them in all sorts of conversation, giving them space if they need it, or reciting entire chapters if they’re bored and unwilling to run around and explore.

The one downside is that they have to rest more often because Ptolemy cannot keep up. But that’s still perfectly fine, and Phainon can make fun of him for it all he wants. They have a six-week limit to get back. With their tempo, it should be two and a half weeks spent on walking, then one week at the fortress, and again two and a half weeks as they make their way back.

It’s going so well that Phainon nearly dies on the spot from the way his stomach drops all the way to his feet when a rustling sound comes from a distance as they try to fall asleep. As if someone is taking a step. Then another one. He rises to his elbows and sees Ptolemy’s silhouette sitting up in alarm, squinting in the dark. Mydei is already up and crouched low, positioned slightly ahead of Phainon. It’s awfully familiar.

And Phainon, Phainon is frozen.

He knows the adrenaline should kick in, make him jump into action, and confront whatever threat might be there.

Their camping spot can hardly be called a forest, but multiple thick trees litter the ground they chose for this. And they were just joking around a few minutes back, finally lying down to rest properly. Not a single thought spared for danger.

And he knows they are plenty strong now, both he and Mydei. They can keep up with experienced warriors of Kremnos; there probably isn’t much they cannot confidently face.

And yet, and yet Phainon remains frozen.

His breathing is fast but shallow, and his eyes are glued to the darkness. The trees aren’t close together, and yet nothing shows between them. Was it just some animal running through? A squirrel, maybe?

And as the thought passes through his mind, a person comes out of the tree. Phainon gasps sharply, scrambling up into a sitting position. His eyes squeeze shut without any input from his brain, and the only thought running through his brain is ‘not again, please,’ stuck on a painful loop.

“Phainon,” Mydei’s voice tears through quickly, soft and lacking any urgency. Slowly, Phainon feels him sit back down next to Phainon, coaxing his hands away from his head, where they somehow ended up, and began tugging on the white strands of hair. He continues quietly, almost a whisper, “There is no danger. Open your eyes.”

“By Titans, what in the world were you thinking?!” Ptolemy’s screeching echoes through the wilderness, but it’s not in fear. Rather, in disbelief and anger.

Phainon finds himself complying with Mydei’s request and blinks his eyes open. Only to find Hephaestion standing near that one tree, too busy wincing as Ptolemy shouts to glance over at Phainon and Mydei. Some of the tension leaves him, and his breathing slowly evens out. Ptolemy is still going off, and Phainon focuses on that as Mydei stays glued to his side, thumbs tracing random patterns against Phainon’s palms.

They’re fine. This isn’t a forest; there is no danger. Even if there were, it wouldn’t have been difficult to resolve. Even if there happened to be two men with axes, Phainon and Mydei would’ve been able to defeat them effortlessly. What are two mortal men against them? Phainon has killed people. He is as dangerous as they were. More dangerous than they could ever be, probably. Mydei had already reached that point before Phainon pulled him out of the sea, and he is only stronger now, Phainon almost his equal.

Something loosens in his chest, and he almost feels a click in his brain. There is nothing to be afraid of. At the pace they are going, soon there won’t be anything left that he should be afraid of. He desperately hopes this will be the last time he’s thrown into this state as a consequence of the past experience. He knows it might not be.

“What else am I supposed to do?” Hephaestion bites back finally when Ptolemy stops to catch his breath from the tirade, the strap of his backpack clenched tightly in his fingers. “I’m the same age they were, and all I hear is that I will have to wait until I’m at least fourteen to do easier assignments than they ever did.”

“You cannot compare yourself to them,” Ptolemy says, shaking his head.

“Because what, they are different? And so what? I can keep up!”

Ptolemy doesn’t appear moved by the words, a scowl set firmly on his face. “You are a kid.”

‘An ill one,’ goes unspoken. Hephaestion continues without acknowledging it either. Ignoring his dysfunctional heart, as always.

“So were they!” He shouts in frustration, and Phainon can see the desperation in his eyes. The exact same drive to improve, all other consequences be damned. “I’m the same age they were. And I’m ahead of everyone else, just as they were. And maybe I’m not meant to be as great and mighty as Mydei and Phainon, whatever.” He rolls his eyes forcefully, but it’s clear he truly means it. He doesn’t care for their golden blood. “But

you cannot tell me that if they never came to the settlement, I wouldn’t have been sent out already. But no, instead the bar is set impossibly high now.”

“Hephaestion,” Ptolemy calls, slightly calmer and cautious. “It’s not Mydei and Phainon’s fault.”

“I know that!” Hephaestion’s arms rise in agitation, one foot skidding on the ground a little. “I’m not blaming them. I’m blaming the people who won’t let me out alongside them. What else can I do but force them to acknowledge I’m also capable enough? Lady Archidamia doesn’t spare me a glance. My parents still think I should switch my field. Be an engineer like my grandmother. Or anything that doesn’t include fighting.”

“That doesn’t change the fact that you cannot just pull something like this.” Ptolemy groans loudly, scrubbing his face with his hands. “Do you have your medication?”

“Perdikkas gave me enough to last two months, just in case. For both,” Hephaestion says, giving him a thumbs-up. He loses most of the anger now that Ptolemy switched from reprimanding him to finding out more about the situation at hand, eager to be allowed to participate in their journey.

“That explains why he shoved that many remedies and brews into our packs,” Ptolemy sighs, swiping hair out of his face. “Do your parents know?”

“…They will find a letter eventually.”

“Hephaestion!”

Are you alright? Phainon refocuses as Mydei signs at him, the newly sparked argument between the other two fading into white noise.

I’m okay. He gestures back. He can tell his heartbeat is still too fast, but it’s no big deal. He pushes an open palm at his own chest and purposely flinches away from it. Scared me.

Mydei sighs a little. Phainon knows it’s not out of annoyance at him but rather in sympathy. Golden eyes sweep around their surroundings, stopping on a few trees. He looks back at Phainon, then tilts his head. Forest?

Phainon glances away, trying to come up with an answer. It’s not just the forest. But it’s okay, he is over it now. Mostly. He hopes.

He makes the mistake of looking at Hephaestion, noting the victorious grin on his face. He must have just convinced Ptolemy to let him stay without making much fuss from now on. Their eyes meet, and his expression shifts into one of confusion, the smile dropping and brows knitting together.

“What’s wrong with you?” Hephaestion asks, scanning Phainon’s face. “You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”

Phainon wants to say he is okay.

Except his lips seem to be glued together, tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. He is significantly calmer now, after watching them argue and having a brief exchange with Mydei. But his hands are still shaking, hidden from view behind his legs. There is a dagger underneath his pillow that he itches to hold, even as he now knows there is no danger.

“You woke him up,” Mydei lies, firmly pushing Phainon back to lie down. “He doesn’t shake off sleep easily.”

Phainon lets out a small oof as he hits the ground, staring up at the treetops and stars shining through them. Now Hephaestion will have one more thing to tease him about. And it’s not even true—he is perfectly decent at waking up on time. No one sane is up and running within seconds of waking up like Mydei. So, it’s not Phainon’s fault that it appears as if he is lagging behind in their house.

Phainon reaches up and yanks Mydei down by his arm, taking satisfaction in how he falls in an uncoordinated heap of limbs. Mydei rises on one elbow, glaring at Phainon and kicking him in the leg. Phainon only smiles at him.

“Come on, you brat,” he hears Ptolemy say, and there’s a rustle like he is getting up. “Let’s get you settled.”

They work quietly, believing in Mydei’s excuse of sleepiness, and attempt to let them rest. With Ptolemy’s cursing and Hephaestion’s angry whispers, it wouldn’t be much of a success. Yet Phainon still finds himself relaxing into his blankets as Mydei slots himself against his side, their arms linked together. Phainon knows the muscles will lock and tingle in a bit, forcing them to change positions. He doesn’t care.

He snakes his other arm around and taps Mydei’s chest twice.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon doesn’t understand why anyone would wear this. Well, no, he gets that it’s for keeping the brain safe. That’s the whole point of a helmet. But with the way his vision is obstructed by the metal edges, doesn’t it worsen the risk of another injury? And it’s stuffy. So, he doesn’t get why they design these things in such a way. Just plain inconvenient. Wouldn’t something resembling a hat be better?

Mydei grabs the helmet and forcefully starts pulling it off Phainon’s head without a word of warning.

“Ow,” Phainon exclaims, hands shooting up to grab Mydei’s to prevent his head from being torn clean off. “Leave it!”

He hears Mydei huff, but the too-rough motion ceases. He carefully slips the garment off and glares at his friend, rubbing the back of his head where the metal dug in. Mydei doesn’t appear guilty in the slightest,

“You looked foolish in it,” Hephaestion pipes up unhelpfully.

“Hey!”

“Alright, let me get this straight. You come from a… rudimentary village,” Ptolemy agonizes as he points at Phainon, brows furrowed together in distress.

All three of them turn to him with varying looks of confusion. He had become more frazzled the closer they got to Castrum Kremnos, muttering to himself and not really paying attention to their conversations when they didn’t explicitly ask him about something.

“What does rudimentary mean?” Phainon asks uncertainly.

Ptolemy doesn’t respond to the inquiry as he usually would, instead pointing to Mydei next. “You haven’t experienced life outside of the Sea of Souls until the age of nine.” Then, he moves to Hephaestion, his other hand runs through his hair, the laurel leaves slightly skewed. “And you don’t recall a single thing from Castrum Kremnos because you were too young when your parents got exiled.”

Hephaestion nods absentmindedly, yanking the helmet out of Phainon’s hands. “I remember just a little bit.”

“Fantastic. Excellent.” Ptolemy nods, lowering his hand to rub his mouth as he stares straight ahead at seemingly nothing. “Splendid. Absolutely insane, how am I supposed to get you three through Castrum Kremnos like this? May Kephale have mercy on my soul.”

“What are you worried about?” Phainon asks with furrowed brows. “What do our childhoods have to do with it?”

“Oh, I’m not so sure,” Ptolemy snarks with an eye roll. “Perhaps the fact that in two days you are all about to witness the magnificent marvel that Kremnoan architecture and technology are, when your baseline so far has been the equivalent of sticks and rocks?”

“Rude,” Phainon mutters, watching as Hephaestion fiddles with the red fur bit on top of the helmet. Plume, Ptolemy called it. Phainon doesn’t know what relation plums have to it. Even the color isn’t right.

“It’s true,” Ptolemy shrugs, entirely unapologetic. His knee still bounces up and down anxiously. “Even when you take into account the settlement’s advanced structure, what you’ve seen so far is still merely child’s play. Only Okhema could try her hand at competing with Castrum Kremnos’ might, and that’s solely because of the advantage the teleslates allow them for.”

Privately, Phainon suspects Ptolemy must be playing it up. All Kremnoans appear to have that overly high image of Castrum Kremnos. Sure, Phainon himself may have had a glorified view of it in his childhood when he proclaimed he would travel to the place called Cream Nose, and he doesn’t doubt it’s a sight to behold. But to this extent? They all must be exaggerating because they miss it or something.

“What’s a teleslate?” Hephaestion asks.

Ptolemy replies without dropping the desperate tone, “A communication device.”

“Wouldn’t that be more convenient than this entire thing?” Mydei asks with a faint hint of confusion. Now that Phainon thinks about it, it’s a good question.

“Well, we are not allied with Lady Goldweaver for her to allow us the use of said devices. Though, since you two are Chrysos Heirs, I’m sure she would have looked at you more favorably because of it.” Ptolemy sighs, a bit regretfully. Is it about the prophecy? The… flame chase? Phainon’s interest is piqued immediately, but Ptolemy quickly continues, “We’re getting off track. That’s something to consider on another day, possibly years from now. For now, let’s focus on the present.”

Ptolemy waves his hands in the air as if to chase the unrelated subjects away, forcing Hephaestion to duck if he wants to avoid being hit. Phainon still doesn’t understand what he’s so stressed about.

“Okay, let’s start with the most important,” he says, and turns to Mydei sharply. “You already know that you must have bandages wrapped around any part of your body that shows those red markings. The helmet does not

come off anywhere you might stumble upon a Kremnoan, your resemblance to the late Queen is too striking. But, as so happens, your name is also too recognizable.” Ptolemy pinches the bridge of his nose with another sigh. “I would normally pick you an entirely new one that wouldn’t spark any suspicion, but that makes room for slip-ups. So, we’re going to stick with Dei. That way, it’s familiar enough that it should be easy to use, and the vague nature gives plausibility to be excused as a nickname for something else, like Deiphobus.” He glances between Phainon and Hephaestion expectantly. “Do you two understand? Not a single Mydei or Mydeimos is to fall from your lips.”

They both nod quickly. When Ptolemy is in such a mood, any delay might result in a lengthy lecture. They would all prefer to avoid that.

“Phainon,” Ptolemy directs at him, “It’s very obvious you are not Kremnoan. Starting with your appearance.”

“I am not wearing a helmet,” Phainon immediately protests before Ptolemy can get another word out. That thing is dreadful, he is not capable of going through that.

“Nor was I about to request that of you,” Ptolemy rolls his eyes. “It might not come up, but if someone questions you on it, you can claim one of your parents hails from another city-state. We will refine the details tomorrow until you remember them by heart.”

Phainon nods again, scratching the back of his head. Having to lie about his origins doesn’t sit right with him. It feels like he might be betraying Aedes Elysiae. But… Those are just words. It’s worth it if it means protecting his friends.

“What about me?” Hephaestion prompts, a bit excited. It’s a little cute just how eagerly he wants to be a part of a mission by any means.

“You?” Ptolemy repeats, blinking at him, before he simply waves him off. “You’re fine. Kremnoan in looks and behavior, fitting name. The only reason for the exile is that you are your parents’ progeny. You aren’t known.”

“But that’s boring,” Hephaestion whines at him, grabbing his arm and jostling it roughly.

“You’ve got more freedom. Be glad for it,” Ptolemy replies, acting like he doesn’t even feel the motion despite the way his entire body is moved with it. “There is more to talk about, but I will get to it once we find Leonnius and convince him to join us. My biggest worry as of this moment is that you won’t be able to contain your amazement. But I can’t prepare you for that, can I?”

And, as Phainon and Mydei exchange a skeptical look, Ptolemy sighs for the hundredth time this day.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Whatever Phainon may have expected out of Castrum Kremnos, it never reached the heights of being this grand. The fortress is gigantic, somewhat level with a cliffside, but otherwise floating in the air entirely. Which is so strange and impossible that Phainon’s brain doesn’t fully comprehend what he is seeing all the way to it.

Ptolemy exchanges a few quiet sentences with two guards keeping watch at the entrance, and they are let in with little fuss. They walk into a huge circular building, then step onto a platform at the very center of an otherwise rather barren room. Ptolemy presses a button, and it instantly moves up, a small field appearing around the edges.

Phainon lurches forward before catching his feet again. Hephaestion and Mydei both latch onto him to keep their balance as Ptolemy laughs at their reaction. This is a lift? He stares up. And then regrets doing so. He can barely even see the ceiling. Are they supposed to go that high up? What if something malfunctions? Are these lifts safe?

It takes a few minutes until the three of them relax, watching their surroundings as they slowly ascend. There are murals stretching all across the walls, going up and up and up, and creating a story which Phainon cannot decipher. When he looks even further up, he can see golden statues ingrained into the stone. And this is just the very first building. There is more?

They come to a stop eventually, and Ptolemy leads them out of the tower, opening the heavy door into a long path with a gigantic sword pointed down at the gates. Or maybe even at something beyond them. It’s hard to tell from this perspective, just like once he couldn’t tell where exactly the star was leading him above the expansive waters.

“This is the Path of Conquest. At least try not to look overly shocked,” Ptolemy says quietly with thinly veiled desperation when they cannot take their eyes off a giant being with weird grey skin. “For the thousandth time, you’re supposed to live here, you know?”

Chastised, all three of them turn to keep their gaze straight forward, even if Phainon has to actively keep his jaw from dropping as shiny objects fly over his head. There are also light fixtures attached to the columns and statues, bearing a strong resemblance to the ones in the settlement. The red flames crinkle in the air, and Phainon already knows they don’t burn upon touching. They appear a bit more advanced than the ones he is familiar with, convincingly simulating daylight if it wasn’t for the dark skies above.

And then another guard approaches them, a bewildered expression on his face as he stares at the oldest teen.

“Ptolemy?” He asks uncertainly, squinting a bit. “The mad scholar?”

“No great mind has ever existed without a touch of madness,” Ptolemy mutters to himself. Then he inhales deeply, glancing up at the dark sky as if asking for patience. “I’m sorry, do I know you?”

“Me? Don’t suppose you’d remember me of all people.” The man shrugs and then chuckles. “But your dramatic performance as you exited through

these very gates was the talk of the year. I was one of the fortunate few who witnessed it.”

“Congratulations,” Ptolemy comments, dry as a bone. “Now, may we pass?”

“It’s a miracle King Eurypon didn’t exile you on the spot,” he still continues, and Ptolemy only sighs tiredly. His gaze finally drops down to the three of them, quickly surveying them before moving back to Ptolemy. “You a nanny now?”

“Do I look like I’ve got nothing better to do than wrangle a bunch of kids?” Ptolemy scoffs, and Phainon notices Hephaestion glare up at him, somewhat offended. Phainon fights against the need to point out he was the one who was in charge of them the most throughout the years, just to contradict his words. “They sneaked out of the fortress, and I found them as I was going in. Thought I’d bring them back in before their parents decide their offense warrants more than a verbal reprimand.”

“Aren’t you so caring,” the guard hums, eyes falling back down to stare at Hephaestion. Their friend meets his gaze head-on, unflinching under the scrutiny until it shifts to Mydei. A grin spreads across his face when he takes a closer look, amused by the shiny helmet. “Ambitious young warrior we’ve got here, eh?” His cheerful expression changes into a frown when his eyes fall on Phainon, though. “You sure this one is Kremnoan, Ptolemy?”

“You’re asking me?” Ptolemy asks incredulously, and Phainon feels himself start to sweat. Great.

“You haven’t just used an opportunity to sneak into Castrum Kremnos unauthorized, have you? Our punishments are severe, kid,” he warns sternly. Phainon gets the impression that he is trying to give him the last chance to leave unharmed. “Who are your parents?”

“My dad is an accomplished engineer,” Phainon claims, feigning being insulted. “My mom was born in Aurelia, and I’ve been told I look like her. She’s an architect. But I don’t want to follow in their footsteps—I will become the greatest warrior. Like a true Kremnoan!” He tacks on for good

measure when his nerves get the better of him. He hears Ptolemy sigh yet again.

The guard examines him for a little longer, his eyes sliding over Phainon’s neck to his attire, the same robes Hephaestion and Mydei are wearing. Very standard for trainees in Castrum Kremnos, apparently. His gaze doesn’t linger, and Phainon slumps in relief.

Peucesta gave him a necklace thing that wraps around the base of his neck, the black color a stark contrast to his pale skin. And the golden star underneath it. His markings don’t stand out and aren’t as recognizable as Mydei’s, but they’re still out of the ordinary, all things considered. The necklace—combined with the robes pulled slightly higher over his shoulder —successfully makes it less eye-catching. Phainon has to thank Peucesta for it once they are back. He might even keep it; he quite likes the look.

“Your physique does suggest a proper training regimen,” the man muses in the end, shrugging as he looks back at Ptolemy. Phainon tries not to appear overly relieved. “What are you really for here, Ptolemy? You would never come back without a good reason.”

“I am in dire need of some incredibly specific source materials,” Ptolemy explains easily. “Nothing holds up to the Garbaniphoro Library in that regard.”

“…I suppose I don’t have any grounds on which I can stop you,” the guard hums, smiling widely.

Ptolemy gives him the flattest stare Phainon has ever seen. And he’s been on the receiving end of quite a few of those. “My sincerest thanks for wasting so much of my precious time.” With that, he begins walking again without a warning, leaving the three of them to scramble after him.

“Hey, I’m just doing my job!” The guard calls after them in dismay. “I have to question everyone who comes forth. Also, Ptolemy? You had a point back then, you know,” he adds in a much quieter tone, barely audible.

“Even a fool may be wise after the event,” Ptolemy says loudly over his shoulder, seeming unaffected, but his eyes are downcast as they continue forward.

“You are a funny one, Ptolemy,” the man laughs, “Good luck with whatever you’re doing!”

Chapter End Notes
