chapters.title: Chapter 8: and traverse what remains
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

"How long do you think until someone notices if these are gone?" Hephaestion asks obnoxiously, pointing to the display.

Leonnius' eyes rapidly go from said display to Hephaestion, then back again. He exhales and closes his eyes, already accepting his fate. Phainon is impressed by how quickly he adjusted to their little group. It's not often someone goes along with everything they say if it isn't due to feeling pressured to adhere to the prince's whims.

"Why?" Ptolemy asks as he squints at Hephaestion.

Chapter Notes

It’s nearing the beginning of the Parting Hour by the time they manage to make their way to the spot indicated by Peucesta. Ptolemy was doubtful they’d find the teen in the spot Peucesta recalls from years ago. People’s schedules change within days, not to mention years, he had argued.

“Shut up,” Ptolemy says mournfully before either of them can open their mouths when they arrive at one of the hundreds of Kremnoan training grounds and see a boy with green hair jogging back and forth. Difficult to miss.

“Now what?” Mydei asks, crossing his arms.

Phainon observes as Ptolemy looks down at the prince, then to presumably Leonnius, and then his eyes drift over the people milling around the site. “Now, I will get him to come over. You will have to show him your face, so we need to be discreet.” Ptolemy gestures to the way they came from. “Go around the corner and wait. Do not get into trouble.”

“What could we possibly even do in five minutes?” Hephaestion questions under his breath as Ptolemy walks off.

They watch him approach the teen and exchange some words, Leonnius shaking his head. It lasts for maybe half a minute before Mydei sighs and grabs their wrists, dragging them back around the corner like Ptolemy instructed.

“What if he doesn’t want to leave with us?” Hephaestion asks, peeking around.

“Then we convince him. Duh,” Phainon replies as Mydei yanks their friend back behind the wall.

Hephaestion rolls his eyes but decides to stay put between them. “I’m not sure I would have left in his place,” he admits.

“You wouldn’t?” Mydei asks, head tilted slightly. “You always do what you want. What would have stopped you?”

“Well, if a pretty prince personally asked, maybe I would go,” Hephaestion says wistfully before slapping a hand over his mouth with alarm, like something he shouldn’t have said slipped out. It is objectively true, though. Mydei is pretty. And Phainon would do a lot if he asked. Just about anything, actually. Hephaestion coughs lightly, looking at an empty wall with too much interest. “I mean. Going off into the unknown is exciting, so maybe I would. It’s just that the adults always talk about Castrum Kremnos as if it’s the best place one could ever live in. If they all want to go back here so badly, who would ever willingly leave it?”

Phainon thinks that if someone is exiled from their homeland on the grounds of personal beliefs or, like, not dying in a battle when victory hasn’t been achieved, then maybe it’s not a place worth coming back to. But what does he know? He still struggles to comprehend how the Kremnoan brains seem to rationalize things. Excluding Mydei, but he is different. Almost as much of an outsider as Phainon is, except forcefully integrated into the Kremnoan hierarchy due to his title. Kremnoan to the core, but also not.

Mydei makes a noise of consideration. “You would also choose to go back like them? Despite not experiencing life in the fortress yourself?”

“It’s just King Eurypon that sucks. The rest must be fine,” Hephaestion shrugs, unconcerned. “So, you must take his place and lead us home, our future king.” Hephaestion grins at Mydei earnestly, already excited about the mere prospect.

Phainon thinks Mydei might be taken aback by the words. It’s hard to tell without being able to take a look at his expression. He keeps himself entirely still, though, which is a sure sign of being unsure how to proceed.

Ptolemy saves him from having to come up with a reply by rounding the corner, Leonnius curiously trailing after him. The stranger looks at all of them one by one, then waves cheerfully.

“So, what’s this about?” He asks, bouncing on his feet.

The first thing Phainon notices is that he is short. Shorter than Phainon and Mydei both, which would put him maybe above a hundred and fifty centimeters. They are thirteen. He is supposed to be, what, fifteen? Sixteen? Will he even grow anymore? Only Hephaestion is just slightly shorter than that.

And he has green hair. Phainon knew about it from Peucesta, but he still feels almost bewildered by it until he remembers Cyrene had bright pink hair. His white is somewhat unusual as well, but not as much. He just got so used to everyone around having shades of blond, brown, and black that he forgot some people have more colorful hair. And then, there’s Mydei with his two tones of hair. Red and blond. Perhaps the green isn’t strange at all, in comparison.

“Just a second,” Ptolemy says, and guides them further away until they reach an even more secluded spot. He then positions himself in such a way that he can notice anyone who might be walking in their direction long before they could hear or truly see them. “Alright. Please, take your helmet off.”

Mydei does so without having to be told twice, breathing out in relief once the metal no longer obscures his face. His hair is flattened from it, but it’s quickly back to its original shape when Mydei shakes his head vigorously. Like a dog. A stark contrast to his usual cat-like behavior.

Leonnius considers him carefully, taking in his features with curiosity. “You look familiar,” he finally settles on.

They all only blink at him for a second. That’s it?

Maybe Mydei isn’t as recognizable after all. But then it’d make no sense how he got identified so quickly in the settlement. They did say he looks very similar to his mother, so maybe Leonnius just isn’t really aware of the Queen’s appearance?

“Have you not seen the grand portrait of the royal couple in their prime?” Ptolemy asks eventually, his expression shrouded in disbelief. “Or has it been taken down by now?”

“It’s been moved, but it’s still up for everyone to see,” Leonnius replies, now squinting at the prince.

Mydei and Phainon exchange a look. It’s a dubious one. If Leonnius doesn’t even recognize Mydei, then who’s to say he will care enough to follow them? Mydei shrugs, not entirely concerned. Phainon supposes they do have a week to work this through. He isn’t keen on finding out what Archidamia’s reaction would be if they came back empty-handed.

They glance back at Leonnius at the same time, just in the perfect moment to watch as the realization clicks.

“Wait,” he says as his eyes widen in surprise. His voice gets progressively louder as he continues, “Didn’t Queen Go—”

Hephaestion lurches forward and frantically covers his mouth with one hand. “Keep it down,” he hisses. A muffled sound that vaguely resembles ‘sorry’ comes from beneath Hephaestion’s fingers before he releases the teen.

“Sorry,” Leonnius repeats. He is a bit more shaken now, like he’s ready to bolt at any moment. Phainon hopes he doesn’t. If what Peucesta says is true, then they would never catch up. “I don’t really look at that painting much. It’s pretty sad.” He glances at Mydei with uncertainty. “You resemble her.”

“That’s understandable,” Ptolemy replies, though Phainon knows by now he must be itching to call Leonnius unappreciative of the culture or something. “But yes, you are correct. A striking resemblance to Queen Gorgo, as he is her son.”

“Isn’t the Crown Prince supposed to be dead?” Leonnius asks cautiously, looking over his shoulder toward the training grounds. He takes one small step back. “Even if not, what does that have to do with me? You wouldn’t be so secretive if this didn’t pose danger. What if I get into trouble for conspiring?”

Ptolemy considers him for a few seconds, then a mild smile spreads across his face. “Well. If you choose not to accept our request, you should be fine as long as you don’t mention it to anyone, shouldn’t you? King Eurypon isn’t known for his rationality nowadays. Only Titans know what punishment he would settle on, were he to find out you’ve been in talks with his presumably deceased son.”

Leonnius visibly pales, his body stilling. “Can I, can I get back?” He asks quietly, a bit scared, and with his gaze averted. “What do you even want from me? Why even me?”

Phainon watches as Ptolemy’s face becomes pinched. He probably relied on the fact that Peucesta vouched for his friend.

“There is a settlement for the Kremnoan exiles. We fight in battles and wars for hire, and we push back against the black tide,” Mydei speaks up quietly for the first time since Leonnius showed up, his voice is filled with earnest confidence. “I have participated in some of them, but I cannot progress further without a capable enough messenger. I am Crown Prince Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos, and I would be honored if you, Leonnius, joined us in our expeditions.” He tilts his head down, eyes lowered respectfully in the same manner as when someone makes a request of him back home.

Ptolemy watches on, smiling with something akin to pride. Phainon vaguely recalls some lessons in diplomacy, given to them by both Ptolemy and some members of the Council. He doesn’t think any of them ever entailed Mydei presenting himself this humbly, though. Pride is one of the core Kremnoan values.

His attention is brought back to the matter at hand when Leonnius flinches back at the action, eyes even wider in shock. “Don’t bow your head to me, you are royalty,” Leonnius panics, waving his hands in the air, his fear momentarily forgotten. “I— I am flattered, Lord Mydeimos. But I don’t think I’m very suitable for the role. I’m not very brave, not like the others.”

“He is courageous who endures and fears the right thing, for the right motive, in the right way and at the right times,” Ptolemy quotes easily. “To be scared is only natural; it means you are not stupid enough to overestimate yourself in the face of danger. But I assure you, these three are the most promising warriors you will ever meet. You are an excellent runner yourself. You have nothing to worry about.”

“I don’t know,” Leonnius still hesitates. “Fear doesn’t have any place in a fight.”

He doesn’t look very convinced, like he might refuse regardless of any argument they might come up with. Phainon sure hopes Ptolemy will think of something believable over the next few days. Can they maybe take him by force and try to change his mind after the fact? It’s a two-week walk, that’s plenty of time.

Phainon stops and reevaluates his thoughts.

That’s way too Kremnoan. The ‘do first, worry later’ approach. Maybe not the greatest plan, after all.

Leonnius swipes his hair away from his eyes, just for the green strands to fall right back down. “Who told you about me?”

“Our friend back at the settlement,” Ptolemy replies with a small sigh. “He seemed confident that you would agree to follow us, but it doesn’t appear to

be quite as easy. Perhaps we made a mistake which resulted in your apprehension, Peucesta wou—”

“Peucesta?!” The teen exclaims, his entire energy shifting like a switch flipped. His brows rise in excitement, and he takes two steps toward them, bringing him even closer than before. “You know Peucesta?”

“Yes?” Hephaestion replies when Ptolemy doesn’t, the scholar blinking as if he’s recalculating.

“Peucesta is my best friend!” Leonnius elaborates with enthusiasm, his body language the most relaxed since Ptolemy first approached him. His gaze almost shines with intensity, and he grins. “Well, I haven’t seen him in years. But he’s still my best friend, you know?”

“He couldn’t come with us due to his exile, as you know, but he is waiting for you back home,” Ptolemy says with a smile. It’s the one he uses when he’s trying to convince Phainon and Mydei that whatever knowledge he’s trying to shove into their brains will come in useful in the future. “He told us a lot about you; it’s clear he cares a lot.”

“Does he?” Leonnius asks, his eyes dimming a little. “He is the only person I have left, but I was too much of a coward when he was sentenced. I regret not leaving with him.”

“Nothing that cannot be redeemed,” Ptolemy reassures him.

“What about your parents?” Hephaestion asks bluntly.

“Always been an orphan,” Leonnius shrugs, not minding the insensitive question. “It’s how I got to know Peucesta at all—we were both admitted to the same group of orphaned children. I’ve been assigned to some couple for a while now, but we aren’t on the best of terms,” he trails off vaguely. “Uh, I don’t really have anything holding me back here. I’m still unsure whether I’m the right fit for the role, but I can come with you if you take me to Peucesta.”

That would still leave them with enough time to convince him he’s what they need on the way back, without the kidnapping. And Peucesta could weigh in after they arrive if they don’t manage. Sounds good, doesn’t it? Phainon, Mydei, and Hephaestion look up to Ptolemy, waiting for him to take direction.

“That’s perfectly alright. We are more than happy to bring you back with us,” Ptolemy says, sending Leonnius the most genuine smile so far. He must be confident in this, then.

Leonnius nods in agreement, bouncing up and down on his feet. His anxiety seems to have mostly faded.

Phainon, meanwhile, finds this conclusion to be very underwhelming. “That’s it?” He asks skeptically. “Isn’t this too easy?”

“Can’t you just be glad and keep quiet?” Mydei rolls his eyes, shifting the helmet to hold it with one hand against his hip. “You’re gonna attract trouble.”

“I’m just concerned,” Phainon defends with a huff. He has learned by now that things rarely ever proceed so easily.

“How is this ever going to convince Lady Archidamia that I’m suitable for expeditions?” Hephaestion, meanwhile, despairs from Leonnius’ side, and Mydei sighs in resignation. “I walked all this way, talked to a guy, and then we came back. She will laugh at me!”

Archidamia wouldn’t laugh. She would raise an eyebrow at Hephaestion before turning him away immediately. Phainon’s been there.

“Well,” Ptolemy cuts in drily, “You don’t think I’m about to leave without my research, do you?”

“Am I the only one who wishes to get this over with as quickly and peacefully as possible?” Mydei asks with a frown.

Ptolemy pats him on the head with a grin, still taller by quite a bit, and Mydei glares up at him in a way that makes Phainon think that currently Mydei wishes for nothing more than to grow taller than him and make the gesture awkward to perform, preferably right in this moment. Ptolemy’s grin only widens. “Oh, but that’s why you are going to be our esteemed leader in the near future.”

“When do we leave, then?” Leonnius asks, gliding right past their bickering. He does look amused at it, though.

“We’ve got a week,” Ptolemy shrugs. “Archidamia should find it sufficient if you get through such a long expedition in hostile territory,” he says to Hephaestion. “We just need to find someplace to sleep, but I figure that we can camp out in the library in the worst scenario.”

“My guardians are on a mission currently, set to come back in roughly two weeks. You could use our quarters?” Leonnius offers spontaneously, looking as if he’s not sure it’s a good idea himself. “There are just two beds, but we can share. Or something. I can sleep on the floor?”

Ptolemy stops. “That’s awfully convenient,” he says slowly. “But Peucesta vouched for you. Rather insistently, might I add. Which means quite a lot, coming from a man of few words that he is.”

“It’s safe, I swear to you,” Leonnius tries to reassure them, a smile blooming on his face at Ptolemy’s words. “Any friends of Peucesta are my friends.”

Phainon thinks it’s a good idea to take him up on the offer. He doesn’t seem like the type to betray them, even on the sole fact that he’s way too anxious for it. And the fact that they know Peucesta appears to have bumped them up several levels in importance.

Not to mention, Phainon is pretty confident they can get away from any real trouble before it crashes down on their heads. In this fortress, swarming with warriors of the same competence as at the settlement. Possibly more skilled. Yes.

“Any friend of Peucesta is our friend,” Mydei echoes back wholeheartedly.

Leonnius beams at him, anxiety quelled entirely. Phainon can almost see those little threads of connection and affection forming as the older boy looks at Mydei. It makes sense. Mydei has a talent for causing people to cherish him quickly. And those that do tend to be fiercely loyal.

Hephaestion was interested from the very moment he saw them in the forest. Ptolemy took them under his wing thoroughly by the second week, Mydei and Phainon growing to be much more than just one kid and a half that he has to tutor. Peucesta, who barely ever entertains requests for an encore, granted Mydei’s wish within a second on their first meeting.

Even Dametrius, who took one glance at them and decided to give his whole house away to the Crown Prince. He made sure to check in on the progress Mydei was making with speech on a weekly basis, simple words of encouragement ready at any moment.

Phainon smiles as another person sees past Mydei’s firm exterior and offers themselves to him without realizing.

One word that comes to mind after entering Leonnius’ quarters is decent. Another one would be sparse.

It’s just two bedrooms, a bathroom, and a kitchen. Going by size alone, it might actually be comparable to Phainon’s old home back in Aedes Elysiae. Except he slept in the same room as his parents, while Leonnius has to walk through his guardians’ bedroom to reach his own smaller one.

It is quickly determined that Phainon, Mydei, and Hephaestion are taking the large bed in the main bedroom for themselves. Ptolemy briefly tries arguing against himself on the decision due to safety, but stops at the realization that they are the strongest fighters among the five. Phainon grins brightly at hearing the words, walking behind Mydei to finally yank that cursed helmet off and throw it into a random corner.

He would have thrown it down the large drop along the Path of Conquest if it wasn’t still needed.

Ptolemy will be staying in Leonnius’ room. It’s not very clear which one of them is taking the bed just yet. Phainon wouldn’t be surprised if both of them ended up sleeping on the floor at this rate. Is every single Kremnoan so painfully stubborn? Is that a requirement for the bloodline?

“Let’s quickly review everything for clarity’s sake,” Ptolemy says as he stands before the large bed, hands resting on his hips and his eyes wandering around the bedroom absentmindedly. “As you know, I will be holing up at the Garbaniphoro Library from the Action Hour until the end of the Parting Hour. Very irresponsible of me, but I will allow you to wander around during that time. You deserve to know more about the fortress, especially Mydei.”

He exhales and zeroes in on Leonnius, who is leaning against the wall.

“Mydei has had a rotation of guards who shadow him closely throughout the expeditions he is allowed to participate in. If he is to lead armies on his very own, outside of the careful watch of the settlement, he will need a permanent royal retinue established sooner rather than later. If you were to ask for my humble opinion, the members have been more or less already selected.” Ptolemy rolls his eyes at the ceiling, clicking his tongue at nothing in particular. “Whether you agree to our offer to be a part of it once we reach the settlement or not, this here is your first assignment. Do you understand?”

Leonnius bites his lip, leaning forward as his heel digs into the wall. “I’m just a stranger you know nothing about. Shouldn’t they stay with you?”

“No, I believe you are perfect for it,” Ptolemy shakes his head with a smile. “Peucesta placed his trust in you, so I will do the same. It’s two simple things, Leonnius. Guide them around the fortress, but do not, under any circumstances, enter the Soul-Forging Zone. Steer them away from the areas King Eurypon frequents and avoid his presence by any means necessary. I permit a broken bone or two to get out of the situation if no other means are available.”

“Will you repeat that to Perdikkas?” Mydei asks drily from Phainon’s left, leaning against the backrest. Phainon has his legs sprawled out atop Mydei’s, and Hephaestion sits cross-legged near the foot of the bed. He nods and points to Mydei.

“What Perdikkas doesn’t know won’t hurt him,” he says haughtily. But his glare lets them know that they had better not repeat the words. Phainon and Mydei wouldn’t. Hephaestion, on the other hand, loves to stir up trouble. “The second thing, the most important one,” he continues as if there weren’t any interruption. “At any sign of danger, you are to run and inform me. No playing a hero, no hiding, no negotiating. You get up, and you run as fast as you can. You are good at running, aren’t you? I know you can do that.”

“I, I will try my best.”

“Don’t try your best, do your best,” Ptolemy admonishes, somehow managing to sound gentle as he does so. “This is your future king we are talking about, on the fast track to becoming the most proficient warrior among the Kremnoans. Trust in him and his companions to buy you enough time to slip out. Trust them to handle themselves for long enough until we arrive.”

Leonnius gives a jerky nod, as if he’s been startled into compliance.

“You three,” Ptolemy rounds back to them, and Phainon slumps back onto the bed. They’ve been over this a hundred times already. “The bandages stay on at all times. The only time they’re allowed to come off is if you’re taking a shower, then we tie them around you first thing in the morning. These rooms are the only spaces you are allowed to be in without a helmet. If you want to eat more comfortably without it, you take your food into a very well-hidden corner, and one of you watches out. Or you deal with it until the end of the day.”

“What’s that got to do with us?” Hephaestion asks, leaning forward and then back again. “It’s all just Mydei.”

“So help me Nikador, if the two of you ever slip up and call him anything other than Dei outside of here,” Ptolemy continues obligingly. “You’d better

keep your head down and not make any problems with your usual shenanigans or, by every Titan’s mercy, I will have Archidamia demote you to babysitting toddlers until you are of age.”

Both Phainon and Hephaestion wisely choose not to comment. Even if Phainon has no doubt that his friend wants to argue just as much. It’s not like they get into their spats on purpose. Hephaestion just has a way of getting under his skin. Mydei, too, sometimes. But that’s different.

“And one last thing,” Ptolemy adds, one of his hands reaching up to scratch his chin. “Not a single word of this to Archidamia, or she will have me executed on sight.” A stilted smile quirks his lips up. “As far as she’s concerned, it took a week to find and convince him. The fortress is big. It was difficult to get him to leave with us. End of the story.”

All of them nod, Leonnius included. He has no clue who Archidamia might be, but his look of concern is as genuine as it gets.

That seems to be the end of the conversation, Ptolemy satisfied enough with it. He will probably return to it tomorrow morning, either to repeat himself or to add a detail. Or two. Or ten.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

One decision that didn’t even register as anything that important, and things could have developed differently.

“Hephaestion,” Hephaestion corrects. Then, adds belatedly, “My Lord.” It comes off less reverent than anyone else’s, but it could be dragged up to nerves. Phainon hopes, at least. Surely there must be people who get nervous around the Kremnoan royalty? Even among the subjects.

Especially among the subjects. Or perhaps not, if they are being punished for showing weakness, last Phainon heard.

“Congratulations,” Eurypon says, not sounding particularly happy or appreciative of Hephaestion’s victory. “I must say, you appear a bit frail for a boy. Not to mention a young warrior who has won a tournament.”

As soon as the condescending words fall from Eurypon’s mouth, Phainon grabs Mydei’s wrist to stop him from taking a step forward. Mydei is protective, Phainon knows it better than most, but it could only bring harm if he were allowed to argue about Hephaestion’s skill with the King in the heat of a moment. And Leonnius would actually faint if that were to happen.

Hephaestion scowls, though it seems he’s trying to keep the expression in check. “My heart doesn’t function properly,” he reluctantly admits.

“Even if that may be so,” the King says flippantly, “It shouldn’t be treated like an excuse.”

Phainon bites on his tongue, grip on Mydei’s wrist tightening to the point where it must hurt. Mydei doesn’t flinch, standing eerily still. Phainon is so glad his eyes are hidden in the shadows of the helmet. He’s seen the predator-like gaze when he’s furious at someone thrice in all the years they’ve spent together, and it would only serve to reveal he isn’t another random kid.

But now, the reason for his tight grasp on Mydei isn’t to keep him back. It’s also to keep himself centered.

Because Hephaestion works harder than anyone Phainon has ever known. He trains day in and day out, and he excels in his fields. He is above his year group, and Phainon would feel confident if he were to participate alongside them in the battles. At the age of twelve and mortal, which is a scary thought. He doesn’t have the raw power Phainon and Mydei possess. But he has the talent and finesse, both slowly and meticulously being polished to perfection, and then a step further. Pushing against the illness despite what anyone else’s opinion may be.

Hephaestion is twelve.

And he has more integrity and drive than most adults Phainon has met. Standing out even among the Kremnoans, the people who infamously stop at nothing when it has to do with the glory gained through battle. It rivals Phainon’s own ambition, and what amazes him even more is that Hephaestion doesn’t have that end goal born from a tragedy to keep him on the course. It’s just the way he is.

Sometimes Phainon wonders what normal twelve and thirteen-year-olds do and think. He and Cyrene were the oldest in Aedes Elysiae, and the next person older than them was a girl seven years their senior. Phainon doesn’t remember her very well, not to mention what she could have been like when she was his age.

“The day I let this thing get in the way of a fight is the day I die,” Hephaestion vows with the most serious look Phainon has ever seen in his eyes. “My Lord.”

“I should hope so,” Eurypon replies, gaze sliding away from Hephaestion and toward them. It settles on Mydei, running over the bandaged limbs. “And you? Are you also ill?”

“Skin condition,” Phainon blurts out immediately, dropping Mydei’s wrist to scratch the back of his head. He smiles awkwardly, aiming for friendly. He’s not sure he succeeds, but it doesn’t matter. Mydei stays put, and the King doesn’t even look at Phainon.

“What a weak generation,” Eurypon scoffs, shaking his head. The man next to him perks up, sensing it might be time to move forward again. “Nikador would be disappointed in the Kremnoans for raising such pitiful children.” And just like that, he deems the conversation to be over. His eyes slide away from their group, and he turns away. “It’s time for us. Krateros must already be awaiting our arrival.”

Phainon has no idea who Krateros is, but the king’s underlings nod solemnly and trail after him when he starts walking away, their fancy robes flowing along in the air. Meanwhile, the four of them stay rooted in place

until the heavy doors creak open, watching as the king disappears behind them.

“I don’t think you look ill,” Leonnius comments, looking in each and every direction. To check whether anyone is paying too much attention to them, Phainon presumes.

“The King would beg to differ,” Hephaestion replies drily, reaching up to swipe his thumb across his bottom lip, catching on his teeth. “But thanks. I guess.”

“No, I’m serious,” Leonnius says with slightly furrowed brows, abandoning his self-imposed task of surveillance to look Hephaestion over. “You’re thin, but that’s good for stealth and speed. I would have thought you made that illness up, but there’s no reason for you to have come up with that lie in the first place.”

“Oh,” Hephaestion says softly. A small smile quirks his lips up. “Yeah, I’ve got hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It makes the walls of my heart really thick. It gets worse with any strenuous physical activity.”

“And you are a… fighter?” Leonnius asks, as if he’s making sure he understands right. His eyebrows rise up in surprise. “Won’t that kill you?”

“Most Kremnoans already die on the battlefield,” Hephaestion replies lightly. “It was discovered when I was very young, so I’ve been taking medication to keep it in check ever since I can remember. I’m not about to let anyone kill me, so yes, I’m most probably going to die from it.”

Leonnius can only offer a sympathetic look at the words. Phainon has heard them already, and he can only wish that perhaps calmer times may arrive before the illness can take Hephaestion’s life. He doubts Hephaestion would have enjoyed a peaceful life regardless of the circumstances. It’s like he’s been born for this, the perfect example of a Kremnoan spirit.

“Ptolemy is never taking us anywhere again,” Mydei comments flatly.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 9: and guide them back
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

An object comes flying straight at his head, and Phainon yelps, catching it in the very last moment before the metal can make contact with his face. With so much force behind the throw, it could've killed him.

"Are you trying to kill me?" Phainon asks angrily, shaking the stupid helmet in his hand. He has half a mind to throw it away this instant. But then Mydei or Ptolemy might want to go find it among the bushes, and that'd be a waste of time.

"Want me to break your nose?" Mydei asks casually as he ignores Phainon's outrage, though he is smirking just a little, and Phainon's eyes narrow. "We can both bleed everywhere, then."

Chapter Notes

“Are you done with your research?” Leonnius asks over the dinner Mydei quickly put together, dropping some meat into his mouth. Leonnius and Ptolemy were sent on a mission to acquire ingredients, leaving the three of them alone in the quarters for about half an hour. “We’re leaving tomorrow, aren’t we?”

“Yes, in the evening. I managed to bid farewell to my parents this time around,” Ptolemy responds, turning pages in the notebook laid out in front of him as he blindly takes a bite out of a sandwich. “And I’m just about done. I have five more books I must get through. I already sorted through which ones I wish to take with me, and they’re stacked on the desk I claimed for myself upon my arrival.”

“Does your girlfriend know about that?” Hephaestion asks, grinning around the fork.

“Not my girlfriend,” Ptolemy replies with a wince, still staring at the pages. “Sevasti would have chopped my head off if she knew. And then she would set my severed head by the front door to serve as a warning. Perhaps she will forget about the missing books by the time we meet again. If we ever meet again.”

“When I finally killed that biggest sea beast, it painted the entire sea red, and no other creatures would approach me for months,” Mydei comments casually between bites. Everyone’s eyes immediately snap to him. “It’s a good strategy.”

“You killed sea beasts?” Leonnius exclaims, visibly excited. “At your age? How come?”

Phainon can see Hephaestion looking their way, impressed as well. He feels pride in his friend’s strength being acknowledged. That’s right, Mydei had been outstanding even before they arrived at the settlement.

“Stranded at the Sea of Souls for close to ten years,” Mydei says, not even looking at any of them, his gaze locked on the plate instead. He doesn’t put any importance on the words, spoken as if it’s a simple fact of life. “Though I was eaten alive by those monsters before I got the hang of evading them. Or killing them.”

And just like that, all Phainon feels is bitterness. He deeply wishes he could throw Eurypon into the Sea of Souls a thousand times over.

Mydei seems oblivious to the silence that falls, Leonnius dropping his fork and Hephaestion growing pale. Ptolemy’s face is still angled down toward his notebook, but it’s obvious he isn’t reading anymore. Phainon, at least, is used to hearing or witnessing Mydei bear the consequences of Thanatos refusing him entry to the Nether Realm. And just for that, Thanatos may be Phainon’s favorite Titan nowadays. As much as suffering the prolonged existence may have caused Mydei, Phainon is selfishly thankful for it if it means he won’t die anytime soon.

Mydei’s fighting style has been developing into something more reckless over the last months of nonstop missions. They only send them with two

handlers at most, even to bigger battles, as Mydei is sure to get rid of any enemies within an hour, regardless of their numbers. That’s not to say Phainon is struggling to keep up; he’s also providing valuable aid that leads to certain victory. It’s just that he doesn’t kill every man who comes too close. And he doesn’t allow a lance to impale him straight through just to have an easier reach to stab someone through the eye. He doesn’t let anyone cut his hand clean off just to roll with the motion and kill a person before they can raise their sword again.

And at first glance, it may look as if Mydei doesn’t feel pain at all. During one of the check-ups with Perdikkas, he revealed it’s simply that he is so used to the sensation that it no longer properly registers in his brain.

So yes, Phainon is used to seeing gore splattered across Mydei, vibrant gold mixing with the dark red. He is used to the sacrifices Mydei makes, refusing to hear a word of it when Phainon and Perdikkas practically beg him to be more careful. It doesn’t seem to go through his skull. He cannot die, and he regenerates fast. He has died twice since they started partaking in the expeditions, and was back up and running within three minutes, before Phainon could even truly panic. In Mydei’s mind, it’s a worthy sacrifice to make.

It doesn’t prevent Phainon’s stomach from twisting in on itself each and every time. Whenever Mydei is hurt seriously, Phainon suddenly finds it easier to drive his sword through an enemy. Anything to get closer to Mydei and protect him, anything to end the battle as soon as possible and allow Mydei to recover.

Someone once said that sending both of them is overkill. And perhaps that’s why Archidamia agreed so easily to this mission. Maybe she also thinks it’s time to send them off to something more difficult, see what happens if they let loose.

“I’ve been meaning to ask,” Mydei speaks up again, as if the tension in Leonnius’ quarters hasn’t thickened so much that it’s a little suffocating. Phainon isn’t entirely certain whether he simply cannot sense it or if he just doesn’t care. “How did Peucesta get exiled?”

He takes a sip of the pomegranate juice, eyes fixed on Leonnius. And it’s as if a bubble pops, everyone’s attention redirected to the new subject. It’s not like there’s anything else they can ask about in relation to him being eaten alive, and it felt awkward to randomly bring something else up.

And it is a good question, Phainon can acknowledge after he forcibly shoves the new information into an already overflowing box of things that create the foundations of the staggering loathing he feels toward Eurypon. With each passing day, Phainon thinks he might kill the man himself if Mydei decides not to.

Well, that’s for the future him. Now, he’s got Peucesta’s exile to think about. He isn’t sure he ever questioned the teen’s presence in the settlement. Phainon half-assumed he was the same as Hephaestion, having arrived so young that he might as well have been born into it. Although, again, no parents to speak of.

“I don’t know either, actually,” Ptolemy admits, finally closing the notebook and setting it off to the side. “I’ve known him for years, but we never spoke about our pasts.”

Alright, that’s surprising. Ptolemy knows most things, even baseless rumors circulating around the settlement. Phainon wonders whether Perdikkas has any idea and simply never shared.

Four pairs of eyes settle on Leonnius with curiosity.

“Normally, I’d say to ask him since it’s not my place to tell you,” Leonnius huffs, rolling his eyes. But he has a soft smile plastered to his face, like he does at every mention of Peucesta. “But I know he would’ve just relegated the task to me. It’s not really a secret either; I’m sure there are people in your settlement who know as well.”

“Peucesta has garnered something akin to popularity thanks to his talent in music,” Ptolemy comments. “I’m confident that if there were people aware of his past to that extent, they wouldn’t have been able to resist the urge to spread the gossip forward.”

“They could just respect him too much to break his trust,” Leonnius shrugs. He picks his food back up, taking a bite, chewing, and swallowing it down. “He killed three Kremnoan soldiers.”

Huh.

Peucesta doesn’t seem the type. Phainon supposes exile is a fitting punishment for such a crime. He is surprised they weren’t harsher on him, even. Three soldiers who no doubt had some reputation from past battles, and Peucesta, who doesn’t even partake in such things. Unless he did, but Phainon finds it hard to imagine. If he does the math, Peucesta would’ve probably been too young for it anyway.

“The reason was, uh,” Leonnius continues, frowning down at the plate. “Sexual harassment?”

Huh?

This is only getting more confusing by the second.

Phainon glances over just in time to see Ptolemy turning to Mydei with a conflicted expression. “I don’t think we covered much in terms of these subjects in our lessons,” he says, eyes wandering over to Phainon and Hephaestion. “But it’s when someone forces themselves onto another person, making unwanted advances of a sexual nature. To put it most simply and quickly, as the term implies.”

Mydei nods, a little stilted.

The whole topic of sex was very briefly touched upon. Ptolemy decided the elaboration on it would be moved up to an unspecified date in the future, when they are old enough for the content to be age-appropriate. The one thing Phainon really remembers Ptolemy emphasizing is that anything sexual should only ever be conducted between two or more willing parties. Consent and comfort are the most important, and they should wait until they’re sure about the other person before proceeding. And he explicitly forbade them to engage in such things until they are sixteen at the very least.

Which, now that he thinks about it, is in less than three years. He wonders whether that elaboration will come sooner than that. If it wasn’t going to, it probably will now.

Phainon has a rough idea of it. Well, he knows how babies are made. He’s seen people who date around the settlement, and there’s the recent incident with Sevasti. And also, he’s been steadily ignoring certain bodily urges that seem to appear every now and then. It just feels awkward and embarrassing. Especially since he is never alone. Anyway.

Phainon refocuses on the situation at hand, noting the way Hephaestion’s nose is wrinkled up in disgust. Mydei is frowning, and Leonnius looks a little uncomfortable. Maybe it was the wrong question to ask.

“By Kremnoan law, sexual harassment is punishable by death, so Peucesta hasn’t done anything wrong,” Ptolemy muses, rekindling the subject instead of letting it die or changing it. “How come he still got exiled in the end?”

“The evidence was too ambiguous to reach a straightforward conclusion. It didn’t help that he killed them in their sleep, which is seen as disgraceful.” Leonnius picks up a bun and starts tearing it into small pieces, each one thrown onto the now-empty plate. “The victim wasn’t very credible, as there had been numerous claims made before, all of them resolved. In that one, witnesses confirmed some suspicious behavior, but nothing conclusive. If Peucesta was deemed guilty of unjust killing, his life would have been taken. If he were absolved of his crimes, he would have been able to lead his life as if nothing happened. No one knew what to do when he was stuck somewhere in between, so he’d been banished into exile.”

Oh. In that case, perhaps exile was the best option. Who’s to say someone wouldn’t have paid to fabricate evidence against him sooner or later? It’s not so long ago that the Council attempted to teach Mydei about bribes and how to handle them. Namely, to never accept them, regardless of circumstances. As if Mydei ever would have done that in the first place.

“You aren’t happy here,” Mydei speaks up again, as blunt and random as ever. Phainon almost stops him from continuing in fear of him touching another unpleasant subject. “Why haven’t you gone with him?”

He glances at Phainon once, like he can barely comprehend the idea of leaving him behind. It warms something deep inside Phainon, making him just a little giddy.

“He offered, but I was too much of a coward.” Leonnius smiles at them, but it appears painfully bitter. He throws a bit of bread into his mouth. “Didn’t think the life outside of here was for me. I was afraid that I would only slow him down or accidentally get us into trouble. People always get mad at me for not being able to stand my ground, so I thought I would only drag him down like that.”

“I think everyone should do what they want,” Hephaestion pipes up defensively. “So what if someone told you that you’re not fit for it? And so what if you fail? If you wanted to go, you should’ve gone.”

“I was exactly your age when it happened, I think. I wish I had seen things in that light back then,” Leonnius replies with a sigh. “He looked devastated upon my refusal to leave with him, and it haunts me to this day. But I can’t change the past, unfortunately.”

Oh, what Phainon would’ve given for such a power. He would have prevented Aedes Elysiae’s destruction. He would have dragged them all the way to the Sea of Souls and begged them to search for a boy who’s drowning somewhere in its depths. He would have led them to the settlement and hoped the Kremnoans would be willing to take them in.

He has long since stopped yearning for a miracle of such magnitude, though.

“No, but we can take you back to him,” Phainon says with a bright grin. “And you can work hard to fix the past mistake.”

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon’s eyes snap open when something collides sharply with his leg.

He spares a single thought of gratitude that he didn’t startle enough to fall out of the bed, and then the sight of golden eyes right in front of him registers. Mydei looks alarmed, one arm angled over his head in such a way that his face is shielded from anyone’s view outside of Phainon since they are lying face-to-face.

Mydei’s eyes dart to the side, then back to Phainon. Frantic. He blinks twice in quick succession.

Uh. Alright. Potential danger. No big deal.

Actually, it’s a very big deal. Mydei’s face is—

Phainon sits up in one sharp movement, blinking owlishly at the two people who seem to have just entered the room. They blink back, their weapons drawn. Phainon knows they can close the distance within a second, and those swords can strike them at any given moment. It doesn’t matter that they are children. Perhaps rightfully so, considering how dangerous they are.

“Um,” he says very intelligently. He can feel the exasperation radiating off the body next to him.

“Who are you?” The woman barks, inching closer.

Phainon slowly puts his hands up in surrender, breathing out in relief when the two halt to watch his movements closely. Titans bless the Kremnoan caution. “We mean no harm,” Phainon says, very loudly and a bit stilted. That’s the point, though, if he wants to alarm Ptolemy somehow.

“There are three of you sleeping in our bed,” she points out angrily. “The only conclusion to reach is that you are thieves. That alone gives us the right to kill you.”

They are teenagers, can’t they just sleep over at their friend’s? Phainon opens his mouth to argue.

“Are these Queen Gorgo’s jewels?” The man gestures with his sword to the nightstand on top of which are, in fact, various pieces of Mydei’s mother’s jewelry.

Phainon closes his mouth.

Shit, he allows himself to think. There is no explaining that, is there? They are thieves. But, well, thieves are better than traitors, he thinks. Or finding out a prince is lying in the bed right beneath those covers. With his bandages off and no helmet.

“I like relics,” Phainon argues faintly. “These are replicas?”

Phainon is certain Hephaestion is no longer asleep either. He is doing a surprisingly good job of pretending otherwise. What’s taking Ptolemy so long, though?

“Are you asking me?” The man asks harshly.

Should Phainon just yell for Ptolemy? He and Mydei can definitely hold these two back for quite a while. But he doesn’t particularly want Leonnius’ guardians to be dead, and that’s the only outcome he can foresee if he goes for it.

What if he—

The door bangs open, and Leonnius almost runs out of it, putting himself between the bed and the two adults. Phainon allows himself to look to the side for a moment, watching as Ptolemy sneaks out of the room as well, a backpack filled to the brim and securely strapped to his back. Were they packing up their belongings all this time?

“Leonnius? What’s the meaning of this?” The woman asks, sword still raised. Phainon has a feeling they won’t be as forgiving and kind as Ptolemy’s mother was.

“They are my friends?” Leonnius says, sounding uncertain as he bounces up and down on his feet. They are all so bad at this. Phainon needs to get

better at convincing and lying to people.

For now, he thinks of the helmet that rests on the floor right below the nightstand, and that the priority is to get it to Mydei. Not many people—if any at all—may recognize his markings, as they are unique to him alone and haven’t been seen by the Kremnoans since his infancy. His face, as has been proven countless times over, is a dead giveaway.

“We’re supposed to believe you finally got close to someone amidst your endless moping?” The woman scoffs openly, shooting him a warning glance before her eyes lock onto the bed, keeping Ptolemy in her field of view at all times while at it. Curse Kremnoan caution. “What’s happening here, Leonnius?”

“If you put your weapons down, we could perhaps come to an understanding?” Ptolemy offers smoothly, stepping closer to everyone and subtly shuffling one of their bags closer to the bed with his foot. “As you can see, Leonnius trusts us enough to offer shelter. I promise we don’t mean to cause you distress.”

“The kid is foolish and naive,” the man says, and Leonnius stills immediately. From this angle, Phainon can see his expression dropping from anxious to hurt. “He would have done anything you could ask for within seconds if you just threatened him.”

Ptolemy’s eyebrows rise, lips parting to no doubt make a sarcastic comment. Leonnius is faster to speak.

“Why do you never trust me?” He asks, narrowly avoiding a voice crack. “I’ve done everything I could to stay out of your way and not be a bother. I know you only took me in because of my parents’ dying wish, but what good is that for if you never support me in anything?”

Unexpectedly, the woman falters just slightly at the words. For a second, Phainon thinks this might take a turn for the better. Until he notices the man doesn’t seem moved by Leonnius’ distress, gazing behind him at the rest of them with hostility. “You’ve got one last chance to surrender yourselves.”

“Please. For all these years, this is the only thing I will ever ask of you, and you will never see me again,” Leonnius pleads with them, stepping in the line of sight of his guardian to block the view of the rest of them. “Let them get up, and we will leave immediately. You’ll never see them or me in Castrum Kremnos again.”

Phainon has a sneaking suspicion that they will, in fact, visit Castrum Kremnos in the future. Unless King Eurypon finds out Mydei is alive and decides to hunt him down in the wild for whatever reason, before they can manage to do so first. But that’s neither here nor there, and still a few years away.

The woman’s resolve seems to harden at her partner’s words. “You can help us detain them, and all of this will be forgotten. Or you will be arrested and tried along with them as an accomplice,” she says with no remorse. “The choice belongs to you.”

“Really. Really? You won’t even allow me this?” Leonnius asks in disbelief. “I’ve known them for not even a full week, and they’ve treated me with more respect than you ever did. Maybe I’m stupid and naive, but I would rather die with the delusion that I’m doing something good than remain here. I’m beyond glad you never had a child of your own,” he finishes harshly, and Phainon feels his own brows rising. He didn’t know Leonnius had it in him to stand up for himself. Maybe he is braver than he is giving himself credit for.

The man’s grip on the sword trembles. Leonnius must have hit a sore spot. “How dare—”

“I see you’ve made the decision,” the woman interrupts and goes for a strike without another warning. Leonnius’ speed works in his favor, helping him dodge with relative ease even as his entire being radiates with anxiety.

Using the distraction, Phainon quickly jumps down from the bed and throws some clothes at Mydei, followed by the helmet. He notices Leonnius trying his best to keep his guardians’ attention solely on himself, and feels appreciation grow inside of him.

“Grab only the essentials. We can make do without most things,” Ptolemy tells them quickly before he also joins in the fight with his dagger.

As if Phainon and Mydei would ever do that instead of getting involved in the fight themselves.

Figuring they’re about to be forced into leaving rather quickly, Phainon allows himself to throw on his clothes first. The shirt and shorts are quickly put on, but he curses quietly as he sets to halfheartedly tie his sandals.

From the corner of his eye, he watches as Hephaestion scrambles to his feet, frantically rummaging in his own backpack to make sure all of his medication is still stored there. Mydei only slips his robes back on, keeping his face angled away from the fight until he can put the helmet on. Quick and to the point. Just as Ptolemy hisses in pain, Phainon’s eyes immediately zero in on the red line blooming to life on his forearm. Oh, they’d better hurry.

Mydei is of the same mind, rushing to aid them without any shoes on. Phainon should have figured. He only gets to his feet when Mydei’s hand already slips into the space between the blade and Ptolemy’s arm before it can connect again. Phainon also rushes forward, just as the golden blood starts pouring out. He grabs the sword lying on the dresser, glad for the Kremnoans and their habit of hoarding weapons, and engages the man in battle. It’s more difficult than the regular fights he and Mydei go through on the expeditions, given the standard Kremnoan training. Still nothing that would require his full attention. Not when Phainon fights Mydei regularly, and the few two-on-one spars with Archidamia as of late.

I don’t care if you get sick of me; you made that offer once, and you said it’s standing even if I refuse, so I’m taking you up on it, and you have to deal with it.” They catch the tail end of what appears to be a rambling apology delivered at the speed of light.

They stand above them as Peucesta lies completely prone with a much smaller teen clinging to him desperately. Leonnius sits with one— impressively—muscular leg on each side of Peucesta’s waist, hands fisted in the musician’s white robes. Peucesta only stares up at the starry sky with a dazed expression and doesn’t even look over when they approach.

“I know you must be mad at me, but can you say something?” Leonnius continues, his voice cracking a little. “I will make it up to you! Just please let me know if you can ever forgive me. I’m sorry. I’m really sorry. I know I will never forgive myself, I just wasted years doing nothing. And the only thing I may have to show for it is you hating me. I would give anything to go back and leave with you.”

Throughout the last few weeks, Phainon has learned that Leonnius is chatty when the mood strikes him. Which is often. When he isn’t too tired or anxious about something, he will grin endlessly, yammering about the smallest of things and retelling stories or rumors. He will move around on quiet feet, quickly enough that within a second of having one’s attention turned away, he may already be on the other side of the room.

It’s a sharp contrast to Peucesta, and it made Phainon wonder how the two of them could’ve been best friends in their childhoods. But perhaps that’s precisely what Peucesta needs, as his hand snakes up to rest at the back of Leonnius’ head, and he props himself up on one elbow. Leonnius’ mouth clicks shut, green hair half-covering his wide eyes.

Peucesta sighs, a little red in the face. “…HKS.”

Leonnius inhales sharply at the word. And exhales slowly with a breathless chuckle. Like a switch flipped, a grin spreads across his face, his relief so palpable that Phainon can feel it himself, happy for the teen he met so recently that this reunion seems to be going so well. Leonnius surges forward into the embrace, almost knocking them back into the ground if not for Peucesta planting his elbow more firmly in the dirt.

“You are small, but it doesn’t change that you are too old for this,” Peucesta mutters into the green hair.

Phainon watches, and his mind goes back to Peucesta’s first word.

Hai..? No, with what he’s seen of Kremnoan over the years, it’d probably be something like HKS.

His understanding of the language is close to nonexistent. Only a vague word or two at the best of days, mostly curse words thrown around in training. He had briefly set his eyes on a book of Ptolemy’s written in the old Kremnoan tongue. It’s only ever been a result of boredom, raking his eyes over the words that make no sense until a better activity came to mind.

Kremnoan isn’t even used widely across the settlement. It’s mostly older people switching to it when they want to say something the children shouldn’t hear, but it’s rarely done in Mydei’s presence out of respect for their prince. Common still seems to be preferred in daily use. It makes sense if Phainon thinks about it. Castrum Kremnos is a mobile fortress, and the Kremnoans fight against and with countless nations. Something more universal, such as Common, would be more handy to be fluent in, even for kids.

Personally, Phainon is of the mind that Mydei should learn more of Kremnoan. It’s in the same way that he fears forgetting the dialect they spoke back at Aedes Elysiae. The tongue of your birthplace is something precious and unique.

Yet upon their arrival at the settlement, it had been decided that it was not crucial to Mydei’s development. Something to revisit at a later date, if at all, Phainon recalls. He understands their decision, as Common is more useful

out in the world, and especially for a king who should be able to negotiate with other nations, but by now, there should be something more.

That one word in particular, though, he thinks he may have heard it being yelled. Not often, though. It’s as good a place to start as any. Even if he is unsure whether they will stick with learning the Kremnoan language in the future.

“What does HKS mean?” Phainon asks, too curious to drop it. And if he doesn’t ask now, he will forget about it entirely. There will be other issues once they make their way through.

All four of the full-blooded and raised Kremnoans shift to stare at him. Phainon looks to the side, finding Mydei to be just as confused, head inclined to the side a little. Phainon doesn’t know what that reaction is for. Could it be such a foul word? Why did Peucesta look so affectionate when saying it, then?

Leonnius gets over it the fastest, grinning from ear to ear as he shifts to gaze at Peucesta with his eyes shining brightly and teasingly. “It means he loves me and wants to—”

“Literal translation would point to hyena,” Ptolemy cuts him off, glaring briefly as Peucesta coughs, his hair swishing forward to cover some of his face. “Or scoundrel. But it’s a—”

Without waiting for Ptolemy to finish the sentence, Mydei shifts to the side and, with his free hand, casually points at Phainon. “HKS.”

Phainon feels vaguely offended.

Even if Mydei’s expression says he is no longer invested in their previous argument, either. That means he is doing it solely to be annoying, not because he is still actively angry at Phainon. Well, he might go right back to being angry after Phainon—

“I should have seen this coming,” Ptolemy laments, resting his face in his hands and successfully thwarting Phainon’s slowly forming plan to

retaliate.

Instead of responding, Phainon looks around once more. Peucesta looks exasperated, and Leonnius appears delighted, still sitting firmly on his friend. He’s small, so he probably doesn’t weigh that much. Maybe Peucesta forgot to push him away. Phainon looks up and sees Hephaestion’s gaze jumping between the two of them.

Varying reactions, to say the least. Phainon isn’t sure what to make of it.

“We should get going,” Ptolemy recovers with a pleading look to the sky. As if Kephale could help him when they didn’t bother to lend their assistance with more important calamities. “I don’t want to see any of you for at least a week. And if we don’t get to Archidamia soon, she just might send out that search party.”

They all nod in agreement, and Leonnius finally gets to his own two feet, sticking his hand out and offering it to Peucesta. He takes it without a thought, and then he is pulled up effortlessly.

“Your guardians?” Peucesta asks as he’s dusting his clothes off from the dirt.

Leonnius shrugs helplessly, tracking the movement. “Remained shitty until the very end. Attacked us on the way out.”

Peucesta nods in acknowledgement. His expression gains a more intense emotion as he asks next, “The others?”

Now, Leonnius scratches the back of his head in embarrassment. “We stopped talking a while back,” he says. “But I know they are all alive except one.”

“Alright,” Peucesta says quietly, some of the tension disappearing from his shoulders as Leonnius bumps their shoulders together. His sharp eyes slide over the rest of them until they reach Ptolemy. “Head over to Perdikkas first. I will let Lady Archidamia know you’ve returned.”

Chapter End Notes
