chapters.title: Chapter 23: and rest easy
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

"How can you even estimate that when I know time wasn't a concept for you," Phainon asks with a huff.

"Were you there, Deliverer?" Mydei returns, a bit haughty. As if that makes any sense when they've talked at length about their pasts. They are incredibly familiar with the only points of their lives they spent without one another; they made sure of that.

Sometime soon, they will have spent more time together than apart. Phainon is kind of looking forward to it. Only three more years to go.

Chapter Notes

"I haven't had many nightmares lately," Mydei says conversationally, folding their blanket as Phainon takes care of the bedroll. "Or dreams."

"That's good," Phainon replies, blinking blearily at the way the corners are pushed together unevenly. Oh, well. No one cares as long as it fits into their belongings. "Dreamless nights are pleasant."

"I'm rather sure I've been seeing memories instead."

"That's also good?" Phainon frowns. "Unless they were bad memories. But that's nightmares. But aren't memories also dreams?"

"Phainon," Mydei sighs, as if Phainon is being slow. Phainon woke up ten minutes ago, and he would like to go back to sleep, so he isn't exactly sure what's there to be slow about in this conversation. "They don't fit my memories."

Phainon blinks at him. Three times, because he's not sure what to say to this. "…So, dreams?"

Mydei rolls his eyes and gets up, flicking him on the forehead as he goes to store away the blanket. "It feels different."

Phainon isn't sure what to say about that either. Dreams are weird. Sometimes you wake up feeling like you are in the wrong world or life. It's just how it is.

"Alright," he relents eventually. "What's so strange about them?"

"When it happens, it's as if I have a real memory of an event that hasn't transpired. And once it fades, I can no longer recall much of it unless it was particularly jarring," Mydei says, petting Kokopo on the leg. "It's not always when I'm sleeping either. Everything fades a little as my mind tries to make sense of it for a moment. I just remember things that are impossible to have happened, even if they mostly match our surroundings." He audibly exhales through his nose and scratches his forehead. "I am unsure how else to explain this."

It still doesn't sound excessively strange to Phainon. How many times did he have to take a minute after waking up so that his reality could realign? He gets up to join Mydei next to Kokopo, then tries to halfheartedly shove the bedroll into its compartment.

Mydei clicks his tongue and lightly pushes him away, then takes over the task. "I only know because you are never in them."

"Me?" Phainon asks, traces of sleep fading quicker.

Mydei nods, then sighs. "It's so seamless that I'm not so certain I would have noticed otherwise."

It's… a bit more unusual.

"Does this happen a lot?" Phainon prods, just out of curiosity.

"Difficult to tell." Mydei inclines his head. "I think it's irregular, though. And not always significant at all."

"And I don't appear in a single instance of those… memories?"

Mydei wordlessly shakes his head.

Maybe they should talk to someone about it.

Phainon leans against Kokopo, mentally preparing himself for the day ahead. They should have enough time to hold a longer conversation about this before they set out again.

Phainon, now thoroughly awake unlike half an hour ago, pays more attention when Mydei recounts everything once more.

"It does seem rather peculiar," Ptolemy says around the pencil he is chewing on. "You mentioned you don't retain any information except for a select few instances. May I ask what they are and what's special about them?"

"I know that I chose Kokopo because she seemed familiar in a way she shouldn't be, and that's the first time it happened. Her name also," Mydei admits, brows furrowed. "Certain visions of my mother linger despite the rest of the memories fading. I once had a vivid recollection of living on my own after arriving at the settlement. That's how I realized something might be wrong—I couldn't remember living with Phainon in that timeframe at all despite the fact I knew we had been inseparable."

Phainon listens, a little bewildered. Mydei didn't tell him of the specific memories. He scratches the side of his neck, skin prickling uncomfortably.

"My latest one," Mydei continues, "Isn't really a memory, but a sense of familiarity with Castrum Kremnos. I remember our journey to the fortress, but I seem to recall the details I shouldn't have found out at the time."

"Such as?" Ptolemy prompts, lowering the pencil.

"A tunnel beneath the Hall of Strife that leads to the Soul-Forging Zone," Mydei says. "And a… head of a lion mounted on a wall that speaks? I get a sense that it might be a figure of authority to me. Yet I don't remember ever interacting with such an entity."

Ptolemy rubs his forehead tiredly. "Yes, I heard of that passage from my mother. She and her priestess friend used it on the day we stumbled on them."

Phainon nearly forgot about that encounter. He hasn't thought of it in years, as distressing of an experience as it had been. With everything else going on around them, it's to be expected that some things fade into nothingness until someone reminds them of it.

"And you are talking about Chryseus Leo, I believe. Not to be confused with the stone statues residing in Okhema that go by Verax Leo."

"We've never seen it," Phainon interjects. It's the first time he has heard of some stone lions at all.

"I don't imagine so, even if you know of the lion the head originated from," Ptolemy says wryly. "I explicitly forbade you to enter that area. The tunnel is one of the highly guarded secrets, one I imagine only Krateros and Archidamia could be aware of. You shouldn't know of either of those by any means. I think it's reasonable to assume something is amiss. Though I would be reluctant to call those experiences memories—whose memories would they be?"

"What else would you call it?" Mydei asks flatly. "They are mine. Just… altered."

"When did this start?" Ptolemy asks instead of arguing, pursing his lips. "Don't tell me it took you six years to mention something, or I might strangle you myself, so help me Cerces."

Mydei crosses his arms, and Phainon already knows the answer might not be to his liking. "When we discovered my weak spot."

"So, roughly two years," Phainon says, staring at the side of his head. Mydei doesn't look at him.

All in all, it could have been worse. It still stings a little. They know everything about each other, and Mydei didn't deem it necessary to mention that something might be wrong with his memory all this time.

"It's irregular," Mydei says, a touch defensively. "And I didn't realize at first. I wasn't planning to broach the subject until I was certain something was off. The majority of the time, nothing is out of order. I could have dealt with this on my own."

"Because that would have gone over well if you suddenly woke up with an entire lifetime's worth of different memories," Ptolemy replies, dripping with sarcasm. "It's the most drastic direction this could take, but not entirely unlikely."

"You still could have mentioned something," Phainon says, voice tight.

"I did say I would tell you once I figure it out," Mydei says. His words are tense, and that's as close as they will get to him admitting he sees Phainon's point. "And I did."

"A word or two would have been appreciated regardless."

Mydei's head whirls around to stare back angrily. "If I told you I have a feeling my memory might be altered every other day, you would have called me insane."

"Well, it could be brain damage from the deaths as a whole," Ptolemy talks over them, successfully shutting them up. "Though Perdikkas ran multiple tests ensuring your healing factor covers every area of your body and returns each organ to its full functionality, brain included.

"It could, of course, be purely psychological as well." Ptolemy sketches idly on the sheet of paper, though he isn't focused on it. Nothing more than action akin to fidgeting with an object. "After all the trauma you've gone through, your brain could be creating a version of events that are easier for

you to accept. I'm not sure why it would ever be erasing Phainon of all people since he brings you the most comfort."

"I'm not erasing Phainon out of anything," Mydei says with an edge to his tone.

It's almost comforting that this is his immediate reaction. Phainon knocks his knee against Mydei's, leaving it pressed there.

Ptolemy presses his thumb and index finger to the inner corners of his eyes. "You will both be the death of me." He mutters and straightens up, eyes jumping between them lazily. "Well. It's to be expected at this stage, but your relationship remains anything but ordinary. Congratulations, Phainon. You continue to be the sole anchor for Mydei, tethering him to reality."

Phainon blinks, a bit speechless at Ptolemy's wording.

Suddenly, he doesn't mind so much that Mydei hasn't told him quickly enough. He doesn't have time to process the words properly or get annoyed at the warmth that strangles him from the inside, because Ptolemy jolts, the pencil nearly puncturing the paper.

"The priestess in Castrum Kremnos," he exclaims with wide eyes, as if everything now makes sense. "That was our only contact with a person who can harness the power of a Titan. She offered you a gift, if I recall correctly."

With a newfound vigor, Ptolemy begins scribbling notes. Phainon watches him and gets a feeling his understanding of the conversation won't last very long. Or his interest in it.

"Great philosophers theorized that existence is timeless," Ptolemy rambles excitedly. He is more energetic than they've seen him in nearly an entire year. "Anything that could happen might have happened already, and multiple things might be happening at the same moment. She was a priestess of Oronyx. Could she have given you a link to the prophecies, albeit different than those reserved for the priests of Janus? Or does it have

to do with reaching past the time itself and obtaining knowledge of the countless possibilities it offers? What if the—"

"So," Phainon says quietly so as not to interrupt Ptolemy. He tilts his head at Mydei. "Could it be a version of your past that never happened?"

"It's the most reasonable guess," Mydei replies, humming when Ptolemy grows quiet and runs his eyes over what he's just written. "I don't believe I've ever seen anything of the supposed future, though."

Phainon stays quiet for a long moment, letting Ptolemy's half-crazed words and unfinished sentences wash over him when he starts thinking out loud again.

"I'm not in a single one of those pasts," he rounds back.

"You aren't," Mydei confirms easily, though a bit tense.

"Okay," Phainon says. He isn't sure how to feel about it.

Sometimes, Phainon stares ahead and gets a sense that nothing actually exists, crawling through him and making it difficult to snap back to reality. Ptolemy called it dissociation when he mentioned it, concerned he might be losing sanity at the age of eleven. In a bizarre sort of way, this feels similar to it. Except like Phainon could be the only thing that doesn't truly exist.

But it was Phainon's very existence that made Mydei realize something was amiss in the first place. That has to count for something.

"Would you be willing to write each instance down as they happen?" Ptolemy suddenly asks, his voice louder to alert them to pay attention now.

"No," Mydei answers before Ptolemy is finished speaking.

"Pity," Ptolemy sighs. "May I ask why not?"

"I don't wish to have any recollection of a life I haven't lived," Mydei says, leg twitching against Phainon. "The sooner those foreign memories disappear, the better."

Phainon doesn't blame him, even if it means disappointing Ptolemy and his drive to research all that is unexplored. He wouldn't want to remember a version of his life without Mydei either.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Aias doesn't react as Hephaestion yanks him slightly to the side so that he can avoid tripping over a large rock. He remains unconcerned about potentially becoming intimately acquainted with the ground, much more interested in their conversation.

"Is it true that Lord Mydei was capable of taking down Sea Beasts by the time he was three years old?" He asks, blue eyes nearly sparkling.

"I don't know about three," Phainon comments, a bit amused. Leave it to Aias to have an unrealistic impression of Mydei's strength, which is already way past what's humanly possible.

"I wasn't able to keep track of years until I was ten years of age," Mydei says like it's a normal thing everyone goes through. Aias eagerly nods along as if it is indeed normal, clearly with no awareness of how insane he sometimes seems when the subject at hand happens to be related to combat. "But I would like to say I could freely kill them by the time I was seven."

"How can you even estimate that when I know time wasn't a concept for you," Phainon asks with a huff.

"Were you there, Deliverer?" Mydei returns, a bit haughty. As if that makes any sense when they've talked at length about their pasts. They are incredibly familiar with the only points of their lives they spent without one another; they made sure of that.

Sometime soon, they will have spent more time together than apart. Phainon is kind of looking forward to it. Only three more years to go.

Aias hums in consideration, stretching his arms above his head and then letting his hands slot together against his nape. "I wanted to become the strongest in the world at seven," he reveals with a boyish grin. "I was set up to fail with the two of you walking on the same ground as me."

"You would still challenge the Titans for a fight if you could," Hephaestion grumbles, very obviously listening in despite not offering his input so far.

Mydei, in turn, wouldn't provoke just any Titan simply for the thrill of a fight, Phainon doesn't think. But he has always believed that Mydei would have held up against one of them if the opportunity presented itself, unwavering.

"Wouldn't it be fun?" Aias wonders airily. His gaze then refocuses sharply, snapping from Mydei to Phainon and back. "So, when will one of you fight me one-on-one without holding back?"

"When you become Phainon," Mydei states bluntly. "I'm not fighting anyone with my full strength the way I fight him unless I intend to kill them."

Archidamia was the closest they had to fighting with all their might against someone else back in the day. Now, Krateros comes close in a one-on-one spar, but they are still prone to holding back just in case.

"You say the sweetest things," Phainon says sarcastically, though his smile certainly betrays him. Phainon is special. The only one Mydei can allow himself to let go with and not worry about the consequences, and vice versa. He likes it that way.

"It is very sweet," Aias agrees enthusiastically, already moving past their refusal to a fight. Hephaestion sighs so intensely that his shoulders go up and down with the effort. Aias grins at the two of them, blue eyes glinting and freckles standing out in the moonlight against his pale skin. "You two might be difficult to reach in terms of strength, but for now I am content to remain as formidable as Hephaestion is. It's an honor to be able to match him with ease."

"It's no easy feat to keep up with Hephaestion," Phainon says with a smile of his own. "Especially as a mortal."

Their friend exceeds all expectations, easily leading squads on his own and handling himself well in battle all the while. With some more years, he might surpass Krateros and Archidamia the same way Phainon and Mydei did.

Fed up with having to reach out to drag Aias this and that way, Hephaestion takes hold of Aias' wrist and decides to hold it loosely, adjusting his course gradually instead of yanking him away from a risky path. Phainon cannot begin to guess what kind of expression Hephaestion must be wearing. He easily notices Aias' fingers twitch, though, eyes darting to the side to look at Hephaestion before he seemingly directs them back forward by force.

"Right?" Aias resumes their subject, clearing his throat. His eyes are bright and happy. Their eye colors are so similar, and Phainon wonders if that's the image others see in his gaze, though adorned with a yellow pupil. Chapter Summary

“I can withstand more cold than most,” Phainon reassures Mydei when those fierce golden eyes take on a concerned look. “I will be fine.”

“You cannot regrow appendages,” Mydei scolds with a light glare.

“Not like you do,” Phainon agrees with a small grin. He wiggles his fingers against Mydei’s warm stomach. They no longer feel like they are on fire, though a stinging sensation hasn’t left yet.

Chapter Notes

Phainon and Hephaestion’s eyes meet from a few meters away. For whatever reason, Hephaestion stands over there as opposed to sitting down with the rest of their group. Hephaestion is first to break the eye contact, his gaze jumping to the side, bouncing off Mydei. Phainon struggles to make sense of his expression.

Still, Phainon doesn’t move away because of it like he would have previously. His fingers twitch a little where they slipped beneath Mydei’s waistband, resting calmly against the warm skin of his hip. Their sides are glued together, Phainon’s arm wrapped around Mydei. His head ended up resting against Phainon’s, and he never moved it away, sipping on his pomegranate milk every few minutes.

It’s comfortable.

Peucesta’s music is lively, but the two of them have been up for the last twenty hours, and it’s taking everything Phainon has in him not to fall asleep right this moment. He’s done many more hours before, but that requires adrenaline. Not relaxing with friends. And who knows when the next time they get to do this might be?

Phainon doesn’t have it in him to worry about Hephaestion’s unrequited feelings right now and potentially rubbing it in his face. He will apologize tomorrow or make it up to him somehow.

He sighs, blinking tiredly. He reaches out and slips the glass from Mydei’s fingers to steal a sip from it. The drink has grown on him over the years. It’s not his favorite by any means, but he can still enjoy it well enough.

He turns his head, feels Mydei’s own shift against his, and presses a kiss to Mydei’s bare shoulder. He blindly returns the glass to its rightful place and shifts to his previous position to take a glance around.

People have slowly begun gathering around their group, attracted by the music. Kids laugh and pull each other around, dancing to the tune. The adults watch on fondly, some clapping to the rhythm.

A familiar burst of orange catches his attention, and Phainon looks back at Hephaestion just in time to see Aias approach him, one hand extended as if in an invitation for a dance.

Hephaestion grins in response, performing the mockery of a curtsy that he likes so much. From that short distance away, Phainon still sees his eyes light up when Aias mirrors the gesture.

“I love your music,” Leonnius says loudly over the catchy melody. Four sets of eyes settle on him, one pair soft and adoring. “I don’t think I could live without it again.”

“Music is a moral law,” Ptolemy quotes without missing a beat. “It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything.”

Leonnius wrinkles his nose. “Alright, that seems like a bit much,” he says.

“No one appreciates the art of spoken word anymore,” Ptolemy bemoans, pulling his knees to his chest.

It’s sweet. And relatable.

Phainon could trace Mydei’s red markings in his sleep, and he still loves them as much as he did years ago. He can count on the beat with Mydei’s resting heartbeat, and it’s still one of the most calming things he’s ever found.

It’s unimaginable to live without those little things by his side.

Leonnius beams at him, holding himself up to press a kiss to the nearest spot, which just so happens to be Peucesta’s knee.

A familiar giggle gets Phainon to look back Hephaestion’s way. He easily spots Thera, laughing freely with her hands linked with Aias and Hephaestion both. The three of them spin in a circle, Hephaestion’s long hair flowing with the motion. His attention is solely on the two people next to him, a grin stretching his lips wide as he tugs Aias to speed up.

Well. With how happy Hephaestion seems right now, Phainon might not need to apologize for anything tomorrow after all.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

They can afford to stop only for a minute or two to take in the new weather phenomenon; otherwise, they’d risk impairing the group behind them. It’s a little like rain. Wet spots dot his skin. Much lighter, though. And prettier, the white dots of various sizes dancing in the wind.

And colder.

Everyone but Mydei has taken to wearing full pants and long sleeves, boots instead of sandals. Mydei, with his outrageous tolerance of extreme temperatures, continues to walk around nearly half-naked. At least he’s got longer pants on as well.

Peucesta adjusts his gloves, careful to keep his hands warm and protected, and Leonnius runs around them all with Thera, helping her get rid of the excess energy. She stops now and then, fascinated by the imprints she leaves on the white powder scattered across the ground.

“We all get sick.”

He looks like he is about to launch into a lecture, but Aias plucks Thera out of her route and holds her up in the air, squeezing lightly when she attempts to squirm away.

“No one is getting sick, and especially not you,” he tells her seriously. He shakes her for good measure. “Right, Thera?”

“I’m not getting sick,” she squeals. “I promise!”

“Do you pinky promise, though?”

She nods eagerly and holds her pinky up. Since Aias is still holding her with both his hands, Hephaestion reaches over and completes the pinky promise.

“Now, you cannot break that promise,” Hephaestion tells her as seriously as he can, though a wide grin spreads across his face. “Or there will be consequences.”

“I know,” Thera chirps. “Aias told me my pinky finger will fall off, and that my tongue will be cut off in a serious battle! I’ve never broken a promise, don’t worry,” she reassures Hephaestion with all the confidence of a ten-year-old.

Phainon… cannot exactly tell whether it’s a Kremnoan saying or not. He and Mydei haven’t been making pinky promises with anyone growing up, so they haven’t been told anything of the sort. But no one reacts to Thera’s words, so perhaps it is a Kremnoan thing?

“It’s a lucky coincidence you named your dog accurately,” Mydei chimes in quietly, going unheard by anyone but Phainon.

“Excuse me?” Phainon bumps into him. “I knew all along what snow was like.”

“Now, did you?” Mydei asks, voice dripping with skepticism. “In Aedes Elysiae? One of the few areas benefiting from the Dawn Device?”

Phainon nods happily.

His father told him it’s supposed to be white, cold, and wet.

Snowy’s fur was white, and his nose was cold and wet. They found him on the same day that the conversation happened, so his four-year-old brain latched onto the recently learned word.

It’s close enough to knowing all along.

Mydei’s gaze says he doesn’t entirely believe him. Phainon grins and presses close to him to steal a kiss, then runs away when Mydei tries to grab him in fear that he will be thrown into a pile of snow.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon tries to spit out the snow, only for it to melt as it gets inside his mouth. Mydei yanks him down to take cover before the next projectile can hit him in the face. It would be the sixth now. Or at least he thinks so. It might have been more; his nose and ears are getting numb. Hephaestion’s aim is brutal.

Mydei glares at him, and Phainon interprets it as an, I was getting to it. He rolls his eyes back at him. Mydei lets out an annoyed sigh.

Mydei really took to throwing lances.

Phainon follows its trajectory and sees Hephaestion jump out of the way, landing in a nearby snow pile in his desperation. Leonnius is at his side immediately, pulling him up and toward a more sturdier cover.

Hephaestion yells at Mydei, who only shoots another, much less successful snowball in response. Phainon would be almost insulted at how easily they forgot his presence, except every now and then he sees Hephaestion’s head whirl back to check on where he’s last seen Phainon with suspicion before Mydei pulls his attention away again.

It gets more difficult to avoid being noticed as he gets closer, but he thinks he does a good enough job. Up until the last moment, when Leonnius spots him. It takes exactly a second of awkwardly staring at each other before

Leonnius shrieks, and Phainon mourns their plan’s failure. If he runs off, they will never be able to catch him.

In a perfect timing, a snowball hits Leonnius right in the face. Stupefied, he remains frozen for long enough that Phainon manages to close the short distance separating them. He does the only thing he can think of, and heaves Leonnius up to prevent him from getting away.

A few steps away, Hephaestion looks at him in alarm, hands still reaching for a snowball, as if he is torn between throwing one at him or running away while he still can.

Admittedly, Phainon doesn’t think much as he throws Leonnius at him. He does it gently, though. Relatively gently. He would have definitely thrown an enemy differently, aiming to harm.

Now, Leonnius falls in a heap at Hephaestion, who yelps when he doesn’t manage to get away in time, too close to Phainon to have any chance of it.

“You bastard!” Hephaestion yells at him after a groan of pain or two, a mess of limbs and possibly a new collection of bruises ready to bloom.

Phainon cannot help but burst out laughing at the sight, only waving his hand when he notices Mydei slowly making his way over. He’s always known they make a good team.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

He is on the third out of four small braids, and has complained at least a dozen times about the awkward length of Mydei’s hair so far. It’s so layered

that some strands keep slipping out despite Phainon’s best efforts to keep them in place.

“What’s my reward, then?” Mydei asks with little inflection. Leonnius laughs to the side when Phainon stares at the back of Mydei’s hair in disbelief.

A movement catches his attention, and he looks away from Mydei to see Aias entering the tent, his ginger hair nearly red in the candlelight. He is bundled up in a coat and a blood-red scarf that he pulls below his chin as he

steps inside, shaking the snow off his shoes. The tents aren’t that much warmer than the outside, but at least the wind isn’t blowing in their faces.

“I dare you to try,” Mydei says and successfully regains Phainon’s attention, followed by a hmph. “See what happens.”

He wouldn’t. Because he values his life somewhat, and Mydei looks utterly breathtaking with his hair tied in the more intricate of hairstyles. He wouldn’t deprive the world—and, most of all, himself—of that sight.

There is something about seeing your beloved adorned with what you’ve created. If it can even be put that way. Phainon thinks it’s fitting. He doesn’t have as much talent as some others, but on Mydei, it looks like a work of art.

Kremnoans were onto something when making this a tradition.

Officially, they wear more complex braids to battle, and it’s customary to help your loved one out. Ensure their vision is unobstructed during the fight.

Unofficially, Phainon gets the idea that it might be to stake your claim on someone. Couples often wear smaller matching braids or have a piece of cloth or jewelry woven into their hair that came from their partner.

Out of all things, this might be Phainon’s favorite among all other Kremnoan traditions.

“Sit down,” Aias says, and Phainon glances over to see him press his hands down on Hephaestion’s shoulders, nearly forcing him into the chair. “I’ve been looking forward to this.”

Hephaestion makes a strangled noise when Aias runs his fingers through the long brown strands. The beginning of a blush takes over his face, and he hastily covers it with his hands. Aias laughs, patting him on the top of his head once before he gets to work.

“You’re together!” Phainon exclaims, his own hands frozen as he tracks the movement.

It’s—

Phainon thinks they fit together well, actually. A little unexpected, given the nature of Hephaestion’s feelings toward Mydei. It’s been some time since their conversation, so they could have faded, of course. Phainon is rather sure they haven’t, though.

Well, it’s not any of Phainon’s business unless Hephaestion wishes to talk about it in depth. If this is what Hephaestion wants, then Phainon is all for it.

“Congratulations, Hephaestion,” Peucesta says with a proud smile. Leonnius nods eagerly at his side, nearly jumping up and down.

“I’m happy for you,” Mydei says softly, his particular brand of sincere.

Ptolemy only sighs. “It’s a bit young, but… Just be safe, you two.”

“We are sixteen,” Aias snorts, eyes focused on his work. The corners of his lips are pulled up. “I heard certain Lords got to it at a similar age.”

“Certain Lords are a terrible example to follow in all romantic matters,” Ptolemy despairs. He presses the hardcover of a book against his forehead before letting it drop to his lap. “I would greatly appreciate it if you were healthier about one another.”

“Hey,” Phainon protests lightly. They aren’t that bad. Mydei doesn’t bother saying a single word on the matter.

“That’s right,” Aias hums. He lets go of Hephaestion’s hair, slipping his hands over his shoulders and hugging him from behind. He toys with the button of Hephaestion’s jacket, a wide and somewhat smug grin parts his lips. “We are both healthy and growing boys. I think we are doing just fine. Aren’t we?”

It’s quiet for a moment as the words sink in and get digested.

Mydei huffs quietly, and Peucesta resumes the braiding of his own hair while Leonnius snorts. Phainon bites his lip.

Hephaestion lets out a sound between a squeak and a whine. “I will kill you, Aias,” he croaks.

“Do try, please,” Aias says, then returns to his previous position and sections off Hephaestion’s hair again. “Let me do your braids first, though.”

Ptolemy continues to stare at them in utter distaste. “Damn Perdikkas for dying and leaving me to deal with this,” he mutters angrily as he clumsily gets to his feet. He pulls his clothes tighter around himself, glaring at the room at large. “I will go and… bother someone until they threaten my life or something.”

He doesn’t wait for a response, out before Leonnius can so much as bark out a laugh.

“Deliverer,” Mydei drawls, looking over his shoulder with fond amusement. “Will you be sending me to battle with half my hair undone?”

“What?” Phainon glances at him, then down at his hands, still holding the three strands. “Ah. I mean, if anyone could pull it off, it would be you?” He says sheepishly, then gets back to work.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Most of the detachment that will head into the battle is set to be divided into four under Mydei, Archidamia, Krateros, and Tyche. Then they will split into smaller groups, which will be assigned to other generals. They are meant to overwhelm Aidonia from different directions at once.

Archidamia approaches them just as discussed, Krateros hanging back, though his gaze follows.

“Lord Ptolemy,” she begins, inclining her head slightly. “You are to lead a cavalry in this expedition”

Archidamia looks straight into his eyes, unwavering. “You’ve done exceptionally well last time.”

It’s a rare praise from Archidamia. Phainon smiles as Ptolemy’s gaze narrows. Archidamia’s praise is one of the few Ptolemy wouldn’t bask in.

“Titans forbid you become competent in anything,” Ptolemy snarks as he rolls his eyes. He folds the paper twice over, then slips it into his satchel. “I haven’t heard anything of this when we were picking all suitable leaders to fight in Aidonia.”

“We held that discussion after you took your leave,” Archidamia clarifies calmly. Sometimes it works in their favor that Ptolemy is the first one out the moment a meeting is concluded.

Ptolemy remains silent in his disbelief. Then rubs one hand down his face in obvious annoyance. “Fine,” he concedes. “I will be in charge of them. However, I am running at the first sight of danger to my person. I am a scholar, not a general.”

“When need calls, you are whatever your King requires you to be,” Archidamia informs him. Phainon thinks it might be solely to rile him up.

“He who cannot be a good follower cannot be a good leader,” Ptolemy stubbornly argues back with a quote.

“The willing are led by fate, the reluctant dragged,” Archidamia responds smoothly, a self-satisfied smirk growing.

Ptolemy’s mouth parts and his eyebrows rise in shock. He sputters right after, not expecting Archidamia of all people to be the one to quote something back at him.

Leonnius pats him on the back, openly laughing at his reaction. “If she rendered you speechless, I think she deserves your cooperation.”

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

As a general rule of life, Ptolemy is always right. If not fully, then at least partially. And that’s enough for it to be an accurate statement, as he has often argued.

Snow might have been fun and pretty when they first stepped into this new land. It proves to be beyond frustrating the moment they engage a single Aidonian squad and get swarmed within minutes.

It’s ridiculously easy to slip. The grounds turn into puddles when run over too often. Drenched clothes do more harm than good in these temperatures. It’s easier to be spotted when snow reflects the light, and harder to hide. The tracks are nearly impossible to quickly cover up, enabling the experienced Aidonian knights to find them with no effort at all.

What good is momentary fun when soon after you have to fight for your life and take others’ in a difficult terrain?

Not much. And certainly not worth the trouble.

Phainon develops an intense dislike for the snow when they stumble upon the corpses of their own people who got separated from them a few hours

earlier. Blood in a shade of red brighter than Phainon has ever seen it against the backdrop of snow.

Fun.

For the next three months, the definition of the word eludes Phainon as a whole.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon’s hands are enveloped in a firm grip, then slipped beneath a thick shirt before he can realize what’s happening. He touches the scalding hot skin with his freezing fingers, and Mydei doesn’t so much as blink at what’s essentially become icicles touching him.

Phainon, meanwhile, nearly jumps away when it feels like boiling water being poured over his hands. He hisses, shoulders hunching. He keeps his hands in place, though.

full advantage of the freezing temperatures that prevent dead bodies from decomposing. As if they’re trying to use death to repel them.

Archidamia may have overestimated the detachment’s capabilities when choosing this place as the middle point of their campaign.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Or, more accurately, death by the inattention brought on by it and all the other consequences it would have on their bodies. Phainon and Mydei take all the night watches they can to give their people as much rest as possible. They stalk the areas over which people are spread out and

watch for the smallest disturbances. Five night-time Aidonian ambushes taught them what to look for.

The game is sparse. They’ve hunted down some animals since the beginning, mostly dire wolves as of late, but as they entered the swamps, it’s become all the more difficult to scavenge for food.

If something doesn’t give, this campaign will end right at its middle point. And they are so close.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon’s coat is soaked through, and the snow-covered ground of the swamps gives him the impression he is sinking into it with each passing minute. The branches falling low from the nearby bush tangle with his hair. It’s no matter. He is the least likely to be spotted as he stares at the rather large group of Aidonians who are in the way of their escape, and the rest of his friends sit with their bodies pressed low to avoid detection.

It’s the last step, and the victory will be theirs.

Their forces took over every Aidonian base so far, meticulously reducing their numbers. They sent off their cavalries to rejoin Archidamia outside of the swamps as she gets ready for a confrontation with the leaders of Aidonia.

“You cannot go in,” Ptolemy repeats for the thousandth time, whispering to Mydei somewhere behind the large stone behind which they took cover. “You could kill them and let us leave, yes. But you are more likely to be murdered by them again, and this time we won’t be able to recover your body. It’s not an option.”

Phainon makes a quiet noise. “I can—”

“No. If they could kill me,” Mydei interrupts him, accompanied by a harsh tug on his leg, “They will kill you.”

Well, that’s uncalled for. Phainon is better than Mydei. Sometimes. He has as much of a chance to succeed as Mydei does. They could also attempt it together, as they usually do, but Ptolemy would have actually died of an aneurysm if both of them endangered themselves like this. It says something about their uncertainty whether they would be successful that they don’t ignore his warnings and set out anyway.

“I’m the best at stealth,” Hephaestion offers with determination.

Phainon watches three Aidonians stare directly at the spot where they are hiding. He barely dares to swallow, even if there is no recognition in their faces. They talk casually, words carrying easily in a language he doesn’t understand.

“I just reminded you not even two minutes ago that the moment one of us stands up, much less walks out of the cover, they will notice,” Ptolemy says angrily. He takes a moment to calm himself down, no doubt noticing the way Phainon stiffens at the slightly too loud tone of his voice. “We need a distraction, nothing more or less.”

They could wait them out. But it might take days, which they cannot afford. They don’t have any provisions, and while Mydei and Phainon could manage, the rest of their friends wouldn’t be in any condition to defend themselves should something happen on the way back.

In any other part of Amphoreus, this wouldn’t have been an issue to deal with. They are still weak if they can be held back by something as silly as weather and traps.

“Peucesta,” Leonnius calls quietly, insistent shuffling heard at the other end of the rock. “I love you. I loved you my entire life, and I will love you beyond it.”

Wait—

It takes everything Phainon has not to whirl onto his back and sit up to see what’s going on. Instead, he very slowly backtracks behind the rock, careful not to raise alarm.

“What are you—”

“I will sing your songs to everyone in the nether realm,” Leonnius cuts Hephaestion off. Phainon finally finds himself behind the cover, hunched over at an awkward angle to stare with wide eyes as Leonnius’ trembling hands hold on to Peucesta’s. “And, and when you join me, you will show me more of your beautiful music. And save everyone from my awful voice.”

Peucesta shakes his head desperately, clutching Leonnius back. Leonnius slips one hand out of the grip, then stabilizes Peucesta’s face and kisses him. It’s harsh and rushed. Phainon can tell from experience that their teeth must clank together from the force of it.

“Never stop playing, okay?” He requests with a sniffle, eyes red, and a broken smile quivering on his lips. “Thank you for gifting me the opportunity to live my life with pride and not as a coward.”

“This is unnecessary,” Peucesta says, finally finding his voice.

Leonnius turns away from him, though he allows their hands to remain linked. His eyes find Mydei easily, and he shows them a toothy grin.

“This is perfect, Mydeimos…” Leonnius trails off, his voice shaking. Phainon feels as if the cold winter finally succeeded and froze his body solid. “I can finally deliver the news of you ascending the throne to the nether realm…”

He chuckles, a nervous thing rather than laced with any humor. His eyes squeeze shut as if he takes a fortifying moment to gather himself, and—

“Leonnius, don’t.”

It’s Peucesta’s plea that sends them into action. Mydei and Phainon both dive forward to grab hold of anything that can keep Leonnius in place. Hephaestion tries as well, the most agile and fastest of them aside from their messenger.

But there is a reason Leonnius is the runner serving directly under the Crown Prince. He’s been training alongside Hephaestion nearly since Perdikkas’ death; he knows how to evade.

And so they all land in the wet snow just as Leonnius runs off, fast enough to make a commotion in a spot a few meters away that, when the Aidonias look over, their attention is directed away from the rock they are hiding behind. Leonnius runs toward them, avoiding the arrows immediately sent his way by a hair.

After that, everything happens too fast.

Phainon scrambles up to have a clear view, suddenly not as concerned with being spotted. It doesn’t matter, given how much ruckus Leonnius’ presence evokes.

One minute, they are watching him run circles around the Aidonians, catching himself at the last moment after stepping on a trigger to some contraption. Reinforcements are called, which Phainon only barely registers approaching from their right and leaving an unguarded path for them to proceed through.

Then, Leonnius is tackled to the ground. He screams, then babbles desperately as they hold him down mercilessly, heavy boots weighing on his limbs. They all watch, transfixed, as Leonnius is hauled up, then tied to a tree. More words are exchanged, people gesturing and searching for something.

A large sword is brought up. A short bark of laughter as Leonnius sobs. A man with the weapon positioned, ready to cut.

Phainon cannot look away, just as he couldn’t when he was barely ten years old, and someone tried to behead Mydei.

He watches silently. Cannot tell what his friends are doing, whether they are still watching too. Cannot spare a thought whether they are already making their way to safety and he is the only one stuck in place.

Leonnius screams, louder and more gut-wrenching than anything Phainon has ever heard in his life, his right leg slowly cut off in the middle of his thigh.

Phainon wants to throw up, feels his stomach clenching and throat spasming. He would have, if only he wasn’t half-starved. This image and sound will be forever seared into his brain.

Someone makes a noise, something between choking and sobbing, but it’s drowned out by Leonnius.

“Damn it. Fuck. Fuck,” Ptolemy mutters to himself quietly, and Phainon finally glances to his side.

Hephaestion and Peucesta are both scarily pale, the latter’s cheeks wet with tears. Hephaestion is on his knees, no longer looking over at the scene past the boulder. Mydei, however, begins rising to his feet with a terrifying expression.

“Mydei!” Ptolemy whisper-shouts, hesitating only for a moment before he grabs his wrist. “Cease this.”

“I will kill them,” Mydei says, deathly quiet. “I know I can.”

“You will do no such thing,” Ptolemy hisses. He yanks harder, trying to get Mydei to back down.

He looks to Phainon with desperation, silently asking for help. Phainon doesn’t. He watches, and feels barely conscious. His thoughts are muddled, his head one giant mess. But he knows that if Mydei goes off to fight them, Phainon will follow suit immediately.

“They will raise alarm. They’ve done it before,” Ptolemy continues desperately. “We have to leave right now.”

Leonnius lets out another scream, impossibly louder and nearly resembling a howl. It ends in more of the loud sobbing and heaving. Phainon doesn’t look that way, not brave enough to face him and witness the sight of a second leg being cut off.

But Mydei does. Red mist clings to him just as the metallic tinge of blood does. He takes a step with the intent to go over, and— and he cannot save Leonnius anymore, so perhaps get as much revenge as he can until his body gives out, and let their enemies do with it as they see fit. Some adrenaline trickles through Phainon’s veins, ready to follow suit.

Ptolemy doesn’t enjoy the idea very much. He punches Mydei in the back of his knee, making use of the fact Mydei didn’t expect an attack to come from one of his friends, and nearly attaches himself to Mydei’s back as he pushes him to the ground.

“Anything you do now will be at the cost of my person,” Ptolemy says viciously when Mydei tries to shove him away. “Go on. Set your crystals on me to get free and waste the opportunity Leonnius created for us.”

Mydei stops struggling at his words, which Ptolemy seems to count as a victory.

Ptolemy ushers them up and away in the direction the Aidonian knights came from. Even if a few remained at a camp, it will be easy to take care of them in comparison. Phainon doesn’t look Leonnius’ way as they eventually stumble through the bottomless swamp, Ptolemy at the lead and Hephaestion at the back.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Archidamia takes one look at them and closes her eyes for a long moment. She doesn’t acknowledge the missing member of the royal retinue. Krateros

places one hand on Mydei’s shoulder. Phainon watches as he squeezes once before letting go and walking away.

Perhaps it’s better this way.

There is no time for anything else anyway, as they advance toward the heart of Aidonia.

Aias takes Hephaestion away. It’s been happening a lot lately, but this time the situation more than warrants it. Peucesta refuses to interact with any of them, doesn’t even raise his red and swollen eyes from the floor.

It’s painful to watch.

“I swore to make Castrum Kremnos into a place he won’t feel fear belonging to,” Mydei says, voice hoarse. And I couldn’t even keep him alive, goes unsaid. Phainon hears it loud and clear, nonetheless.

“You can still keep your promise,” Phainon says mildly. It’s not the same, he knows.

“It’s not your fault,” Ptolemy says into his hands as they are cover his entire face. His foot is incessantly tapping against the ground. “The… cruelty of it, especially. I suspect one of them could have caught sight of him as he was sabotaging the strongholds previously.” His palms move up and into his hair, dislodging the golden wreath and letting it fall to the ground carelessly. “Recognized him and decided to take revenge.”

“That changes nothing,” Phainon says, tipping over to crash into Mydei’s body. Mydei holds him up with one hand so that he doesn’t slip further down, letting him rest against him. “We should have done something. We could have done something.”

“Phainon, both of you would have died if you did,” Ptolemy responds, a touch angrily as his hands drop.

“Mydei slayed armies of soldiers,” Phainon shoots back angrily, though he mostly feels empty. “This would have been nothing for the two of us.”

“Whether you like it or not, there are certain risks that cannot be taken,” Ptolemy says, tone harsh and signaling he doesn’t want to hear further arguments on the matter. “If we cannot protect you from the enemies, we can at least protect you from your stupidity,” he continues scathingly, eyes blazing. “Let me put it into perspective for you, shall I?”

People yell and cheer in the distance, a preliminary celebration of their victory against Aidonia, which will be in full swing once they leave those miserable snow-covered grounds. Phainon’s stomach lurches at the painful reminder of how similar this is to Perdikkas’ death. They don’t even have a body to bury this time, though.

Ptolemy’s leg stops moving, his body now entirely still in a way it rarely is. Phainon doesn’t like the look in his eyes.

“Mydei is the Crown Prince of our nation, yes?” Ptolemy asks, and a clearly annoyed smile stretches his lips, the one that usually makes an appearance during meetings with the Council. “He just so happens to be the strongest person in our ranks alongside you, the Consort.”

“I know that,” Phainon grumbles, straightening out in his seat. Mydei doesn’t say anything, breathing in and out evenly.

“Do you?” Ptolemy asks with a sharp, humorless laugh. He runs his hands through the blond strands, messing them up further. “Phainon. Mydei is immortal except—” he cuts himself off, visibly biting his lip to prevent himself from revealing the only and most important secret they are keeping from the entire detachment. You never know who might overhear something. “Except his body has to be recovered. Do you imagine what might happen if it isn’t?” He stressed desperately, and Phainon thinks of Aidonians cutting Leonnius’ legs off without a thought to spare. What would they have done if they discovered Mydei’s immortality? “Do you imagine what would happen if you were also gone?”

Phainon curls in on himself, regretting ever engaging in the discussion.

“The rest of you would have found a way to recover me,” Mydei finally responds, bland as his words are.

“And then what? Watch you kill yourself because Phainon is potentially dead?” Ptolemy asks incredulously. “You’ve done incredibly well with regaining the ability to be apart, but if you think you can be separated like that, you’ve got another thing coming.”

Ptolemy breathes out heavily, his hand twitching before he picks up his laurels and starts fiddling with them. He glances at the hair tie, worn by the passage of time. He stopped messing with it a while ago, perhaps anxious it would break off. Peucesta still doesn’t say a word, and Phainon quickly looks away from him the moment his eyes begin prickling with tears.

“As I was saying,” Ptolemy continues, more in control of himself. “If something were to happen to Mydei in such an event, Phainon is the one to take over the detachment. It technically shouldn’t come into effect until marriage, but we are an army detachment. The rules don’t exactly apply, though we’ve been trying our hardest to implement them as if they were. Mydei technically remains exiled and disowned as well, but he is treated with the same regard as a Crown Prince would be, and so you are as good as a Consort would be.”

Ptolemy calms down further as he rambles about the laws and protocols. The information he relays becomes more objective rather than their previous arguments on should-haves.

“Putting me at the lead would be pointless,” he comments flatly when Ptolemy falls silent. “I would have dedicated my everything to get Mydei back.”

“And say that Mydei is impossible to recover,” Ptolemy hypothesizes, gesturing with his laurels. Meaning, Mydei is dead. “What do you do then?”

Revenge for Mydei. Revenge for his village. And then… then, what?

Kremnoans aren’t his people by birthright.

They would still accompany him on his quest to spill the blood of those who wronged him, though. A new target for the spearhead the detachment forms.

“Well, it wouldn’t happen anyway,” Phainon snaps with finality, deciding he’s had enough of the worst of hypotheticals.

Ptolemy only huffs and shakes his head.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Phainon cannot sleep.

Leonnius’ screams ring in his ears, and he curses himself over and over again for not reacting faster. They could have stayed put for longer. If two days passed and they didn’t return, Archidamia would have no doubt sent reinforcements. It would have allowed them to escape with no casualties.

Someone should have said something and stopped Leonnius from sacrificing himself.

Phainon’s hand remains on Mydei’s stomach, rising up and down along with his breaths. When asleep, Mydei’s breathing pattern is unbelievably even. He doesn’t snore, he doesn’t sigh, he doesn’t even open his mouth. Unlike Phainon, who wakes up with his lips parted and drooling more often than not. And on the scant few occasions they weren’t sleeping beside each other, Mydei didn’t even move until woken up by the slightest of sounds.

Phainon enjoys thinking about it. The fact that Mydei reacts to his presence in his sleep so much. It’s a much more preferable subject to occupy himself with than the current reality.

Mydei’s legs twine with his of their own accord. He periodically shifts throughout the night to bury closer to Phainon. He doesn’t stir awake unless Phainon makes an effort to rouse him.

His breathing never changes unless he is plagued by a nightmare, which is followed by other signs.

So it’s not a shocking revelation that Phainon immediately notices when his hand remains in the upward motion for a moment too long for the third time, as if Mydei is holding his breath.

“You aren’t asleep,” Phainon whispers, making a small circle with his fingers against Mydei’s skin. He still sleeps shirtless despite the weather. Phainon doesn’t feel cold in his sweater only because of the heat Mydei exudes.

Peucesta and Hephaestion are out. Ptolemy is snoring softly in the corner. They are moving forward in, what, three hours?

“Astute observation,” Mydei replies, and Phainon can easily imagine the eye roll. He pinches him and gets lightly kicked. “You aren’t either.”

“What is it?”

Mydei doesn’t answer immediately. He rolls over onto his side, Phainon’s hand shifting along his waist, settling on the small of his back. There aren’t any lights in the tent; he can barely make out the vague shape of Mydei’s head in the dark.

Phainon waits him out.

He asked a stupid question, he is aware. Leonnius died. What else could it even be?

Why is Phainon awake? Because he still feels guilty. Because he doesn’t know what to do and how to help. He feels useless.

Ptolemy resorted to alcohol after Perdikkas died. A kind of misery Phainon has never witnessed before. What will Peucesta do? How will he cope? Can they help him in any way?

Ptolemy didn’t want any outright help. Phainon wouldn’t have wanted it either. Not unless it’s related to bringing your beloved back.

They’ve relied on their friends so much throughout the years, and they cannot even soothe their pain when it matters.

“I don’t think my life should be prioritized over others,” Mydei tells him so quietly that Phainon nearly misses half the words. “It’s no more precious than anyone else’s.”

Phainon knows what he means, but…

“Would you prioritize my life over others?” He asks because he thinks he knows the answer.

Because Phainon would. It’s awful; no life carries more weight or importance than another. Perdikkas made sure to teach them that. He died because he stepped out onto the battlefield to take care of a woman he’s spoken to perhaps once.

But Phainon would choose Mydei over that woman. He wouldn’t even think about it.

“That’s different,” Mydei protests. His hands clench on Phainon’s sweater, pulling on it a bit. Phainon leans forward until his head collides with Mydei’s softly. He angles it up a little, pressing their foreheads together.

“I don’t think so,” Phainon sighs. “If we can do that, why can’t they?”

Perdikkas wouldn’t have liked it, but it’s the truth.

Kremnoans look up to Mydei. They stake their future and death on him. Phainon is certain that some of them don’t imagine their lives without their beloved Crown Prince leading them forward.

They are not so different. The Kremnoans and Phainon.

Mydei doesn’t have a response to that.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

An Aidonian messenger finds them as they wander forth, fearless in the face of people who wish him death, same as the rest of his now-deceased peers. He carries a plea for peace from the Usurper, who took advantage of the discord sown by the foreign army on the outskirts, slowly picking out the entirety of the Aidonian armed forces.

Archidamia grins when she hears the news and reads over the official letter herself, a sharp and satisfied thing. Mydei doesn’t wait for her opinion as he agrees to the terms, and they set course for the walls of the city-state.

˖✧ 𖤓 ✧˖

Their arrival marks twenty days since Leonnius’ death.

They still travel in the set-out groups, simply for propriety’s sake, until they reunite with the rest of the detachment once the situation is truly under control. Perhaps it will still be within this very city. A runner had been sent to update their people on the status of the campaign, and another will follow tomorrow at the latest.

Archidamia is at the head once more, followed by Tyche, then Mydei, and Krateros brings up the rear. Even then, they are still divided into their cavalries, with Hephaestion being first in line. Phainon and Mydei travel together, as they always do, their cavalries merged into one. Behind them steps Ptolemy, then Peucesta. It’s a loose arrangement, though the soldiers stick to their sides as best they can.

Early in the day, not many civilians are outside to see them pass. Those who stare out of the windows seem to harbor curiosity rather than fear and hatred, as they are used to.

It’s calm. Until,

“Fire!” Shouts reach them from the back, echoed through the crowd by the soldiers to let the news carry forward.

Phainon and Mydei turn in unison, catching sight of a bright flash of color and smoke rising. Isn’t it right where—

“Ambush!” “It’s falling—” “Lord Ptolemy’s cavalry.”

A construction not too far away trembles, and just as it begins to fall, the other calls register. Phainon curses under his breath, and they take off running. They shove past the small crowd already gathering near the site, unsure what to expect when they get there.

People yell for their friends, ones stuck behind the debris, separating them from the rest. Another column falls, blocking those inside from escaping, buildings trapping them on the sides.

“Ptolemy, move!” Mydei commands, uncaring of how the scholar is nowhere in sight. He sounds nearly fearful.

Phainon swallows.

Move. Move where?

They rush closer to the debris, finding a spot where the stones fell in such a way that they allow for a view in. The soldiers are scattered, searching for any potential way out. Some are already dead, boulders crushing their bodies. Phainon sees a person stumble away in shock, one arm clearly torn off.

A body crashes into Phainon and Mydei both, worming closer in and panting with exertion. “Ptolemy!” Hephaestion yells into the gap, nearly at the top of his lungs.

Each of them calls for their friend. Minutes pass and only the crackling of fire and fragile structures threatening to give in echo back, drowning among the cries.

Phainon bangs his fist against the thick stone in frustration, Hephaestion’s fingers desperately trying to find purchase in another spot to dislodge them and make the gap bigger. It’s not very successful, and it must hurt as he repeats the action, but he doesn’t stop.

They need just a glimpse of Ptolemy to confirm his location. If they know where he is, then something can be done. They lived through so much; this isn’t even a particularly dangerous situation. It’s not a big space, he should be somewhere nearby.

It takes a few minutes, but miraculously, a familiar figure stumbles forward, stepping in their direction tiredly. Ptolemy has a cut on his cheek, and his robes are covered in gray dust, singed by fire at the bottom. His arm is colored with an angry red shade, like he might have had it burned.

Hephaestion rests his forehead against the stones in relief. Phainon only feels fear as he struggles to find a way to get their friend out of there.

“It’s the rebels,” Ptolemy informs them immediately once he is close enough. “Acting out because they think we are allied with the Usurper. We found one of them right after she set fire and got information from her. She may not have feared death, but I’m being told I can be rather persuasive.”

Ptolemy grins grimly as people yell all around them. He seems to have accepted the reality faster than they ever could.

“The obelisks are rigged,” he continues, voice heavy. He breathes in deeply, looking away from them and up at one of the structures. “Nothing we can do in time before they collapse and crush us all to death.”

“Something can always be done,” Hephaestion snarls at him, fingers clenching on the stone.

Ptolemy gazes at them, and Phainon recognizes grief in his features. “Let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.”

The quote lacks his usual enthusiasm. And Phainon feels tears prickle at his eyes. Unthinkingly, he joins Hephaestion in trying to do something.

“Not much left for me to do, though, is there?” Ptolemy laughs bitterly, brushing his hair back and skewing the laurel leaves. “But I would like everyone to know I died courageously, alright?”

“Ptolemy,” Mydei finally croaks out, and Phainon’s heart breaks twice over at his tone.

Ptolemy’s face falls immediately, and he squeezes his eyes shut, coughing into his hand to regain composure.

“Nothing can be done about this,” Ptolemy repeats, resolute.

As if to agree with his words, a loud creak resounds. Ptolemy’s gaze snaps up again, taking a step back to see the nearby obelisk better. His shoulders slump in resignation. Phainon looks above the debris and finds it trembling just so, but nothing else seems to be out of the ordinary. When he looks through the gap again, though, he notices the subtle hue of flames.

Mydei suddenly punches the rock, and leaves a golden splatter on its rough surface among slight cracks. He pays it no mind, repeating the action. Hephaestion and Phainon keep attempting to find any crease that will allow them to pull out a single rock. Just one is enough. Then some more will follow, and Ptolemy will be able to squeeze through. They can make it in time. Just for this one person to be saved. They cannot lose Ptolemy.

“Listen to me, alright?” Ptolemy calls, a few steps closer than he had been the last time Phainon glanced his way, too busy with his task. He looks over his shoulder and up, then frantically regards them again. Still calmer than the situation warrants. “You three are the best thing that could have ever happened to me.”

“We are not!” Hephaestion yells at him, choked up. “You keep calling us brats, remember? We give you nothing but trouble, and you keep us in check. So get the fuck out of there, please.”

“…Take care of my journals, will you?”

“Take care of them yourself,” Phainon shoots back, not caring as he watches one of his nails break on the stone. “We are throwing them into the water.”

“You are the most resilient person I’ve ever had the pleasure to meet, Hephaestion,” Ptolemy ignores them both, smiling even as his eyes turn red. “Never lose sight of yourself.”

“Shut up,” Hephaestion pleads, rubbing harshly at his eyes with one hand while still fighting the rocks with the other.

Red powder scatters in the air as Mydei tries to use his crystals to break the stones. It leaves only a small dent, always used for piercing rather than breaking things apart with blunt force.

Ptolemy’s gaze finds Phainon, and it takes everything in him not to look away. “I think you are meant for greater things than our detachment, Phainon,” he simply says. “The Kremnoans cannot repay you enough for bringing our Crown Prince to us and taking care of him. We will always cheer you on.”

Phainon grits his teeth, feels wetness on his cheeks. Ptolemy cannot die. It’s just rocks. Another creak, and Phainon catches in the corner of his eye several tall obelisks shaking. Soldiers yell in the distance, loud crashing as more rocks no doubt fall across the soon-to-be ruins.

“You shall be the wisest King of Kremnos. My last advice to you will be something simple, my apologies,” Ptolemy says, and his own tears slip past. His hand shakes where it’s balled into a fist at his side. He grips his own wrist, right over the hair tie he’s been carrying on him for so long. “You must do what you think is right. Your heart guided you well so far, hasn’t it?”

The creaking grows in volume, and Mydei strikes a few more times. His hand looks mangled.

Ptolemy laughs once more, and it’s freer than the last few Phainon has heard from him. It still retains a hint of despair, trailing off into a choked noise.

“Mydeimos, please tell my family: It was not cunning schemes that vanquished Ptolemy, but the immense weight of Amphoreus’ entire history.”

They watch as Ptolemy bows dramatically, then walks backward, disappearing among the soldiers that await their demise.

Phainon punches the stone, even more useless without a power like Mydei’s backing it up. Hephaestion yells desperately after him, blood from his own fingertips adding red to their gold. Marking what’s about to become Ptolemy’s tombstone.

When Perdikkas died, Phainon felt grief fill him immediately.

With Leonnius, there was no time. There still isn’t time to think about it properly past Peucesta’s silence and dimmed eyes.

And now, as he watches Ptolemy about to be buried under the rocks, he feels cold dread.

One of the obelisks begins to fall, kicking off another wave of thick dust as it snaps. It covers their view, falling right where Ptolemy just stood, and they can do nothing as a second one falls not too far, and the next one. The crashes are loud enough to make Phainon’s ears ring, eyes stinging.

It’s silent, then. Not a single soldier on the inside speaking or calling for help. They can no longer look through the gap and see whether there are any survivors.

Until all three of them yell Ptolemy’s name, hoping for anything, and lurch forward as one, redoubling their hopeless efforts to rescue their dear friend. Phainon isn’t sure how long they remain in that state, only that he can no longer feel his fingers. The first stone is broken by Mydei, only to give way to another.

A hand settles on Phainon’s shoulder, and he lashes out instantly, stopped by Archidamia’s hand catching his wrist. His body reacts on instinct, twisting his own arm and spinning her around, then kicking her knees out. He isn’t sure whether she lets him do it, or if she didn’t expect him to act out in such a way.

He lets go as if burned once he realizes, gaze searching out his friends immediately.

Hephaestion is now held by Peucesta, sobbing as he tries to break free and resume their efforts to dig Ptolemy out somehow. Peucesta’s arms are tense around Hephaestion, expression pained even while he remains the most composed out of them.

Phainon looks to the side and finds Krateros standing a few steps away, his forearm bleeding from a fresh, large cut. Mydei kneels beside him, fingers digging into the ground. His shoulders are shaking, and Phainon moves to reach him before a thought can even form.

“Kremnoans do not grieve,” Krateros only says, directed to Phainon and Mydei both, and perhaps Hephaestion as well. Disapproving. Phainon sometimes wonders if it’s the only emotion he can openly feel and show.

“I know that,” Mydei snaps, raising his head to glare at him. Tears run down his face, some slipping from his chin down onto the ground. Phainon only grabs his elbow, offering any form of subtle support that he can. He sniffs, tastes salt.

“Precisely. Your friend is dead,” Krateros continues, eyes hardened. He isn’t bothered by the red streams of blood flowing down his forearm freely, falling off his fingers and disappearing into the cold ground the same way Mydei’s tears do. “It’s not the first death you experienced, nor will it be the last. Get over yourselves.”

Phainon’s blood boils. Get over themselves?

Leonnius is dead.

Now, Ptolemy is also dead. On a random day, when they haven’t even fought a single opponent. On their way to negotiate peace. They are prepared for deaths to follow when they engage an enemy. But out here, in a peaceful spot as they walked forth? How is that fair? Ptolemy should be standing next to them right this moment, getting on Krateros’ nerves.

“Have you even felt a thing when Queen Gorgo died?” Phainon asks, taking immense effort not to spit the words out in fury that burns him from the inside. He feels his gaze boring into Krateros with too much intensity. He cannot be bothered to cover up the rage, already doing everything in his power not to let it take too much control from him. “Grief? Remorse? Guilt?”

Krateros’ lip curls, disbelief mixing with anger. “Excuse me?”

“You heard me,” Phainon scoffs, hand tightening on Mydei. It says something that his partner doesn’t intervene. “Have you always been a heartless bastard? Kremnoans do not grieve, but do they also not possess a shred of empathy? I assume that’s a quality unique to you.”

It’s not often a Kremnoan falls into the clutches of grief. Ptolemy did, though he didn’t break apart in such a way that would warrant a reaction from others. They all drink, and Ptolemy has enough gall to make everyone turn a blind eye. Peucesta is handling it remarkably well, as did Aias and Thera. As Kremnoans often do.

It might be frowned upon to mourn. It might be shamed quietly, a reprimand in the privacy of one’s home. Phainon has yet to actually witness someone make a scene about it the same way Krateros does right now.

Krateros’ hand tightens into a fist, face entirely red. Phainon has never taken so much glee in being despised before. “You are seventeen, you insolent child, what could you possi—”

“Krateros,” Archidamia interrupts him tiredly, then speaks even louder when he doesn’t stop. “Let the boys be.”

The man sputters as she walks over. He stares at her in astonishment, shaking his head. “You cannot be serious. You know better than anyone else that this is not the example Kremnoans should be led by. Our Crown Prince cannot be held back by such frivolous matters.”

“Oh, but I am,” Archidamia says, standing tall and unwavering, stepping in front of Phainon and Mydei. She and Krateros are the same height. “The man who raised them into the Kremnoan culture just died. They weren’t born into it, must I remind you? You were there when Lord Mydeimos was deprived of such opportunity.”

Krateros’ mouth clicks shut, eyes narrowing. “It is no excuse.”

Archidamia inclines her head. “I agree that it doesn’t fit with our tradition. However, to have such expectations in this case is simply foolish.” She turns around to address the large crowd Phainon didn’t realize had formed, countless eyes fretful and expressions uncertain. “I am of the mind that this should serve as a reminder to everyone that Lord Mydeimos has also suffered at King Eurypon’s hands, and this is one of the many consequences.”

Phainon takes advantage of the moment and tugs Mydei to his feet, the hand around his elbow moving a bit lower to his wrist.

Mydei, tears slowly drying on his skin, gazes at his people with eyes set and chin held high. Phainon matches him, tries to even send them a thin smile.

Archidamia’s words seem to have worked. It’s gracious, what she’s just done. It’s what Ptolemy would have done, with a touch of dramatics. She worked the crowd in their favor, making them more sympathetic than they would have been otherwise after this display. It’s much different from Mydei murdering an entire army while delirious from grief.

“Be it as it may,” Archidamia speaks again. “We must continue on. I am giving everyone ten minutes to gather themselves on their own before we set off. We have much to discuss with the Usurper.”

Phainon, uncaring of Krateros’ opinion on the matter, turns them around and decides to make use of those ten minutes. His heart lurches and tears spring into his eyes the moment the ruins come into his view again.

Especially so when he glances at Hephaestion, still crying while he stares blankly at the spot where they last saw Ptolemy, his fingertips ruined.
